While searching for the ox, he climbed Uttaravaḍḑhamāna Mountain. There, a large python caught and coiled around him. He thought, "I will cut off the snake's head with this sharp billhook." Then he thought again, "It is not proper for me to break the precepts I have taken from my venerable teacher." Having thought this up to three times, he decided, "I will sacrifice only my life, but I will not sacrifice the precepts," and threw the sharp billhook on his shoulder into the forest. At that very moment, the python released the Upāsaka and went away. Abstinence by eradication (samuccheda-virati) should be understood as the abstinence associated with the Noble Path (ariya-magga). From the moment that abstinence arises, even the mere thought "I will kill a living being" no longer occurs to the Noble Ones (ariya-puggala). Just as the analysis (vinicchaya) of the ten unwholesome courses of action was understood by five aspects, so should the analysis of these ten wholesome courses of action be understood by five aspects: Dhamma, portion (koṭṭhāsa), object (ārammaṇa), feeling (vedanā), and root (mūla). Among these, the analysis by way of Dhamma is: among these ten wholesome courses of action, the first seven in order can be both volition (cetanā) and abstinence (virati). The last three are only mental factors associated with volition. By way of portion (koṭṭhāsa), the first seven in order are called "courses of action" (kammapatha). The roots are...
147:
Thinking, "I will sacrifice my life, but I will not sacrifice the precept," he threw the sharp bone-handled axe that was on his shoulder into the forest. At that very moment, the great python released that lay devotee and went away.

Abstinence associated with the Noble Path should be known as 'abstinence by eradication' (samuccheda-virati). From the moment that abstinence arises, even the slightest thought of "I will kill a living being" does not arise in Noble Persons (ariya-puggala).

Now, just as the analysis of the unwholesome courses of action was known, so too the analysis of these wholesome courses of action (kusala-kammapatha) should be known by way of these five aspects: (1) by way of state (dhamma), (2) by way of portion (koṭṭhāsa), (3) by way of object (ārammaṇa), (4) by way of feeling (vedanā), and (5) by way of root (mūla).

Therein, the analysis 'by way of state' (dhamma) is as follows: Among these wholesome courses of action, in sequence, the first seven can be either volition (cetanā) or abstinence (virati). The final three are only states associated with volition.

The analysis 'by way of portion' (koṭṭhāsa) is as follows: In sequence, the first seven are only courses of action (kammapatha) and not roots (mūla). The final three are both courses of action and roots. When non-covetousness (anabhijjhā) reaches the level of a root, it becomes the wholesome root of non-greed (alobha-kusalamūla). Non-ill-will (abyāpāda) is the wholesome root of non-hatred (adosa-kusalamūla), and right view (sammā-diṭṭhi) is the wholesome root of non-delusion (amoha-kusalamūla).

The analysis 'by way of object' (ārammaṇa) is as follows: The objects of unwholesome states such as killing living beings are the very objects of these wholesome courses of action. This is because what is called 'abstinence' (veramaṇī) occurs only from the objective field that is to be transgressed. Just as the Noble Path, which has Nibbāna as its object, abandons the defilements, so too these courses of action, which have the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) and so forth as their objects, should be understood to abandon immoralities (dussīlya) such as killing living beings.

The analysis 'by way of feeling' (vedanā) is as follows: All courses of action are either accompanied by pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā) or neutral feeling (majjhatta-vedanā). This is because at the level of wholesome states, there is no such thing as painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā).

The analysis 'by way of root' (mūla) is as follows: In sequence, the first seven courses of action have three roots by way of non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion for one who abstains with a consciousness associated with knowledge (ñāṇa-sampayutta-citta). For one who abstains with a consciousness dissociated from knowledge (ñāṇa-vippayutta-citta), there are two roots. When non-covetousness occurs with a consciousness associated with knowledge, it has two roots; when it occurs with a consciousness dissociated from knowledge, it has one root. Non-greed itself cannot be its own root. The same method applies to non-ill-will. Right view has only two roots by way of non-greed and non-hatred. These are the ten wholesome courses of action.
148:
## Discussion on the Comparison of Courses of Action

Now, at this point, what is called the comparison of the courses of action (kammapatha-saṃsandana) should be understood. Indeed, non-restraint (asaṃvara) arising by way of the five sense-contact doors (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body) is only unwholesome mental action (manokamma). However, non-restraint arising by way of the mind-contact door (manophassa-dvāra) can be all three types of action. If that non-restraint reaches the point of movement (copana) in the body-door, it is unwholesome bodily action (kāyakamma); if it reaches movement in the speech-door, it is unwholesome verbal action (vacīkamma); if it does not reach movement in either, it is unwholesome mental action. Non-restraint arising by way of the five doors of non-restraint is also only unwholesome mental action. Non-restraint arising by way of the body-door of non-restraint with movement is only unwholesome bodily action; that arising by way of the speech-door of non-restraint is only unwholesome verbal action; that arising by way of the mind-door of non-restraint is only unwholesome mental action. The three types of bodily misconduct are only unwholesome bodily action; the four types of verbal misconduct are only unwholesome verbal action; the three types of mental misconduct are only unwholesome mental action.

Restraint (saṃvara) arising by way of the five sense-contact doors is also only wholesome mental action. This restraint arising by way of the mind-contact door, like non-restraint, can be all three types of action. Restraint arising by way of the five doors of restraint is also only wholesome mental action; restraint arising by way of the body-door of restraint with movement is only wholesome bodily action; restraint arising by way of the speech-door of restraint is only wholesome verbal action; restraint arising by way of the mind-door of restraint is only wholesome mental action. The three types of bodily good conduct are only wholesome bodily action; the four types of verbal good conduct are only wholesome verbal action; the three types of mental good conduct are only wholesome mental action.

Unwholesome bodily action does not arise by way of the five sense-contact doors; it arises only by way of the mind-contact door. Unwholesome verbal action is the same. Unwholesome mental action, however, arises by way of all six sense-contact doors. If that mental action reaches movement in the body-door and speech-door, it becomes unwholesome bodily and verbal action; if it does not reach movement, it is only unwholesome mental action. Just as it does not arise by way of the five sense-contact doors, so too unwholesome bodily action does not arise by way of the five doors of non-restraint; it arises only by way of the body-door and speech-door of non-restraint with movement, and not by way of the mind-door of non-restraint. Unwholesome verbal action also does not arise by way of the five doors of non-restraint; it arises by way of the body-door and speech-door of non-restraint with movement, and not by way of the mind-door of non-restraint. Unwholesome mental action, however, certainly arises by way of the eight doors of non-restraint. The same method should be understood for wholesome bodily action and so forth.
149:
This is the distinction: just as unwholesome bodily and verbal actions do not arise by way of the door of mental non-restraint, these (wholesome bodily and verbal actions) are not like that. Indeed, these (wholesome actions) do arise even at the door of mental restraint for one who undertakes the precepts without moving the bodily or vocal organs.

Among those (doors), the wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara-kusala-citta) arises by way of the three doors of action (kammadvara); it does not arise by way of the five doors of consciousness (viññāṇadvara). By the method, "Whatever feeling arises—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—conditioned by eye-contact," it arises by way of the six doors of contact (phassadvara). It does not arise by way of the eight doors of non-restraint (asaṃvaradvara); it arises by way of the eight doors of restraint (saṃvaradvara). It does not arise by way of the ten courses of unwholesome action (akusalakammapatha); it arises by way of the ten courses of wholesome action (kusalakammapatha). Therefore, whether this consciousness arises by way of the three doors of action, the six doors of contact, the eight doors of restraint, or the ten courses of wholesome action, it is so. When it is said, "A wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere has arisen ... etc. ... (taking) a visible object ... etc. ... or a mental object," everything has been stated.

## The Discussion on Doors is Finished.

Regarding the phrase "yaṃ yaṃ vā panārabbha," the construction is as follows: among the visible objects and so forth mentioned below, it means "beginning with a visible object," or "having made it the object." It arises beginning with an audible object ... etc. ... or a mental object. By this much, it is as if only one of these objects is permitted for this consciousness. This (consciousness) arises for one person at one time beginning with a visible object, and again at another time for another person, it arises beginning with any other object among audible objects and so forth. For this consciousness thus arising, there is no such sequence as: first, in one existence, it arises beginning with a visible object, and later with an audible object. Even among visible objects, there is no such rule as: first a blue object, and later a yellow object.

Thus, to show the state of having all these as objects, the state of having no fixed sequence, and the state of having no fixed rule even among blue, yellow, and so forth despite the lack of sequence, he said, "yaṃ yaṃ vā panārabbha." This is the meaning: it is not just any single one among these visible objects and so forth; rather, it arises beginning with whichever object. Even when it arises thus, it does not occur in a sequence such as "first beginning with a visible object, then an audible object," but arises beginning with whichever object. The meaning is: "It arises by making this or that object among visible objects and so forth, whether in reverse order, in direct order, or by the method of skipping one, skipping two, and so forth." Even among visible objects...
150:
It means that it arises by taking any one of the visible-form objects such as blue or yellow, without being restricted by the rule "first the blue object, then the yellow object." The same method applies to sound objects and so on. This is one yojanā (interpretation).

This is another yojanā: It is called rūpārammaṇa because the visible form is the object of this consciousness... It is called dhammārammaṇa because the mental state is the object of this consciousness. Having stated that consciousness arises with a visible-form object or a mental-state object, it is said again, "taking whatever object." The meaning of that statement is: among these objects like visible forms, it arises by taking any one of them according to the method mentioned below. In the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, however, it is said: "There is nothing new in the yevāpanaka (miscellaneous) states; only what was taken below is taken again." It is mentioned only this much: "This is said to show that it arises by taking a visible-form object... or a mental-state object, or this or that object."

## Dhammuddesavāra
## Phassapañcamakarāsi-vaṇṇanā

The phrase "Tasmiṃ samaye (at that time)" is a statement that specifically points out the time which was previously indicated in a general way. Therefore, the meaning should be understood as: "At whatever time a sense-sphere wholesome consciousness arises, at that very time contact (phassa) occurs... non-distraction (avikkhepa) occurs." In this context, just as consciousness arises, so too among contact and the rest, contact occurs. What kind of contact occurs? The construction (yojanā) should be made according to the terms available, such as: "It is of the sense-sphere, it is wholesome, it is arisen (uppanna), it is accompanied by joy (somanassa)," and so on. Because the term "accompanied by joy" cannot be obtained for feeling (vedanā) [as it is the feeling itself], and "associated with knowledge" cannot be obtained for the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya), it is said "according to the terms available." This is the opinion of teachers outside the Commentaries; however, it should not be regarded as essential.

Why is contact mentioned first here? Because it is the first impact of consciousness on the object. Since there is the first impact of consciousness on the object, contact arises while touching the object; therefore, it is mentioned first. Having touched with contact, one feels with feeling, perceives with perception, and wills with volition. Thus it is said in the Suttas: "Bhikkhus, being touched, one feels; being touched, one perceives; being touched, one wills."
151:
In another way, this thing called contact (phassa) is like a pillar in a palace, which is a strong condition for the remaining wooden structures. Just as the beams, tie-beams, walls, foundations, pinnacles, rafters, ridge-poles, and brackets (or bosses) are connected to the pillar and rest upon the pillar, even so, contact is a strong condition for the conascent associated states. Contact is like a pillar. The remaining states are like the wooden components. For this reason also, it is mentioned first. However, this is not the primary reason. Among the states that have arisen in a single moment of consciousness, it cannot be said, "This state arose first, this state arose later." Even in contact being a strong condition, the temporal cause is not seen. Contact is mentioned first only by way of the order of teaching (desanā-vāra). For it would also be proper to teach by considering: "Feeling occurs, contact occurs; perception occurs, contact occurs; volition occurs, contact occurs; consciousness occurs, contact occurs; feeling occurs, perception occurs; volition occurs, initial application (vitakka) occurs." However, it should be understood that contact is mentioned first according to the order of teaching. Just as in the case of contact, a sequence of priority should not be sought in the remaining states either. The ultimate realities should be investigated only by way of their etymology (vacanattha), characteristics (lakkhaṇa), functions (rasa), and so on.

Namely: It is called contact (phassa) because it touches. It has the characteristic of touching (phusana-lakkhaṇa), the function of impingement (saṅghaṭṭana-rasa), the manifestation of concurrence (sannipāta-paccupaṭṭhāna), and the proximate cause of an object that has entered the range (āpāthagata-visaya-padaṭṭhāna).

Although this is a mental state (arūpa-dhamma), it is said to have the characteristic of touching because it proceeds in the manner of touching the object. And although it does not adhere to a single part, it has the function of impingement because it impinges on the consciousness and the object, just as the eye impinges on the visible form and the ear on the sound. Or, it should be understood to have the function of impingement in the sense of "attainment" (sampatti) because it arises from the impingement of the base and the object. For it is said in the Commentary: "Among the contacts occurring in the four planes, there is none that does not have the characteristic of touching. But the function of impingement exists only in the contact of the five doors. The contact of the five doors is named both as having the characteristic of touching and the function of impingement. The contact of the mind-door is named only as having the characteristic of touching, not the function of impingement."

To state this, the following Sutta analogy is brought forward: "Great King, suppose two rams were to fight. One ram should be regarded as the eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda), the second ram as the visible-form object (rūpārammaṇa), and their collision as contact (phassa)." Thus, contact has both the characteristic of touching and the function of impingement. "Great King, for example..."
152:
In the clashing of two bowls... or the clashing of two hands, the eye should be seen as one hand, the visible form as the second hand, and contact (phassa) as the meeting of those two hands. Thus, contact has the characteristic of touching and the function of impinging (saṅghaṭṭana). This is explained in detail in the Milindapañhā.

Alternatively, just as in the texts beginning with 'having seen a form with the eye,' eye-consciousness and so on are referred to by the name 'eye' and so on, so too here they should be understood as being referred to by the name 'eye' and so on. Therefore, in phrases such as 'thus the eye should be seen,' the meaning should be understood in this way: 'thus eye-consciousness should be seen.' This being so, because of the impinging of the mind and the object, the meaning 'having the function of impinging' (saṅghaṭṭana-rasa) is established in this sutta as well, in the sense of its function.

Because it is declared by way of its own cause, known as the conjunction of the three (base, object, and consciousness), it is called 'having conjunction as its manifestation' (sannipāta-paccupaṭṭhāna). For indeed, in various places, this contact is declared by way of its cause thus: 'The meeting of the three is contact.' The meaning of this sutta passage is that contact arises because of the meeting of the three; it should not be understood that the mere meeting itself is contact.

Because it is declared in this way, it is said to have 'conjunction as its manifestation' because it appears to knowledge in that very mode of the meeting of those three. However, as a manifestation in the sense of its effect, it is called 'having feeling as its manifestation' (vedanā-paccupaṭṭhāna). This means it causes feeling to appear, i.e., it produces it. In producing feeling—just as externally, heat (tejo) dependent on the element called lac, though having heat as its cause, produces softness only in its own support, the lac, and not in its cause, the external flameless embers—so too, although there are other causes called the base (vatthu) and the object (ārammaṇa), because it is dependent on the mind, this contact produces feeling only in its own support, the mind, and not in its causes, the base or the object. Furthermore, because it arises without obstruction in an object prepared by appropriate attention (samannāhāra) and the faculties (indriya) such as the eye, it is said to have 'an object that has come into range as its proximate cause' (āpāthagata-visaya-padaṭṭhāna).

Feeling (vedanā) is so called because it feels. It has the characteristic of being felt, the function of experiencing, or the function of enjoying the desirable aspect of the object. It is manifested as mental gratification and has tranquillity (passaddhi) as its proximate cause.
153:
Among the feelings occurring in the four planes, there is no feeling that does not have the characteristic of being felt (vedayita-lakkhaṇa). Although it is said that the function of experiencing the taste of the object (anubhavana-rasa) is obtained only in pleasant feeling, that view is then rejected, and it is stated that whether it be pleasant feeling, painful feeling, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, all feelings have the function of experiencing the taste of the object. This meaning is illustrated as follows: having reached the point of experiencing the taste of the object, the remaining associated states (sampayutta-dhamma) experience only a single portion. Indeed, for contact, there is only the act of touching; for perception, only the act of perceiving; for volition, only the act of coordinating; for consciousness, only the act of cognizing. But certainly, by way of sovereignty, capability, and mastery, feeling alone experiences the taste of the object.

For feeling is like a king, and the remaining states are like a cook. Just as a cook, having prepared food of various tastes, places it in a bowl-basket, seals it, brings it to the king, breaks the seal, opens the basket, takes the best of all the dishes, places them in a dish, and swallows them to test whether they are faulty or faultless, and then serves the food of various excellent tastes to the king; the king, being the master with sovereignty and capability, eats whatever he desires. In this analogy, the experience of a portion of the object's taste by the remaining states is like the cook's testing of the food. Just as the cook tests only a portion of the food, so too the remaining states experience only a portion of the object's taste. But just as the king, being the master with sovereignty and capability, eats according to his wish, so too feeling, by way of sovereignty, capability, and mastery, experiences the taste of the object. Therefore, it is said to have the function of experiencing (anubhavana-rasa).

In the second alternative meaning, the feeling intended here enjoys only the desirable aspect of the object in whatever way; therefore, it is said to have the function of enjoying the desirable aspect (iṭṭhākāra-sambhogarasa). Because it is a state of gratification dependent on the mind, this feeling is said to have 'mental gratification as its manifestation' (cetasika-assāda-paccupaṭṭhāna), referring to its appearance to knowledge by its own nature of gratification. Because it is said, 'One with a tranquil body feels pleasure,' it should be understood as having 'tranquillity as its proximate cause' (passaddhi-padaṭṭhāna).

Perception (saññā) is so called because it perceives an object distinguished as blue, etc. It has the characteristic of perceiving and the function of re-cognizing (paccābhiññāṇa-rasa) by means of a sign previously noted. Indeed, perception occurring in the four planes, which is said not to have the characteristic of perceiving...
154:
There is no perception (saññā) that does not have the characteristic of perceiving. All perception has the characteristic of perceiving. Among the perceptions occurring in these four planes, that which perceives by signs such as blue, yellow, long, or short is said to have the function of re-cognition (paccābhiññāṇarasa), which is the act of recognizing again by a sign previously noted. Its occurrence should be understood through the example of a carpenter who, having made a mark on wood, recognizes that wood again by that mark; or a man who, having noted a mark such as a mole or a birthmark on another man, recognizes him again by that mark, saying, 'This is the one named so-and-so'; or the king's treasurer in charge of ornaments who, having tied a name-tag to various ornaments, when ordered to 'Bring such-and-such an ornament,' lights a lamp, enters the treasure chamber, reads the tag, and brings that specific ornament.

Alternatively—perception, which has the characteristic of perceiving by way of grasping the whole, has the function of making a sign as a cause for recognizing again (punasaññāṇapaccayanimittakaraṇarasa). It is like the carpenter and others with regard to wood and so on. It has the manifestation of producing misinterpretation (abhinivesakaraṇapaccupaṭṭhāna) as 'This is the very thing' by the power of a previously grasped sign. It is like blind men who, having felt parts of an elephant, describe the elephant. Or, because it does not penetrate the object, it has the manifestation of not lasting long (aciraṭṭhānapaccupaṭṭhāna), like lightning. It has the proximate cause of the object as it appears (yathāupaṭṭhitavisayapadaṭṭhāna). It is like the perception of 'man' that arises in young deer regarding a scarecrow made of grass. Among these, the perception associated with knowledge follows knowledge itself. It should be understood that in the case of the earth-element with its components (sasambhārapathavī) and so on, the remaining states follow the earth-element and so on.

It is called volition (cetanā) because it coordinates; the meaning is that it coordinates associated states with itself upon the object. It has the characteristic of coordinating (cetayitalakkhaṇa); the meaning is it has the characteristic of the state of volition. It has the function of accumulating (āyūhanarasa). Among the volitions occurring in the four planes, there is none that does not have the characteristic of coordinating. All volition has the characteristic of coordinating. However, the function of accumulating (āyūhanarasa) occurs only in the wholesome and unwholesome. When it reaches the stage of accumulating wholesome and unwholesome kamma, the function of the remaining associated states is only partial, but volition has excessive zeal and excessive effort—double zeal and double effort. Therefore, the ancient teachers said: 'This volition stands in the nature of a landowner.' A landowner means the owner of a field. Just as a man who is the owner of a field, taking fifty-five strong men, enters the field together saying, 'I will harvest.' His zeal is excessive and his effort is double. He says things like, 'Grasp it continuously,' points out the boundaries, manages the liquor, food, perfumes, and garlands for them, and carries out the field work equally. This is the completion of this simile.
155:
The completion of this simile should be understood. Indeed, volition is like the landowner. The fifty-five wholesome states that arise by way of mental factors are like the fifty-five hired workers. Just as the time when the landowner exerts double zeal and double effort, when volition reaches the stage of accumulating wholesome and unwholesome kamma, it has double zeal and double effort. Thus, its function of accumulating (āyūhanarasa) should be understood.

Furthermore, it manifests as directing (saṃvidahanapaccupaṭṭhāna). Indeed, it appears as directing, accomplishing its own task and the tasks of others, like a senior pupil, a master carpenter, and so on. For example, a senior pupil, seeing the preceptor coming from afar, while reciting himself, makes the other young students also engage in their own recitation. When that senior pupil begins to recite, they also recite, following him. And just as a master carpenter, while he himself is hewing, makes the other carpenters also engage in their own hewing. When that master carpenter begins to hew, they also hew, following him. And just as a general, while he himself is fighting, makes the other soldiers also engage in the act of combat. When that general begins to fight, they also fight without retreating, following him.

In the same way, when this volition occurs on an object through its own function, it makes the other associated states also occur in their respective functions. When it has begun its own task, those associated with it also begin. Therefore, it is said: 'It accomplishes its own task and the tasks of others, like a senior pupil, a master carpenter, and so on.' It should be understood that in remembering urgent tasks and so on, this volition becomes evident as it occurs in the mode of urging the associated states.

The verbal definition of consciousness (citta) has already been stated by way of 'it thinks of an object.' By way of characteristic and so on: consciousness has the characteristic of cognizing (vijānanalakkhaṇa), the function of being a precursor (pubbaṅgamarasa), the manifestation of connecting (sandahanapaccupaṭṭhāna), and the proximate cause of mentality-materiality (nāmarūpapadaṭṭhāna). Among the consciousnesses occurring in the four planes, there is none that does not have the characteristic of cognizing. All have the characteristic of cognizing. However, when reaching a sense-door and making the object clear, consciousness is the precursor and the forerunner. One cognizes a visible object seen with the eye-door only through consciousness... one cognizes a mental object known with the mind-door only through consciousness. Just as a city guard sitting at a crossroads in the middle of the city observes and determines the people coming and going, saying, 'This is a resident, this is a visitor'—this should be seen as the completion of this simile. This was also said by the Great Elder: 'Just as, O Great King, a city guard sitting at a crossroads in the middle of the city sees a person coming from the east, sees a person coming from the west, the south, and the north; in the same way, O Great King, whatever visible object one sees with the eye-door, one cognizes that object with consciousness. Whatever sound one hears with the ear-door, whatever smell one smells with the nose-door, whatever taste one tastes with the tongue-door, whatever tangible object one touches with the body-door, whatever mental object one knows with the mind-door, one cognizes that mental object with consciousness.' This shows that in making the object clear, consciousness alone is the precursor; consciousness is the forerunner. Therefore, consciousness is said to have the function of being a precursor (pubbaṅgamarasa).
156:
“Great King, just as a city guard sitting at the crossroads in the middle of the city would see a man coming from the east... from the west... from the south... from the north; even so, Great King, whatever form one sees with the eye, one cognizes it with consciousness. Whatever sound one hears with the ear, whatever smell one smells with the nose, whatever taste one tastes with the tongue, whatever tangible one touches with the body, whatever mental object one cognizes with the mind, one cognizes it with consciousness” (as taught in the Milindapañhā). Thus, in the context of reaching the door and manifesting the object, the mind alone is the forerunner and the precursor. Therefore, it is said to have the function of being the forerunner.

This mind, as it arises subsequently, appears to the knowledge as connecting the preceding states without interruption; thus, its manifestation is connecting. In the five-constituent existence (pañcavokāra-bhava), its proximate cause is name-and-form (nāmarūpa); in the four-constituent existence (catuvokāra-bhava), its proximate cause is name (nāma) alone. Therefore, it is said to have name-and-form as its proximate cause.

Is this mind the same as the one previously mentioned, or is it different? It is the same. If it is the same, why is the previously mentioned mind stated again? This was not investigated in the Commentary. However, the logical reason here is as follows: Just as the sun and so on, which are designated based on form and so on, are not essentially different from form and so on—for this reason, when the sun rises, its form known as radiance (teja) also rises—even though it is said so, there is no such thing as a 'sun' distinct from form and so on. The mind is not like that; although it is designated based on states such as contact (phassa), in essence, it is indeed distinct from those states like contact. Therefore, it should be understood that this mind is stated again to demonstrate this meaning: 'At whatever time the mind has arisen, at that time, it is certainly distinct in essence from contact and so on.'

For example, in such passages as: 'At whatever time one develops the path for rebirth in the fine-material sphere... the earth-kasiṇa, at that time there is contact, there is feeling,' the person who develops at the time determined by the developer does not arise in essence. For that reason, in that passage, it is said 'there is contact, there is feeling,' but it is not said 'the one who develops, he exists.' But in passages such as 'At whatever time a wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere has arisen,' the mind determined by the time, at the time determined by the mind, is not thus in essence...
157:
...not that it does not arise. It should be understood that this mind is stated again to show this meaning: just as at that time contact exists and feeling exists, so too the mind exists.

The conclusion here is: this mind is stated again for the purpose of inclusion in the Summary Section (uddesavāra) and for the purpose of analysis in the Exposition Section (niddesavāra). The reason is that by the first word 'mind' (citta), only the occasion (samaya) is determined. To show those states such as contact that exist at that occasion determined by the mind, the passage beginning with 'there is contact' (phasso hoti) is undertaken. The mind also certainly exists at that occasion. Therefore, for the purpose of including that mind as well, it is stated again. If the mind were not mentioned in this place, it would not be possible to analyze it in the Exposition Section by asking 'What is the mind at that time?' In such a case, the analysis of this mind would be omitted. Therefore, it should be understood that it is stated again also for the purpose of analyzing that mind in the Exposition Section.

Alternatively, in the phrase 'has arisen' (uppannaṃ hoti), the words 'the mind has arisen' (cittaṃ uppannaṃ) are merely the head of the teaching. However, it is investigated in the Commentary that the mind does not arise alone. Therefore, here too, in the phrase 'the mind has arisen,' the mind is taken together with the fifty-five wholesome states, not just the mind alone. Thus, having taken all the states of mind and mental factors in brief in that place, the passage beginning with 'there is contact' is undertaken here to show them according to their nature and classification. Thus, it should be understood that the mind is also stated just like contact and so on.

## The Summary of States (Dhammuddesavāra)
## Description of the Group of Jhana Factors (Jhānaṅgarāsi-vaṇṇanā)

It is called 'initial application' (vitakka) because it thinks of the object. Or, the act of thinking is 'initial application.' It means 'lifting' (ūhana). It has the characteristic of directing the mind onto the object. Indeed, it directs the mind onto the object. For example, just as someone enters the palace by depending on a relative or a friend who is a favorite of the king, even so, the mind enters the object by depending on initial application. Therefore, it is said to have the characteristic of directing the mind onto the object. But the Elder Nāgasena said: 'Initial application has the characteristic of striking (ākoṭana).' He said: 'Great King, just as when a drum is struck, thereafter the sound reverberates and echoes; even so, Great King, initial application should be understood as being like the striking. Sustained application (vicāra) should be understood as being like the subsequent reverberation and echoing.' It has the function (rasa) of hitting and thumping. For that reason, it is said that the practitioner makes the object hit by initial application and thumped by initial application. It is manifested as bringing the mind to the object.
158:
The mind explores the object by means of that [applied thought]; therefore, it is called sustained thought (vicāra). Alternatively, the act of exploring the object is vicāra. It means the continuous wandering upon the object. This vicāra has the characteristic of repeatedly exploring the object. Its function (rasa) is to yoke conascent states to that object. Its manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna) is the continuous anchoring of the mind to the object.

Although vitakka and vicāra are inseparable in certain types of consciousness, vitakka is the initial impact of the mind on the object, like the first strike of a bell, because it is grosser than vicāra, precedes it, and has the sense of directing the mind toward the object. Vicāra is the continuous anchoring of the mind to the object, like the subsequent resonance of the bell, because it is subtler than vitakka and has the nature of repeatedly exploring and reflecting on the object.

Between these two, vitakka is characterized by vibration; it has the nature of vibration during the initial arising of the mind. It is like the flapping of wings by a bird wishing to fly into the sky, or like a bee whose mind is attached to the scent diving toward a lotus. Vicāra has a peaceful occurrence; it is the nature of the mind without excessive vibration. It is like the bird that has flown into the sky spreading its wings, or like the bee that has dived toward the lotus hovering over the top of the flower.

In the Commentary, however, it is stated: Vitakka should be understood as the state of directing the mind toward the object, like a large bird flying in the sky catching the wind with both wings and then steadying them. For that vitakka, being one-pointed, fixes the mind. Vicāra should be understood as the state of exploring the object, like the flight of a bird flapping its wings to catch the wind. It is said that vicāra explores the object; this statement is extremely appropriate regarding the continuous occurrence of the mind upon the object. The distinction between vitakka and vicāra is evident in the first and second jhānas.

Furthermore, vitakka is like the hand that firmly holds a tarnished bronze bowl with one hand, while vicāra is like the other hand that rubs it with a mixture of powder and oil. Similarly, vitakka is like the hand of a potter that presses the lump of clay while turning the wheel with a stick to make a vessel, and vicāra is like the hand that moves back and forth [to shape it]. Likewise, vitakka is like the fixed pin in the center used by one drawing a circle, which directs the mind to the object, while vicāra is like the outer pin that revolves around, exploring the object.

It is called joy (pīti) because it gladdens. That pīti has the characteristic of endearing. Its function (rasa) is to refresh the body and mind, or to pervade. Its manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna) is the elation of the mind. This pīti is of five kinds: minor joy (khuddikā pīti), momentary joy (khaṇikā pīti), showering joy (okkantikā pīti), uplifting joy (ubbegā pīti), and pervading joy (pharaṇā pīti). Among these five, minor joy is only able to make the hair on the body stand on end. Momentary joy occurs frequently like a flash of lightning. Showering joy enters the body and breaks repeatedly, like waves breaking upon the seashore. Uplifting joy is powerful and reaches the extent of being able to lift the body and make it leap into the sky. Indeed, Elder Mahātissa, residing in Puṇṇavallika village, went to the courtyard of the shrine on a full-moon evening and, seeing the moonlight, faced the Great Shrine (Mahācetiya). Thinking, 'At this time, the four assemblies will be worshipping the Great Shrine,' he aroused uplifting joy directed toward the Buddha through the power of the object he had previously seen...
159:
Among those five types of joy, minor joy (khuddikā pīti) is only able to cause the hair on the body to stand on end. Momentary joy (khaṇikā pīti) occurs like flashes of lightning at every moment. Showering joy (okkantikā pīti) descends upon the body and breaks, like waves breaking upon the seashore. Uplifting joy (ubbegā pīti) is powerful and reaches the extent of being able to lift the body and make it leap into the sky. To illustrate this, Elder Mahātissa, living in Puṇṇavallika village, went to the courtyard of the shrine on a full-moon evening. Seeing the moonlight and facing the Great Shrine, he thought, 'At this time, the four assemblies will be worshipping the Great Shrine.' Through the power of the object he had naturally seen before, he aroused uplifting joy directed toward the Buddha. Like a colorful ball struck against a plastered floor, he rose into the air and landed right in the courtyard of the Great Shrine.

Similarly, a young woman of a noble family in Vattakālaka village, depending on Girikaṇḍaka Monastery, once leaped into the sky through powerful uplifting joy directed toward the Buddha. It is said that her parents, when going to the monastery in the evening to hear the Dhamma, said, 'Dear, you are heavy with child and cannot travel at an unseasonable time. We will share the merit with you after hearing the Dhamma.' They then departed. Although she wished to go, she could not disregard her parents' words. Staying at home and standing at the doorway, she looked at the courtyard of the Ākāsa Shrine at Girikaṇḍaka by the moonlight and saw the offering of lamps at the shrine. She saw the four assemblies worshipping the shrine with flowers and perfumes and circumambulating it, and she heard the sound of the community of monks chanting in unison. Then, while looking at the shrine which was like a heap of pearls, uplifting joy arose in her as she thought, 'How fortunate are those people who can go to the monastery, wander in such a shrine courtyard, and hear such sweet Dhamma talk!' She leaped into the sky and, arriving at the shrine courtyard from the air even before her parents, she worshipped the shrine and stood listening to the Dhamma. When her parents arrived, they asked, 'Dear, by which path did you come?' She replied, 'I came by the sky path, not by the ground path.' They asked, 'Dear, only those who have destroyed the taints (khīṇāsava) travel by the sky; how could you come?' She said, 'As I stood looking at the shrine by the moonlight, powerful joy directed toward the Buddha arose. At that time, I did not even know whether I was standing or sitting, but by the sign I had grasped...'
160:
“I have leaped into the sky and am standing on the courtyard of the shrine.” In this way, uplifting rapture (ubbegā-pīti) has the capacity to make one leap into the sky.

When pervading rapture (pharaṇā-pīti) arises, it continuously permeates the entire body, like a bladder filled with air or like a mountain cavern flooded by a great torrent of water. This fivefold rapture, as it matures and reaches fulfillment, brings to completion the two kinds of tranquility (passaddhi): tranquility of body (kāya-passaddhi) and tranquility of mind (citta-passaddhi). As tranquility matures and reaches fulfillment, it brings to completion the two kinds of happiness (sukha): bodily happiness (kāyika-sukha) and mental happiness (cetasika-sukha). As happiness matures and reaches fulfillment, it brings to completion the three kinds of concentration (samādhi): momentary concentration (khaṇika-samādhi), access concentration (upacāra-samādhi), and attainment concentration (appanā-samādhi). Among these types of rapture, excluding the one that fulfills attainment concentration, the other two (which fulfill momentary and access concentration) are also associated with this [great wholesome consciousness].

It is called happiness (sukha) because it causes ease; the meaning is that when it arises in someone, it makes that person happy. Alternatively, it is called sukha because it thoroughly consumes or digs out the suffering (affliction) of the body and mind. This is a name for pleasant feeling (somanassa-vedanā). Its characteristics and so forth should be understood in the same way as stated in the section on the aggregate of feeling (vedanā).

Another way: Happiness has the characteristic of being pleasant, the function of intensifying associated states, and the manifestation of repeated grasping [of the object] or assisting associated states. Although rapture (pīti) and happiness (sukha) are inseparable in certain states [such as jhāna], rapture is the delight in obtaining a desired object, while happiness is the experiencing of the taste of the object already obtained. Where there is rapture, there is happiness. However, where there is happiness, there is not necessarily rapture. Rapture is included in the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha), while happiness is included in the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha). Rapture is like the joy of a person exhausted in a desert upon hearing of or seeing a forest and water. Happiness is like the ease felt when entering the shade of the forest and using the water.

For example: Suppose a man traveling through a great desert, exhausted by the heat, thirsty and parched, meets someone on the way and asks, “Where is there drinking water?” That person might say, “Beyond this forest, there is a natural lake and a grove; if you go there, you will find it.” Upon hearing those words, the man would be extremely delighted. As he continues, seeing lotus petals, stalks, and leaves fallen on the ground, he would become even more delighted. As he proceeds, he would see people with wet clothes and wet hair, hear the sounds of wild fowl and peacocks, see the dark green forest grove near the lake resembling a net of jewels, see the blue, red, and white lotuses growing in the lake, and see the clear, transparent water. He...
161:
That exhausted man, becoming increasingly delighted and joyful, would descend into the lake, bathe and drink as he pleases, and with his distress allayed, he would eat lotus stalks and roots, wear blue lotuses and other flowers, and placing lotus fibers on his shoulders, he would emerge from the water. After dressing in his cloth and drying his bathing cloth in the sun, he would lie down in the cool shade where a gentle breeze blows, exclaiming, “Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!” This is how the completion of this simile should be understood.

For that man, the period of delight from the time he heard about the lake and forest until he saw the water is like rapture (pīti), which has the quality of delighting in the object in the preliminary stage. The period when he lies down after bathing and drinking, enjoying the gentle breeze in the cool shade and saying, “Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!” is like happiness (sukha), which consists in the experiencing of the taste of the object that has reached full strength. It should be understood that this is stated because [these qualities] are prominent at those respective times. As for the statement that where there is rapture, there is also happiness, that has already been mentioned.

One-pointedness of mind (cittass'ekaggatā) means the state of the mind having a single point; this is a name for concentration (samādhi). Regarding its characteristics and so forth, it is said in the Commentary: “Concentration has the characteristic of being the leader (pāmokkha) and the characteristic of non-distraction (avikkhepa).” Just as the roof peak (kūṭa) of a house is the chief because it binds together the rest of the wooden structures, so too, because all wholesome states are accomplished through the mind of concentration, concentration is the leader of all those states. Therefore, it is said:

“Just as, O King, whatever rafters there are in a gabled house, they all lead to the peak, incline toward the peak, and converge at the peak, and the peak is called the chief of those rafters; even so, O King, whatever wholesome states there are, they all incline toward concentration, lean toward concentration, and tend toward concentration, and concentration is called the chief of those states.”

And just as a king, upon reaching the battlefield, goes to whatever place the soldiers are faltering, and wherever the king goes, the soldiers are restored, and the enemy forces are broken and follow the king’s will; even so, because it does not allow associated states to be distracted or scattered, concentration is said to have the characteristic of non-distraction.
162:
To state another method: this concentration (samādhi), known as one-pointedness of mind (ekaggatā), has the characteristic of non-wandering or non-distraction. It has the function of unifying co-nascent (sahajāta) states, just as water unifies bath powder. It is manifested as the calmness of the mind or as the manifestation of knowledge. For it was said: "One who is concentrated knows and sees things as they really are." It has happiness (sukha) as its proximate cause. It should be understood as the steadiness of the mind, like the steadiness of a lamp's flame in a windless place.

## Description of the Group of Faculties (Indriya-rāsi-vaṇṇanā)

Faith (saddhā) is that by which associated states believe, or it believes itself, or it is just the act of believing. That faith is a faculty (indriya) in the sense of predominance because it overcomes faithlessness. Or, it is a faculty because it exercises lordship in the characteristic of decision (adhimokkha). Faith itself is a faculty, thus it is the faith-faculty (saddhindriya). That faith has the characteristic of clarifying (sampasādana) and the characteristic of aspiring (sampakkhandana).

Just as when the water-clearing gem of a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) is thrown into water, it causes the mud, weeds, water-plants, and filth to settle, making the water clear, translucent, and undisturbed; in the same way, when faith arises, it inhibits the hindrances (nīvaraṇa), causes the defilements (kilesa) to settle, clarifies the mind, and makes it undisturbed. With a clear mind, the son of a good family who is a practitioner (yogāvacara) gives gifts, undertakes morality, performs the Uposatha duties, and begins meditation. In this way, faith should be understood as having the characteristic of clarifying associated states. Therefore, the Venerable Nāgasena said:

"Great King, just as a Universal Monarch, traveling on a long journey with his fourfold army, might cross a small body of water. That water would become disturbed, turbid, agitated, and muddy due to the elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry. Having crossed the water, the Universal Monarch would command his men, 'Friends, bring me drinking water; I will drink.' The King would possess a water-clearing gem. Those men, replying 'As you command, Your Majesty,' would throw that water-clearing gem into the water. As soon as it is thrown into the water, the mud, weeds, and water-plants would disappear, the silt would settle, and the water would become clear, translucent, and undisturbed. Then they would offer the drinking water to the Universal Monarch, saying, 'May Your Majesty drink the water.'"
163:
"Great King, the mind should be seen as the water. The practitioner (yogāvacara) should be seen as those men. The defilements should be seen as the weeds, water-plants, lotus-husks, and mud. Faith should be seen as the water-clearing gem. Just as when the water-clearing gem is thrown into the water, the weeds, water-plants, and lotus-husks disappear, the mud settles, and the water becomes clear and undisturbed; in the same way, Great King, when faith arises, it drives away and suppresses the hindrances (nīvaraṇa), and the mind free from hindrances becomes clear and undisturbed" (as stated in the Milindapañha).

Furthermore, when people who are afraid reach a great river filled with crocodiles, monsters, sharks, and demons, they stand on both banks. Then a brave hero, a great warrior, arrives and asks, 'Why are you standing here?' When they reply, 'We do not dare to descend because of the danger,' he takes a sharp sword and says, 'Follow me, do not be afraid.' He then descends into the river, wards off all the crocodiles and other dangers that come, and leads the people safely from this bank to the other bank. He also brings them safely from the other bank back to this bank. In the same way, for one who gives gifts, protects morality, undertakes the Uposatha, or develops meditation, faith is the precursor and the leader. Therefore, it is said that 'faith has the characteristic of aspiring (sampakkhandana).'

Another method: Faith has the characteristic of trusting (saddahana) or the characteristic of conviction (okappana). It has the function of clarifying (pasādana) like the water-clearing gem, or the function of leaping forward (pakkhandana) like crossing a flood. It is manifested as non-turbidness (akālusiya) or as decision (adhimutti). It has objects of faith (saddheyya-vatthu) as its proximate cause, or the factors of stream-entry (sotāpattiyaṅga) as its proximate cause. That faith should be seen as a hand, as wealth, or as a seed.

Energy (vīriya) is the state of the brave (vīra) or the action of the brave. It is called vīriya because it is to be initiated or carried out by way of method or means. That energy itself is a faculty (indriya) in the sense of predominance because it overcomes laziness. Or, it is a faculty because it exercises lordship in the characteristic of upholding (paggahaṇa). Energy itself is a faculty, thus it is the energy-faculty (vīriyindriya). That energy has the characteristic of supporting (upatthambhana) and the characteristic of upholding (paggahaṇa). Just as an old house stands by the support of a new pillar, in the same way, the practitioner (yogāvacara), being supported by the support of energy, does not decline or fall away from any wholesome states (kusala dhamma). In this way, energy should be understood as having the characteristic of supporting. Therefore, the Elder Nāgasena said:
164:
## 
Great King, for example, when a house is about to fall, it is supported by another wooden prop, and being thus supported, that house does not fall but remains standing; even so, Great King, energy (viriya) has the characteristic of supporting (upatthambhana). All wholesome states supported by energy do not decrease or perish.

Alternatively, just as when a small army and a large army are engaged in battle, the small army might retreat. Then, upon informing the king, the king sends powerful reinforcements of elephants, horses, and soldiers. Supported by those reinforcements, one's own army is able to defeat the enemy army; even so, energy does not allow the associated states (sampayutta-dhamma) that arise together with it to retreat or shrink back, but instead uplifts and upholds them. Therefore, it is said, "Energy has the characteristic of upholding (paggahaṇa)."

In another way, energy has the characteristic of endeavour (ussāha), the function of supporting (upatthambhana) the states that arise together with it, and it manifests in knowledge as the state of non-faltering (asaṃsīdanabhāva). In accordance with the words, "One who is stirred (saṃvigga) makes a proper effort," it has spiritual urgency (saṃvega) as its proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna), or it has the eight grounds for initiating energy (vīriyārambhavatthu) as its proximate cause. Energy that is properly initiated should be understood as the root of all attainments (sampatti).

They remember by means of that state, or it remembers by itself, or it is merely the act of remembering; therefore, it is called mindfulness (sati). That same mindfulness is called a faculty (indriya) in the sense of predominance because it overcomes forgetfulness (muṭṭhassacca). Or it is called a faculty because it exercises lordship in the characteristic of establishing (upaṭṭhāna) upon an object. Since mindfulness itself is a faculty, it is called the faculty of mindfulness (satindriya). That mindfulness has the characteristic of non-drifting (apilāpana) on the object and the characteristic of embracing (upaggaṇhana) what is beneficial. For example, just as a king's treasurer (bhaṇḍāgārika), while guarding the ten kinds of jewels, reminds the king of his sovereign wealth and glory every evening and morning; even so, mindfulness reminds and makes one note wholesome states. Therefore, the Elder Nāgasena said:

"Great King, just as the treasurer of a Universal Monarch reminds the Universal Monarch of his glory every evening and morning, saying: 'Great King, there are this many elephants, this many horses, this many chariots, this many infantry, this much silver, this much gold, and this much of all kinds of wealth; may the King remember them'; even so, Great King, mindfulness keeps wholesome states from being forgotten, reminding: 'These are the four foundations of mindfulness, these are the four right efforts, these are the four bases of power, these are the five faculties, these are the five powers, these are the seven factors of enlightenment, this is the Noble Eightfold Path, this is calm (samatha), this is insight (vipassanā), this is knowledge (vijjā), this is liberation (vimutti), and these are the supramundane states.' Thus, Great King, mindfulness has the characteristic of non-drifting (apilāpana)."
165:
## 
Just as the advisor-gem (pariṇāyakarattana) of a Universal Monarch, knowing those who bring harm and those who bring benefit to the king, removes the harmful and brings near the beneficial; even so, mindfulness investigates the destinations of beneficial and harmful states, thinking, "These states such as bodily misconduct are harmful," and thus dispels harmful states, and thinking, "These states such as bodily good conduct are beneficial," it embraces beneficial states. Therefore, the Elder Nāgasena said: "Great King, just as the advisor-gem of a Universal Monarch knows the beneficial and harmful persons to the king, thinking, 'These people bring benefit to the king, these bring harm; these are helpful, these are unhelpful,' and then dispels the harmful and embraces the beneficial; even so, Great King, mindfulness, when it arises, investigates the destinations of beneficial and harmful states, thinking, 'These states are beneficial, these states are harmful; these states are helpful, these states are unhelpful,' and then dispels the harmful states and embraces the beneficial states. Thus, Great King, mindfulness has the characteristic of embracing (upaggaṇhana)."

In another way, mindfulness has the characteristic of non-drifting, the function of non-forgetfulness (asammosana), and it manifests as the state of guarding (ārakkha), or it manifests as the state of facing the object (visayābhimukhībhāva). It has firm perception (thirasaññā) as its proximate cause, or it has the foundations of mindfulness such as the body (kāyagatāsati) as its proximate cause. Because it stands firmly on the object, it should be understood as being like a gatepost (esikā), and because it guards the eye-door and so on, it should be understood as being like a gatekeeper (dovārika).

Because it places the mind rightly on the object, it is called concentration (samādhi). That same concentration is called a faculty (indriya) in the sense of predominance because it overcomes distraction (vikkhepa). Or it is called a faculty because it exercises lordship in the characteristic of non-distraction (avikkhepa). Since concentration itself is a faculty, it is called the faculty of concentration (samādhindriya). Its characteristics and so forth should be understood according to the method already mentioned below.

Because it knows in various ways, it is called wisdom (paññā). What does it know? It knows the Noble Truths through the method of "This is suffering," and so on. In the Commentaries, however, it is said, "It is wisdom because it makes things known (paññāpeti)." How does it make things known? It makes them known as impermanent (anicca), suffering (dukkha), and non-self (anatta). That same wisdom is called a faculty (indriya) in the sense of predominance because it overcomes ignorance (avijjā). Or it is called a faculty because it exercises lordship in the characteristic of seeing (dassana). Since wisdom itself is a faculty, it is called the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya). That wisdom has the characteristic of illuminating (obhāsana) and the characteristic of understanding (pajānana). For example, just as when a lamp is lit at night in a four-walled house, darkness disappears and light appears; even so...
166:
Wisdom has the characteristic of illuminating. There is no light equal to the light of wisdom. Indeed, for a wise person sitting in a single cross-legged posture, the ten thousand world-systems become a single illumination. Therefore, the Elder said:

“Great King, just as a man might bring a lamp into a dark house; the lamp, having entered, destroys the darkness, produces radiance, reveals light, and makes forms manifest. Even so, O Great King, wisdom, when it arises, destroys the darkness of ignorance (avijjā), produces the radiance of knowledge (vijjā), reveals the light of insight (ñāṇa), and makes the Noble Truths (ariya-sacca) manifest. Thus, O Great King, wisdom has the characteristic of illuminating” (Milindapañha).

Alternatively, just as a skilled physician knows the suitable and unsuitable foods for patients, so wisdom, when it arises, knows distinctly the states that are wholesome and unwholesome, to-be-cultivated and not-to-be-cultivated, low and sublime, dark and bright, and those that are similar or dissimilar. This has also been stated by the General of the Dhamma (Venerable Sāriputta): “Friends, it is called ‘wise’ because it knows distinctly (pajānāti). What does it know distinctly? It knows distinctly: ‘This is suffering (dukkha).’” This should be expanded upon. Thus, its characteristic of knowing distinctly should be understood.

Another way: Wisdom has the characteristic of penetrating the true nature of things, or the characteristic of unerring penetration, like the penetration of an arrow shot by a skilled archer. It has the function of illuminating the object, like a lamp. It manifests as non-delusion, like a good guide in a forest.

It is called ‘mano’ (mind) because it knows; the meaning is knowing distinctly. But the commentators say: It is called ‘mano’ because it measures, weighs, and knows the object, like measuring with a nāḷi measure or weighing with a great scale. That very mind is called a faculty (indriya) because it exercises lordship in the characteristic of knowing. The mind itself being a faculty is the mind-faculty (manindriya). This is a synonym for the consciousness (citta) mentioned below.

One who has a beautiful mind due to association with zest (pīti) and happiness (somanassa) is called ‘sumana’ (happy-minded). The state of being happy-minded is ‘somanassa’ (joy/mental pleasure). It is called a faculty (indriya) because it exercises lordship in the characteristic of experiencing pleasure. Somanassa itself being a faculty is the joy-faculty (somanassindriya). This is a synonym for the feeling (vedanā) mentioned below.
167:
Those states associated with the life faculty are called ‘life’ (jīvita) because they live by means of it. It is called a faculty (indriya) because it exercises lordship in the characteristic of maintaining. Life itself being a faculty is the life-faculty (jīvitindriya). It exercises lordship over the continuity of the clung-to aggregates (upādinnaka-khandha) as they occur.

By way of characteristics, etc., the life-faculty has the characteristic of maintaining the states (conascent states) that are inseparable from itself. It has the function of making those states occur (persist). It manifests as the establishing of those very states from arising to dissolution. Its proximate cause is the states that are to be maintained.

Even though there are functions such as maintaining, the life-faculty maintains those states only during its own moment of existence. It is like water maintaining lotuses and so on. It also protects the states produced by its own conditions, like a nurse protecting a prince. It persists only through its connection with the states it causes to occur, like a navigator staying with the boat he steers. It cannot cause them to persist beyond their dissolution (bhaṅga) because of the absence of itself and the states to be caused to persist. It cannot maintain them even at the moment of dissolution because it is itself breaking up, like the wick and oil of a lamp that are being exhausted cannot maintain the flame. However, it should not be regarded as being devoid of the power of maintaining, causing to occur, and establishing, because it accomplishes those respective tasks at the stated moment.

## Description of the Group of Path Factors
Among the terms such as Right View (sammādiṭṭhi), it is Right View because of the sense of seeing without distortion. It is Right Intention (sammāsaṅkappa) because of the sense of directing onto the object. It is Right Effort (sammāvāyāma) because of the sense of exerting. It is Right Mindfulness (sammāsati) because of the sense of establishing presence. It is Right Concentration (sammāsamādhi) because of the sense of non-distraction. By way of word-definition (vacanattha): it sees well, or by means of it they see well, thus it is Right View. It intends well, or by means of it they intend well, thus it is Right Intention. It strives well, or by means of it they strive well, thus it is Right Effort. It remembers well, or by means of it they remember well, thus it is Right Mindfulness. It concentrates well, or by means of it they are well-concentrated, thus it is Right Concentration. Alternatively, a praised or beautiful view is Right View. In this way, the word-definitions of these terms should be understood. Their characteristics, etc., are as stated below.

## Description of the Group of Powers
In the case of the power of faith (saddhābala) and so on, faith and the other states have the meanings already stated. They should be understood as powers (bala) because of the sense of being unshakable. Thus, among these, it is the power of faith because it is not shaken by faithlessness (assaddhiya). It is the power of energy (vīriyabala) because it is not shaken by laziness (kosajja). It is the power of mindfulness (satibala) because it is not shaken by forgetfulness (muṭṭhassacca). It is the power of concentration (samādhibala) because it is not shaken by restlessness (uddhacca). It is the power of wisdom (paññābala) because it is not shaken by ignorance (avijjā). Because it is not shaken by shamelessness (ahirika)...
168:
It is called the power of moral shame (hiri-bala) because it is not shaken by shamelessness (ahirika). It is called the power of moral dread (ottappa-bala) because it is not shaken by fearlessness of wrongdoing (anottappa). This is the explanation of the meaning through the combination of the terms (such as faith, etc.) and the term "power" (bala).

Among those (seven powers), the first five, starting with the power of faith, have already been explained below through their characteristics and so forth. Regarding the latter two (the power of moral shame and the power of moral dread): it is called hiri because it feels shame (or disgust) towards bodily misconduct and so forth. This name hiri is a designation for shame (lajjā). It is called ottappa because it feels dread because of those same bodily misconducts and so forth. This name ottappa is a designation for the dread of evil. To show the distinction between these two, hiri and ottappa, this detailed discourse is spoken by setting forth the following matrix (mātikā): "origin, predominance, shame, and the characteristic of fear."

Hiri has an internal origin (ajjhatta-samuṭṭhāna), while ottappa has an external origin (bahiddhā-samuṭṭhāna). Hiri has self-predominance (attādhipati), while ottappa has world-predominance (lokādhipati). Hiri is established in the nature of shame, while ottappa is established in the nature of fear. Hiri has the characteristic of respect, while ottappa has the characteristic of seeing fear in faults and dreading them.

Among them, one arouses hiri which has an internal origin through four reasons: by reflecting on birth, by reflecting on age, by reflecting on heroism, and by reflecting on great learning. How? "Doing this evil is not the work of those well-born; this is the work of those of low birth, such as fishermen and the like. For someone well-born like me, it is not proper to do this work." Thus, first reflecting on birth, one arouses hiri by not committing evil such as taking life. Similarly, "Doing this evil is a work to be done by the young. For someone like me who is at an advanced age, it is not proper to do this work." Thus, reflecting on age, one arouses hiri by not committing evil such as taking life. Similarly, "This evil work is the work of those of weak nature, not of the heroic. For someone like me endowed with heroism, it is not proper to do this work." Thus, reflecting on heroism, one arouses hiri by not committing evil such as taking life. Similarly, "This evil work is the work of the blind and foolish, not of the wise. For someone like me who is wise and of great learning, it is not proper to do this work." Thus, reflecting on great learning, one arouses hiri by not committing evil such as taking life. In this way, one arouses hiri which has an internal origin through these four reasons. Having aroused it, one introduces hiri into one's mind and no longer commits evil. In this way, hiri is said to have an internal origin.
169:
What is moral dread with an external origin (bahiddhā-samuṭṭhāna ottappa)? If you were to do evil, you would be blamed in the midst of the four assemblies.

"The wise will blame you, just as a city-dweller avoids filth;
The virtuous will also avoid you. O monk, how could you do such a thing?"

One who reflects in this way does not commit evil through moral dread that has arisen from an external origin. This is called moral dread with an external origin (bahiddhā-samuṭṭhāna ottappa).

What is moral shame with self-predominance (attādhipati hiri)? Here, a certain son of good family, making himself the chief and foremost, reflects: "For one like me who has gone forth out of faith, who is of great learning, and who is a holder of the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), it is not proper to commit evil," and thus does not commit evil. This is called moral shame with self-predominance (attādhipati hiri). Therefore, the Blessed One said: "He, making himself alone the chief and foremost, abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome; he abandons the blameworthy and develops the blameless; he maintains himself in purity."

What is moral dread with world-predominance (lokādhipati ottappa)? Here, a certain son of good family, making the world the chief and foremost, does not commit evil. As the Blessed One said: "This world-habitation is indeed vast. In this vast world-habitation, there are ascetics and brahmins who are powerful, possessed of the divine eye, and knowers of others' minds. They can see even from afar, and though they are near, they are not seen (if they conceal themselves); they can know another's mind with their own mind. They will know me thus: 'Look, sirs, at this son of good family; though he has gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, he lives mixed with evil, unwholesome states.' There are also deities who are powerful, possessed of the divine eye, and knowers of others' minds. They too can see even from afar, and though they are near, they are not seen; they can know another's mind with their own mind. They too will know me: 'Look, sirs, at this son of good family; though he has gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, he lives mixed with evil, unwholesome states.' ... He, making the world alone the chief and foremost, abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome; he abandons the blameworthy and develops the blameless; he maintains himself in purity." This is called moral dread with world-predominance (lokādhipati ottappa).
170:
Hiri (moral shame) is established in the nature of shame, and ottappa (moral dread) is established in the nature of fear. In this context, shame refers to the mode of being ashamed or disgusted, and the state established by that nature is called hiri. Fear refers to the fear of the woeful states (apāya), and the state established by that nature is called ottappa. Both of these become manifest in the avoidance of evil. For instance, just as a person of good family, while relieving himself, might feel ashamed and reproached upon seeing someone before whom it is proper to feel shame; in the same way, one refrains from doing evil by internalizing the sense of shame. Another person refrains from doing evil out of fear of the woeful states.

In this regard, there is this analogy: Suppose there are two iron balls, one of which is cold but smeared with excrement, and the other is glowing and hot. A wise man would not pick up the cold one because of his disgust at the excrement, nor would he pick up the other because of the fear of being burnt. Here, the non-picking up of the cold ball due to disgust at the excrement should be understood as the non-doing of evil by internalizing the sense of shame. The non-picking up of the hot ball for fear of being burnt should be understood as the non-doing of evil out of fear of the woeful states.

Hiri has the characteristic of respect (sappatissava); ottappa has the characteristic of dreading blame (vajjabhīruka). These two also become manifest only in the avoidance of evil. Some people arouse hiri, characterized by respect, and refrain from evil through four reasons: consideration of the greatness of one's birth (jāti), consideration of the greatness of the Teacher (the Buddha), consideration of the greatness of the inheritance (the Dhamma), and consideration of the greatness of one's fellow practitioners. Some people arouse ottappa, characterized by dreading blame, and refrain from evil through four reasons: fear of self-reproach (attānuvāda-bhaya), fear of reproach by others (parānuvāda-bhaya), fear of punishment (daṇḍa-bhaya), and fear of woeful states (duggati-bhaya). In this context, the considerations of the greatness of birth, etc., and the fear of self-reproach, etc., should be explained in detail.

## Mūlarāsivaṇṇanā
It is called alobha (non-greed) because by this, they do not covet; or it itself does not covet; or it is simply the state of non-coveting. The same method applies to adosa (non-hatred) and amoha (non-delusion). Among them, alobha has the characteristic of the mind's lack of greed for an object, or the characteristic of non-attachment, like a drop of water on a lotus leaf. It has the function of not-possessing, like a liberated bhikkhu.
171:
...It is like that. It manifests to knowledge as the state of non-clinging, like a man who has fallen into filth (and does not wish to be smeared by it). Adosa has the characteristic of non-ferocity, or the characteristic of non-opposition, like a kind friend. It has the function of removing resentment, or the function of removing the fever (of passion), like sandalwood. It manifests to knowledge as a state of peacefulness, like the full moon. Amoha has already been explained below under the term 'faculty of wisdom' (paññindriya) by way of its characteristics and so forth.

Among these three, alobha is the opposite of the stain of stinginess (macchariya); adosa is the opposite of the stain of immorality (dussīlya); amoha is the opposite of the non-development of wholesome states. Here, alobha is the cause of giving (dāna); adosa is the cause of virtue (sīla); amoha is the cause of meditation (bhāvanā). Among them, through alobha, one does not take in excess, because a greedy person takes in excess (perceiving qualities where there are none). Through adosa, one does not take what is deficient, because a hateful person takes what is deficient (by disparaging existing qualities). Through amoha, one takes things correctly without distortion, because a deluded person takes things in a distorted way.

Furthermore, through alobha, one perceives an existing fault as a fault and dwells on the fault; for a greedy person conceals a fault. Through adosa, one perceives an existing virtue as a virtue and dwells on the virtue; for a hateful person disparages a virtue. Through amoha, one perceives the true nature as it really is and dwells on the true nature; for a deluded person takes what is true as false and what is false as true. Through alobha, the suffering of separation from the loved does not occur, because a greedy person has the nature of being attached and cannot endure separation. Through adosa, the suffering of association with the unloved does not occur, because a hateful person has the nature of disliking and cannot endure association. Through amoha, the suffering of not getting what one wants does not occur, because for one who is undeluded, there is the possibility of such reflection as: 'Where can it be obtained in this thing which is subject to aging: "May it not age"?' and so forth.

In this context, through alobha, the suffering of birth (jāti-dukkha) does not occur, because alobha is the opposite of craving (taṇhā) and the suffering of birth has craving as its root. Through adosa, the suffering of aging (jarā-dukkha) does not occur, because for one with intense hatred, aging occurs quickly. Through amoha, the suffering of death (maraṇa-dukkha) does not occur, for death with delusion is suffering, and that does not happen to one who is undeluded. Through alobha, there is happy cohabitation for householders (as there is no dispute over land, etc.); through amoha, for monastics (as there is no dispute over views); and through adosa, there is happy cohabitation for all people.
172:
Among these three qualities, specifically, because of non-greed (alobha), there is no rebirth in the realm of hungry ghosts (peta). For beings are mostly reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts due to craving (taṇhā), and non-greed is the opposite of craving. Because of non-hatred (adosa), there is no rebirth in hell (niraya). For due to hatred, being of a fierce nature, they are reborn in hell which is similar to hatred; and non-hatred is the opposite of hatred. Because of non-delusion (amoha), there is no rebirth in the animal realm (tiracchāna). For due to delusion, they are reborn in the animal realm which is constantly bewildered; and non-delusion is the opposite of delusion. Among these, non-greed prevents attachment through the power of passion (rāga); non-hatred prevents departure through the power of hatred; non-delusion prevents the state of being unable to remain neutral (amajjhattabhāva) through the power of delusion.

Through these three qualities, in order, these three perceptions arise: the perception of renunciation (nekkhamma-saññā), the perception of non-ill will (abyāpāda-saññā), and the perception of non-harming (avihiṃsā-saññā). Also, these three perceptions arise: the perception of foulness (asubha-saññā), the perception of the immeasurable (appamāṇa-saññā), and the perception of elements (dhātu-saññā). By non-greed, there is the avoidance of the extreme of devotion to sensual pleasures (kāmasukhallikānuyoga); by non-hatred, there is the avoidance of the extreme of devotion to self-mortification (attakilamathānuyoga); by non-delusion, there is the practice of the middle way (majjhimā-paṭipadā). Likewise, by non-greed, there is the breaking of the bodily tie of covetousness (abhijjhā-kāyagantha); by non-hatred, the breaking of the bodily tie of ill will (vyāpāda-kāyagantha); by non-delusion, the breaking of the remaining two ties. The first two foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) are accomplished by the power of the first two [non-greed and non-hatred], while the last two are accomplished by the power of the last one [non-delusion] alone.

Among these, non-greed is the cause of health; for one without greed does not consume what is unsuitable even if it is desirable, and because of that non-consumption, one is healthy.
