Non-hatred is the cause of youthfulness; for one without hatred is not burned by the fire of hatred which brings about wrinkles and gray hair, and thus remains youthful for a long time. Non-delusion is the cause of long life; for one who is undeluded knows what is beneficial and what is harmful, avoids the harmful and practices the beneficial, and thus becomes long-lived.

Among these, non-greed is the cause of the attainment of wealth; for the wealth of one without greed is obtained through generosity. Non-hatred is the cause of the attainment of friends; because of obtaining friends through loving-kindness (mettā) and because of not falling away from friends. Non-delusion is the cause of self-attainment; for the undeluded one, doing only what is for one's own benefit, [perfects] oneself...
173:
...perfects oneself. Non-greed is the cause of the divine abiding (dibba-vihāra, the dwelling of devas or jhānas); non-hatred is the cause of the brahma-abiding (brahma-vihāra); non-delusion is the cause of the noble abiding (ariya-vihāra, fruition attainment).

Among these, by non-greed, one is at peace regarding the formations of beings (satta-saṅkhāra) on one's own side; this is because of the absence of suffering caused by excessive attachment when those formations of beings perish. By non-hatred, one is at peace regarding the formations of beings on the other side (enemies); for to one without hatred, there is no perception of "enemy" even among enemies. By non-delusion, one is at peace regarding the formations of beings on the neutral side; for to one who is undeluded, there is an absence of all attachment.

By non-greed, there is the vision of impermanence (anicca). For a greedy person, due to the desire for enjoyment, does not see even impermanent formations as impermanent. By non-hatred, there is the vision of suffering (dukkha). For one with a disposition of non-hatred, having abandoned the grounds for resentment, sees only suffering in formations. By non-delusion, there is the vision of non-self (anatta). For the undeluded one, being skillful in perceiving things as they really are, understands the five aggregates, which have no director (apariṇāyaka), as being without a director. Just as the vision of impermanence etc. arise because of these [non-greed etc.], so also these [non-greed etc.] arise because of the vision of impermanence etc. By the vision of impermanence, non-greed becomes; by the vision of suffering, non-hatred becomes; by the vision of non-self, non-delusion becomes. For who, knowing rightly "This is impermanent," would produce longing for its sake? Or who, knowing formations as "suffering," would produce the further, extremely sharp suffering of anger? And having understood the emptiness of self, where would one again fall into delusion?

## Description of the Group of Courses of Action (Kammapatharāsivaṇṇanā)
It is called non-covetousness (anabhijjhā) because one does not plan to take another's property by way of greed. It is called non-ill will (abyāpāda) because one does not destroy the physical and mental happiness of oneself and others, the welfare of this world and the next, and the fame obtained through the power of virtues. It is called right view (sammādiṭṭhi) because one sees rightly, or because it is a beautiful view. These are just names for non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion. It should be understood that while these qualities were taken as "roots" (mūla) below, here they are taken as "courses of action" (kammapatha).

## Description of the Dyad of World-Protectors (Lokapāladukavaṇṇanā)
Shame (hiri) and fear of wrongdoing (ottappa) were also taken as "powers" (bala) below, but here they are taken as "world-protectors" (lokapāla). Indeed, these two qualities protect the world. As it was said: "Monks, these two bright qualities protect the world. Which two? Shame and fear of wrongdoing. Monks, these two bright qualities [protect] the world..."
174:
...they protect. Monks, if these two bright qualities did not protect the world, then in this world, one would not be known as 'mother,' or 'maternal aunt,' or 'maternal uncle's wife,' or 'teacher's wife,' or 'wife of respected ones.' The world would fall into confusion like goats, chickens, pigs, dogs, and jackals. Monks, because these two bright qualities protect the world, therefore one is known as 'mother,' or 'maternal aunt,' or 'maternal uncle's wife,' or 'teacher's wife,' or 'wife of respected ones' (as taught in Aṅguttara Nikāya, 2.9).

## Description of the Pairs Starting with Tranquility

Tranquility of the body is kāyapassaddhi. Tranquility of consciousness is cittapassaddhi. In this context, 'body' (kāya) refers to the three aggregates beginning with feeling (vedanā). Taking both together, they have the characteristic of quieting the distress (daratha) of the body and consciousness; their function is to crush the distress of the body and consciousness; they manifest as the state of coolness and lack of agitation of the body and consciousness; and they have the body and consciousness as their proximate cause. They should be understood as being the opposites of defilements such as restlessness (uddhacca) which cause the body and consciousness to be unquiet.

Lightness of the body is kāyalahutā. Lightness of consciousness is cittalahutā. These qualities have the characteristic of quieting the heaviness of the body and consciousness; their function is to crush the heaviness of the body and consciousness; they manifest as the state of non-sluggishness of the body and consciousness; and they have the body and consciousness as their proximate cause. They should be understood as being the opposites of defilements such as sloth and torpor (thinamiddha) which cause the body and consciousness to be heavy.

Malleability of the body is kāyamudutā. Malleability of consciousness is cittamudutā. These qualities have the characteristic of quieting the stiffness of the body and consciousness; their function is to crush the stiffness of the body and consciousness; they manifest as the state of non-resistance; and they have the body and consciousness as their proximate cause. They should be understood as being the opposites of defilements such as wrong view (diṭṭhi) and conceit (māna) which cause the body and consciousness to be stiff.

Wieldiness of the body is kāyakammaññatā. Wieldiness of consciousness is cittakammaññatā. These qualities have the characteristic of quieting the unwieldiness of the body and consciousness; their function is to crush the unwieldiness of the body and consciousness; they manifest as the success of the body and consciousness in taking an object; and they have the body and consciousness as their proximate cause. They should be understood as being the opposites of the remaining hindrances (nīvaraṇa) which cause the body and consciousness to be unwieldy. They should be understood as bringing about faith in objects worthy of faith, and as bringing about the state of being capable of application in beneficial actions, like purified gold.
175:
Proficiency of the body is kāya-pāguññatā. Proficiency of the mind is citta-pāguññatā. These have the characteristic of the healthiness (non-sickness) of the body and mind. Their function is to crush the sickness of the body and mind. They are manifested as the state of being faultless. They have the body and mind as their proximate cause. They should be understood as the opposites of defilements such as lack of faith (assaddhiya) and others which cause sickness of the body and mind.

Rectitude of the body is kāya-ujukatā. Rectitude of the mind is citta-ujukatā. These have the characteristic of the uprightness of the body and mind. Their function is to crush the crookedness of the body and mind. They are manifested as non-crookedness. They have the body and mind as their proximate cause. They should be understood as the opposites of defilements such as deceit (māyā) and hypocrisy (sāṭheyya) which cause crookedness of the body and mind.

It is called mindfulness (sati) because it remembers. It is called clear comprehension (sampajañña) because it knows well in various ways; it means knowing thoroughly in all aspects. The divisions of clear comprehension should be understood through these four: clear comprehension of purpose (sātthaka-sampajañña), clear comprehension of suitability (sappāya-sampajañña), clear comprehension of the resort (gocara-sampajañña), and clear comprehension of non-delusion (asammoha-sampajañña). Their characteristics and so forth should be understood in the same way as mentioned under the faculty of mindfulness (satindriya) and the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya). Thus, these two dhammas already mentioned below are taken again in this place by way of their helpfulness.

It is called tranquillity (samatha) because it quiets opposing states such as sensual desire (kāmacchanda). It is called insight (vipassanā) because it sees dhammas in various ways by way of impermanence (anicca) and so forth. In essence, this is wisdom (paññā). The characteristics and so forth of these two dhammas have also been mentioned below. Here, however, they are taken by way of being yoked together (yuganaddha).

It is called exertion (paggaha) because it upholds the co-nascent dhammas. It is called non-distraction (avikkhepa) because it is the opposite of the distraction known as restlessness (uddhacca). The characteristics and so forth of these dhammas have also been mentioned below. Here, however, it should be understood that these two are taken for the purpose of joining energy (vīriya) and concentration (samādhi).

## Explanation of the "Or Whatever Other" (Yevāpanaka) Dhammas

In the sentence, "Or whatever other immaterial dhammas arise dependently at that time, these dhammas are wholesome," it is not only these fifty-plus dhammas shown merely in the order of terms such as "contact arises... non-distraction arises" that are wholesome. In fact, at whatever time the first sense-sphere great consciousness (mahācitta) arises—which is accompanied by three roots, accompanied by joy, and is unprompted (asaṅkhārika)—at that time, there are also other dhammas that exist, occurring in association with those very factors such as contact (phassa).
176:
All these states, which arise depending on their respective suitable causes, and which are called mental states (nāma) because they lack the nature of being deformed, and which are clearly present by their own nature, are also wholesome states (kusala).

Having thus shown the fifty-six states mentioned in the Pali text by way of the constituents of consciousness (cittaṅga) through this sequence of words, the Buddha, the King of Dhamma, also shows nine other states by way of the 'yevāpanaka' (or whatever else) clause. In various Sutta passages, these nine states are found: 'desire-to-act (chanda), decision (adhimokkha), attention (manasikāra), equanimity (tatramajjhattatā), compassion (karuṇā), appreciative joy (muditā), abstention from bodily misconduct (kāya-duccarita-virati), abstention from verbal misconduct (vacī-duccarita-virati), and abstention from wrong livelihood (micchājīva-virati).’ In this great wholesome consciousness (mahākusala citta) as well, there is the wholesome desire-to-act (dhammacchanda) characterized by the wish to perform; however, it is not directly mentioned in the Pali text by way of the constituents of consciousness. That desire-to-act is included here by way of the 'yevāpanaka' clause.

Decision exists; attention exists; equanimity exists. Preliminary loving-kindness (parikamma-mettā) exists; when non-hatred (adosa) is taken, it is already included. Preliminary compassion (parikamma-karuṇā) exists; preliminary appreciative joy (parikamma-muditā) exists. Preliminary equanimity (parikamma-upekkhā) exists; that equanimity is also already included when tatramajjhattatā is taken. Right speech (sammā-vācā) exists; right action (sammā-kammanta) exists; right livelihood (sammā-ājīva) exists. However, it is not mentioned in the Pali text by way of the constituents of consciousness. That right livelihood is also included here by way of the 'yevāpanaka' clause.

Among these nine states, only these four—desire-to-act, decision, attention, and equanimity—are obtained at the same moment; the remaining five are obtained at different times. When one abandons wrong speech with this consciousness and fulfills right speech by way of abstention (virati), then these five—the four starting with desire-to-act and right speech—are obtained at the same moment. When one abandons wrong action and fulfills right action by way of abstention... (similarly) when one abandons wrong livelihood and fulfills right livelihood by way of abstention... when one performs the preliminary work (parikamma) for compassion... when one performs the preliminary work for appreciative joy, then these five—the four starting with desire-to-act and preliminary appreciative joy—are obtained at the same moment. Apart from these instances of fulfilling right speech etc., for one who gives gifts, observes morality, or exerts effort in meditation, only the four invariable constituents (starting with desire-to-act) are obtained.

Thus, among the nine 'yevāpanaka' states, 'desire-to-act' (chanda) is a synonym for the wish to perform (kattukamyatā). Therefore, that desire-to-act has the characteristic of the wish to perform, the function (rasa) of searching for an object, and the manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna) of being in need of an object. That very object is its...
177:
...proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna). This desire-to-act should be understood as being like the stretching out of the mind's hand to grasp an object.

Decision in the object is 'adhimokkha'. It has the characteristic of deciding (sanniṭṭhāna), the function of not wavering (asansappana), and the manifestation of conviction (nicchaya). It has the state to be decided as its proximate cause. It should be understood as being like a boundary pillar (indakhīla) firmly fixed in the object without wavering.

Making in the mind is 'manasikāra'. It is also called manasikāra because it makes the mind (vīthi-citta) different from the preceding life-continuum (bhavaṅga). This manasikāra is of three types: object-directing manasikāra, process-directing manasikāra, and impulsion-directing manasikāra. Among these three, object-directing manasikāra has the characteristic of driving (sāraṇa) the associated states toward the object. It has the function of joining (sampayojana) the associated states with the object. It is manifested as being face-to-face with the object (arammaṇābhimukhabhāva). It is included in the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha). Because it directs the object, it should be understood as being like a charioteer driving the associated states. Process-directing manasikāra is a synonym for the five-door adverting consciousness (pañcadvārāvajjana). Impulsion-directing manasikāra is a synonym for the mind-door adverting consciousness (manodvārāvajjana). These two are not intended here.

Neutrality toward those states is 'tatramajjhattatā'. It has the characteristic of keeping consciousness and mental factors in balance (samavāhita). It has the function of preventing deficiency and excess (ūnādhikanivāraṇa), or the function of cutting off partiality (pakkhapātupacchedana). It is manifested as neutrality (majjhattabhāva). It should be understood as being like a charioteer looking on at well-trained horses that are running evenly.

'Compassion (karuṇā) and appreciative joy (muditā)' will be clearly shown in the exposition of the Divine Abodes (Brahmavihāra-niddesa). The only difference is that the states mentioned there are fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) states that have reached absorption (appanā), whereas here they are sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) states.

Abstaining from bodily misconduct is 'abstention from bodily misconduct' (kāya-duccarita-virati). The same method applies to the remaining two terms (abstention from verbal misconduct and abstention from mental misconduct). In terms of characteristics etc., all three of these abstentions have the characteristic of non-transgression (avītikkama) of the objects of bodily misconduct etc. This means they have the characteristic of not crushing (amaddana). They have the function of shrinking (saṅkocana) from the objects of bodily misconduct etc. They are manifested as non-action (akiriya). They have virtues such as faith (saddhā), shame (hiri), fear of wrongdoing (ottappa), and fewness of wishes (appicchatā) as their proximate cause. They should be understood as the mind's turning away from performing evil.

Thus, the fifty-six states starting with contact (phassa) and the nine states mentioned by way of the 'yevāpanaka' clause total sixty-five states in this exposition of states (dhammuddessavāra). Among those states, sometimes sixty-one occur in a single moment, and sometimes sixty-two. This variation is due to the fulfillment of right speech and so on.
178:
In the occurrence, sixty-one dhammas arise in five places. In one place distinct from those five places, sixty-two dhammas arise.

Excluding the yevāpanaka (miscellaneous) dhammas, if taken according to the Pāḷi text as taught, there are only fifty-six dhammas. Among those fifty-six dhammas, by taking only one of each identical dhamma, there are thirty dhammas in total: the group of five starting with contact (phassa-pañcaka), initial application (vitakka), sustained application (vicāra), zest (pīti), one-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā), the five faculties (indriya), the two powers (bala) of moral shame (hiri) and moral dread (ottappa), the two roots (mūla) of non-greed (alobha) and non-hatred (adosa), and the twelve dhammas such as tranquility of body (kāyapassaddhi) and tranquility of mind (cittapassaddhi).

Among those thirty dhammas, eighteen dhammas are non-differentiated (by various names), and twelve dhammas are differentiated. What are the eighteen non-differentiated ones? They are: contact (phassa), perception (saññā), volition (cetanā), sustained application (vicāra), zest (pīti), life-faculty (jīvitindriya), and the twelve dhammas such as tranquility of body (kāyapassaddhi); these eighteen are non-differentiated. Feeling (vedanā), mind (citta), initial application (vitakka), one-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā), faith-faculty (saddhindriya), energy-faculty (vīriyindriya), mindfulness-faculty (satindriya), wisdom-faculty (paññindriya), the power of moral shame (hiri-bala), the power of moral dread (ottappa-bala), non-greed (alobha), and non-hatred (adosa)—these twelve dhammas are differentiated. Among these, seven dhammas are differentiated in two places, one dhamma in three places, two dhammas in four places, one dhamma in six places, and one dhamma in seven places.

How are they differentiated? Mind (citta), initial application (vitakka), faith (saddhā), moral shame (hiri), moral dread (ottappa), non-greed (alobha), and non-hatred (adosa)—these seven dhammas are differentiated in two places. Among these seven dhammas, mind (citta), when it first reaches the group of five starting with contact, is called 'mind' (citta); when it reaches the faculties, it is called 'mind-faculty' (manindriya). Initial application (vitakka), when it reaches the factors of absorption (jhānaṅga), is called 'initial application' (vitakka); when it reaches the path-factors (maggaṅga), it is called 'right intention' (sammā-saṅkappa). Faith (saddhā), when it reaches the faculties, is called 'faith-faculty' (saddhindriya); when it reaches the powers, it is called 'faith-power' (saddhā-bala). Moral shame (hiri), when it reaches the powers, it is called 'power of moral shame' (hiri-bala); when it reaches the dyad of world-protectors (lokapāla-duka), it is called 'moral shame' (hiri). The same method applies to moral dread (ottappa). Non-greed (alobha), when it reaches the roots, is called 'non-greed' (alobha); when it reaches the course of action (kammapatha), it is called 'non-covetousness' (anabhijjhā). Non-hatred (adosa), when it reaches the roots, is called 'non-hatred' (adosa); when it reaches the course of action, it is called 'non-ill will' (abyāpāda). These seven dhammas are differentiated in two places.

Feeling (vedanā), when it reaches the group of five starting with contact, is called 'feeling' (vedanā); when it reaches the factors of absorption, it is called 'happiness' (sukha); when it reaches the faculties, it is called 'joy-faculty' (somanassindriya). Thus, one dhamma is differentiated in three places.

Energy (vīriya), when it reaches the faculties, is called 'energy-faculty' (vīriyindriya); when it reaches the path-factors, it is called 'right effort' (sammā-vāyāma); when it reaches the powers, it is called 'energy-power' (vīriya-bala); when it reaches the piṭṭhiduka...
179:
Energy (vīriya), when it reaches the piṭṭhiduka, is called 'exertion' (paggaha). Mindfulness (sati), when it reaches the faculties, is called 'mindfulness-faculty' (satindriya); when it reaches the path-factors, it is called 'right mindfulness' (sammā-sati); when it reaches the powers, it is called 'mindfulness-power' (sati-bala); when it reaches the piṭṭhiduka, it is called 'mindfulness' (sati). Thus, these two dhammas (energy and mindfulness) are differentiated in four places.

Concentration (samādhi), when it reaches the factors of absorption (jhānaṅga), is called 'one-pointedness of mind' (cittekaggatā); when it reaches the faculties, it is called 'concentration-faculty' (samādhindriya); when it reaches the path-factors, it is called 'right concentration' (sammā-samādhi); when it reaches the powers, it is called 'concentration-power' (samādhi-bala); when it reaches the piṭṭhiduka, it is called 'tranquility' (samatha) and 'non-distraction' (avikkhepa). Thus, this one dhamma (concentration) is differentiated in six places.

Wisdom (paññā), when it reaches the faculties, is called 'wisdom-faculty' (paññindriya); when it reaches the path-factors, it is called 'right view' (sammā-diṭṭhi); when it reaches the powers, it is called 'wisdom-power' (paññā-bala); when it reaches the roots, it is called 'non-delusion' (amoha); when it reaches the course of action (kammapatha), it is called 'right view' (sammā-diṭṭhi); when it reaches the piṭṭhiduka, it is called 'clear comprehension' (sampajañña) and 'insight' (vipassanā). Thus, this one dhamma (wisdom) is differentiated in seven places.

If someone should say: 'There is nothing new here; it is merely taking what was already taken below and filling in the terms in various places. This disconnected discourse is like goods brought by thieves in a disorganized manner, or like grass trampled on a path where a herd of cattle has passed; it was spoken without knowing.' Such a person should be restrained, saying, 'Do not say so,' and should be told: 'In the teaching of the Buddhas, there is no such thing as being disconnected; it is indeed connected. There is also nothing spoken without knowing; everything is spoken only after knowing. For the Perfectly Enlightened One knows the function (kicca) of each of those dhammas. Knowing that, and presenting the differentiation by the power of function: knowing that eighteen dhammas have one function each, He presented the differentiation in one place each. Knowing that seven dhammas have two functions each, He presented the differentiation in two places each. Knowing that feeling has three functions, He presented the differentiation in three places. Knowing that energy and mindfulness have four functions each, He presented the differentiation in four places each. Knowing that concentration has six functions, He presented the differentiation in six places. Knowing that wisdom has seven functions, He presented the differentiation in seven places.'

In this matter, there is this analogy: It is said that a wise king, having gone into seclusion, thought thus: 'This property belonging to the royal family should not be consumed haphazardly, but in accordance with one's skill...'
180:
"I will increase the wages," he thought. That king gathered all the craftsmen and said, "Call those who know one craft each." When called thus, seventeen people stood up. He had a portion given to each of them and dismissed them. When he said, "Let those who know two crafts each come," seven people came. He had two portions given to each of them. When he said, "Let those who know three crafts come," only one person came. He had three portions given to him. When he said, "Let those who know four crafts come," two people came. He had four portions given to each of them. When he said, "Let those who know five crafts come," not even one person came. When he said, "Let those who know six crafts come," only one person came. He had six portions given to him. When he said, "Let those who know seven crafts come," only one person came. He had seven portions given to him.

In that analogy, the Peerless King of Dhamma is like the wise king. The states (dhammas) that arise by way of the mind and mental factors are like the craftsmen. The classification of those various states by way of their functions is like the increasing of wages according to the craft.

All these states form seventeen groups by way of: the group of five starting with contact (phassa-pañcaka), the factors of jhāna (jhānaṅga), the faculties (indriya), the path factors (magga), the powers (bala), the roots (mūla), the courses of action (kammapatha), the guardians of the world (lokapāla), tranquility (passaddhi), lightness (lahutā), malleability (mudutā), readiness (kammaññatā), proficiency (pāguññatā), rectitude (ujukatā), mindfulness and clear comprehension (sati-sampajañña), calm and insight (samatha-vipassanā), and exertion and non-distraction (paggāha-avikkhepa).

## The Explanation of the Summary of States is finished.

## The Explanation of the Exposition of Wholesome States of the Sense Sphere

Now, in order to analyze and show those fifty-six terms that have entered the Pali text in that Summary of States, the Exposition Section is begun with the method starting with: "What is contact on that occasion?"

In that context, the meaning of the question is: At the time when a great consciousness of the sense sphere that is wholesome, accompanied by joy, associated with three roots, and unprompted arises, at that time...
181:
In the statement "At that time contact occurs," the meaning in all questions should be understood by this method: "What is that contact?"

"That contact which occurs at that time" means the contact that has arisen by way of touching at that time. This term "contact" (phassa) is called a nature-term (sabhāva-pada) because it points out the nature of contact. Phusanā means the mode of touching. Samphusanā is the same mode of touching, but the word is expanded by a prefix. Samphusitatta means the state of having touched. Here, the word-connection (padayojanā) is: that contact which occurs by way of touching at that time, that phusanā which occurs at that time, that samphusanā which occurs at that time, that samphusitatta which occurs at that time. Alternatively: that contact which occurs by way of touching at that time is also called phusanā, samphusanā, and samphusitatta by other synonyms; this is what is meant by "At that time contact occurs." In the expositions of feeling (vedanā) and so on, the word-connection should be understood in this same way.

Here, the general decision on classification (vibhatti) regarding all terms is as follows: When the Blessed One was analyzing and showing the first wholesome great consciousness of the sense sphere, He established these fifty-plus terms by way of the summary (mātikā) and then took each term one by one and subjected them to classification. When these terms undergo classification, they do so through three reasons; when they become distinct, they do so through four reasons. Here, the "further illustration" (apara-dīpanā) reaches two places. How? These terms undergo classification through these three reasons: by way of phrasing (byañjana), by way of prefix (upasagga), and by way of meaning (attha). Among those three, the classification by way of phrasing should be understood as: "anger (kodha), being angry (kujjhanā), the state of being angry (kujjhitatta)"; "hatred (dosa), hating (dussanā), the state of hating (dussitatta)." Here, the single state of anger undergoes classification in this way by way of phrasing. The classification by way of prefix should be understood as: "cāra, vicāra, anuvicāra, upavicāra." The classification by way of meaning should be understood as: "wisdom (paṇḍicca), skill (kosalla), proficiency (nepuñña), erudition (vebhabyā), reflection (cintā), investigation (upaparikkhā)." Among those terms, in the exposition of the term contact (phassa), all three of these classifications are obtained. "Contact (phassa), touching (phusanā)" is the classification by way of phrasing. "Samphusanā" is by way of prefix. "Samphusitatta" is by way of meaning. In this way, the classification in the expositions of all terms should be understood.

Even when they are distinct, they become distinct through these four reasons: distinction of name (nāma-nānatta), distinction of characteristic (lakkhaṇa-nānatta), distinction of function (kicca-nānatta), and distinction of opposition (paṭikkhepa-nānatta). Among those four, "What is ill-will (byāpāda) on that occasion? That which..."
182:
At that time, hatred has the nature of destroying (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 419). In this sentence, both what are called ill-will (byāpāda) and hatred (dosa) are just anger (kodha); they differ only in name. Thus, diversity should be understood by 'diversity of names' (nāma-nānatta).

In the sense of a group, the five aggregates are also just a single aggregate. However, among these five aggregates, matter has the characteristic of being deformed, feeling has the characteristic of experiencing, perception has the characteristic of perceiving, volition has the characteristic of urging, and consciousness has the characteristic of cognizing. Thus, the five aggregates exist by this 'diversity of characteristics' (lakkhaṇa-nānatta). In this way, diversity should be understood by 'diversity of characteristics'.

The four right efforts (sammappadhāna) are also— "Here, a monk... for the non-arising of evil, unwholesome states that have not yet arisen... upholds the mind and strives" (Vibhaṅga 390, Dīgha Nikāya 2.402). Thus, the single factor of energy (vīriya) appears in four instances due to 'diversity of functions' (kicca-nānatta). In this way, diversity should be understood by 'diversity of functions'.

The four 'un-dhamma' (asaddhamma) are also— prioritizing anger is not prioritizing the true Dhamma, prioritizing the disparaging of others' virtues is not prioritizing the true Dhamma, prioritizing gain is not prioritizing the true Dhamma, and prioritizing honor and offerings is not prioritizing the true Dhamma. In such passages (Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.44), diversity should be understood by 'diversity of rejection' (paṭikkhepa-nānatta).

These four types of diversity are not found in contact (phassa) alone; they are found in all states, such as the group of five starting with contact (phassa-pañcamaka). Indeed, the name of contact is 'phassa'... the name of mind is 'citta'. Contact has the characteristic of touching, feeling has the characteristic of experiencing, perception has the characteristic of perceiving, volition has the characteristic of urging, and consciousness has the characteristic of cognizing. Likewise, contact has the function of touching, feeling has the function of experiencing, perception has the function of perceiving, volition has the function of urging, and consciousness has the function of cognizing. In this way, diversity should be understood by 'diversity of functions'.

'Diversity of rejection' (paṭikkhepa-nānatta) does not exist in the group of five starting with contact. However, in the explanation of non-greed (alobha) and so on, it is found in the manner of "non-greed is the state of not being greedy, the fact of not being greedy," and so forth. In this way, diversity should be understood by 'diversity of rejection'. Thus, the fourfold diversity should be understood according to what is obtainable in the explanation of all terms.

Furthermore, 'further elucidation' (apara-dīpanā) reaches two points: either the elucidation of the word's meaning (padatthuti) or reinforcement (daḷhīkamma). Indeed, like one who presses with the tip of a staff, if one says 'phassa' only once, that word is not yet called blossomed, adorned, or beautified. By the power of syllables repeatedly...
183:
When 'phassa, phusanā, samphusanā, samphusitatta' are taught by the power of prefixes and meanings, that word 'phassa' is said to be blossomed, adorned, and beautified. For example, if one were to bathe a young prince, dress him in pleasing clothes, adorn him with flowers, apply collyrium to his eyes, and then place only a single dot of red arsenic (manosilā) on his forehead, that would not yet be called an ornamental forehead mark (citta-tilaka). Only when many dots are made, surrounded by various colors, is it called an ornamental forehead mark. The completeness of this analogy should be understood. This is called 'elucidation of the word's meaning' (padatthuti).

Repeatedly speaking by the power of syllables, prefixes, and meanings is called 'reinforcement' (daḷhīkamma). For example, if one says 'Friend' or 'Sir' or 'Ogre' or 'Snake' only once, it is not called reinforcement. But if one says repeatedly, 'Friend, friend', 'Sir, sir', 'Ogre, ogre', 'Snake, snake', then it is called reinforcement. In the same way, if one says 'phassa' only once, like pressing once with the tip of a staff, that word is not called reinforcement. Only when one says 'phassa, phusanā, samphusanā, samphusitatta' repeatedly by the power of syllables, prefixes, and meanings is it called 'reinforcement'. Thus, 'further elucidation' (apara-dīpanā) reaches two points. By the power of this further elucidation, the meaning should be understood in all explanations of terms (pdaniddesa) where it is applicable.

'Ayaṃ tasmiṃ samaye phasso hoti' means that at whatever time the first great wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere (paṭhama kāmāvacara mahākusala citta) arises, at that time this state called contact (phassa) exists. This is the commentary (vaṇṇanā) on the explanation of the term 'contact'. Hereafter, in the explanations of terms such as feeling (vedanā), I will comment only on the distinctive points. The remaining points should be understood in the same manner as stated here for contact.

In the sentence 'yaṃ tasmiṃ samaye', although it begins with 'katamā tasmiṃ samaye vedanā hoti', it is taught as 'yaṃ' by the power of the term 'sāta' (pleasant). In the phrase 'tajjā-manoviññāṇadhātu-samphassajaṃ', 'tajjā' refers to the mind-consciousness element that is suitable and appropriate for that pleasant happiness. This word 'tajjā' has the meaning of being appropriate (anucchavika). Therefore, it is taught: 'tajjāṃ tassāruppaṃ kathaṃ manteti'. Alternatively, it is called 'tajjā' because it is born from those objects such as visible forms, which are the conditions for this happiness. Mind-consciousness itself is called an 'element' (dhātu) because of its nature of non-self. It is called 'born of contact' (samphassaja) because it is born from contact or born in contact. It is called a 'mental factor' (cetasika) because it depends on the mind.
184:
It is called 'sāta' (pleasant) because of its sweet nature. The meaning is this: when that sense-sphere great wholesome consciousness (mahākusala citta) arises, there occurs a pleasant mental feeling (sāta vedanā) born of contact with the mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu) that is appropriate to that pleasure, according to the sense already described. This pleasant feeling is what is meant by 'feeling' (vedanā) at that time. In this same way, the connection should be understood with all the remaining terms.

Now, in the terms 'cetasikaṃ sukhaṃ' (mental pleasure) and so on, by the word 'cetasika' (mental), bodily pleasure (kāyika sukha) is excluded; by the word 'sukha' (pleasure), mental pain (cetasika dukkha) is excluded. 'Cetosamphassaja' means born of contact associated with the mind. 'Sātaṃ sukhaṃ vedayitaṃ' means a pleasant experience, not an unpleasant experience; a happy experience, not a painful experience. The three subsequent terms are stated by way of the feminine gender: 'sātā vedanā' (pleasant feeling), not unpleasant; 'sukhā vedanā' (happy feeling), not painful. This alone is the meaning in this context.

In the exposition of perception (saññā-niddesa), 'tajjamano-viññāṇadhātu-samphassajā' means born of contact with the mind-consciousness element appropriate to that wholesome perception. 'Saññā' is the name by way of its nature. 'Sañjānanā' is the mode of perceiving. 'Sañjānitatta' is the state of having perceived. In the exposition of volition (cetanā-niddesa) also, the method should be understood in this same way.

In the exposition of consciousness (citta-niddesa), it is called 'citta' because of its variegated (vicitta) nature. It is called 'mano' because it knows (measures) the object. 'Mānasa' is just the mind. For in the passage, "The snare of passion that wanders in the sky, which wanders in the mind (mānasa)," the associated states are called 'mānasa'.

"O Blessed One, why should your disciple,
Delighting in the Dispensation, well-known among people,
A learner (sekha) who has not yet reached the goal (mānasa),
Pass away?"

In this passage, Arahatship (arahattaphala) is called 'mānasa'. However, in this exposition of consciousness, 'mānasa' is just the mind. Indeed, this term is expanded by way of its literal syllables.

'Hadaya' is the mind. In the passage, "I will either scatter your mind (citta) or split your heart (hadaya)," 'hadaya' refers to the physical chest. In the passage, "I think he goes knowing another's heart (hadaya) with his own heart," 'hadaya' refers to the mind. In the passage, "Kidneys, heart (hadaya)," 'hadaya' refers to the heart-base (hadayavatthu).
185:
In this exposition of consciousness, however, the mind itself is called 'hadaya' (heart) because of its internal nature. That same mind is called 'paṇḍara' (bright/white) because of its purity. This term 'paṇḍara' is said with reference to the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). As it was said by the Blessed One: "Luminous (pabhassara) is this mind, O bhikkhus, but it is defiled by adventitious defilements." Just as a river flowing from the Ganges is called the Ganges, and a river flowing from the Godhāvarī is called the Godhāvarī, even an unwholesome mind is called 'paṇḍara' simply because it originates from that bhavaṅga.

In the phrase 'mano manāyatanaṃ', the mention of 'mano' is for the purpose of showing that the mind itself is the base (āyatana). By this, it is shown: "This is not called 'manāyatana' because it is a base for the mind, like a temple is a base for a deity (devāyatana); rather, the mind itself is the base, thus it is 'manāyatana'." In that context, 'āyatana' should be understood by way of the meanings: dwelling place, mine (source), meeting place, place of birth, and cause. For in the world, in such terms as 'issarāyatana' (abode of Ishvara) or 'vāsudevāyatana' (abode of Vasudeva), a dwelling place is called 'āyatana'. In terms like 'suvaṇṇāyatana' (gold mine) or 'rajatāyatana' (silver mine), a mine is called 'āyatana'. In the Dispensation, however, in such passages as "Birds resort to a pleasant āyatana (meeting place)," it means a meeting place. In "Dakkhināpatha is the āyatana (birthplace) of cattle," it means the place of birth. In "When the cause (āyatana) exists, one attains the state of a witness in this or that matter," it means cause. In this exposition of consciousness, all three meanings—place of birth, meeting place, and cause—are appropriate.

Since states such as contact (phassa) arise in this mind, it is an 'āyatana' in the sense of a place of birth. Since external objects like forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles meet in this mind as objects, it is an 'āyatana' in the sense of a meeting place. Since it serves as a cause for states like contact by way of conditions such as the co-nascence condition (sahajāta-paccaya), it should be understood as an 'āyatana' in the sense of a cause. The term 'manindriya' (mind-faculty) has the meaning already described.

It is called 'viññāṇa' because it cognizes (vijānāti). Consciousness itself is an aggregate (khandha), thus it is 'viññāṇakkhandha' (consciousness-aggregate). The meaning of that aggregate should be understood by way of a mass (group) and so on. In the passage, "It is reckoned only as a great mass of water (mahā-udakakkhandha)," 'khandha' is used in the sense of a mass. In "the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha), the aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha)," it is used in the sense of quality (virtue). In "The Blessed One saw a great log of wood (dārukkhandha)," it is used in the sense of a mere conventional designation. In this exposition of consciousness, however, 'khandha' is used by way of common usage (ruḷhī). Indeed, in the sense of a mass...
186:
A portion of the aggregate of consciousness is a single consciousness. Therefore, just as it is said of one who cuts a portion of a tree that "he cuts the tree," so too, a single consciousness, which is a portion of the aggregate of consciousness, is metaphorically called the "aggregate of consciousness" (viññāṇakkhandha).

The "appropriate mind-consciousness element" (tajjāmanoviññāṇadhātu) refers to the mind-consciousness element that is suitable for those states such as contact (phassa). Indeed, in this term, the single mind is referred to by three names: as "mind" (mano) because of its sense of measuring; as "consciousness" (viññāṇa) because of its sense of specifically knowing; and as "element" (dhātu) because of its sense of being a natural phenomenon or its sense of non-being (non-self). Thus, in this group of five states beginning with contact (phassapañcamaka), first, contact is merely contact and not "born of contact with the appropriate mind-consciousness element"; and the mind is merely the "appropriate mind-consciousness element." Therefore, in these two terms, the designation "born of contact with the appropriate mind-consciousness element" (tajjāmanoviññāṇadhātusamphassaja) is not applied. Although it could be obtained in terms such as "applied thought" (vitakka) and others, it is not extracted here because it is disconnected.

The Blessed One performed a difficult task in extracting the designations by distinguishing and analyzing each of these five states beginning with contact. If various waters or various oils were placed in a single vessel and stirred all day, it might be possible to know the difference by seeing, smelling, or tasting the variation in color, scent, and flavor. Even if it were possible, that task is said to be difficult. However, the Fully Enlightened One performed an extremely difficult task in extracting the designations by distinguishing and analyzing each of these immaterial mental states—mind and mental factors—that arise in a single object. Therefore, the Venerable Elder Nāgasena said:

"Great King, the Blessed One has performed a difficult task."
"Venerable Nāgasena, what difficult task has the Blessed One performed?"
"Great King, the Blessed One has performed a difficult task in declaring the distinguishing and defining of these immaterial mental states—mind and mental factors—that arise in a single object, saying: 'This is contact, this is feeling, this is perception, this is volition, this is mind.'"
"Venerable sir, please give an analogy."
"Great King, suppose a man were to go down into the ocean by boat, take some water in his cupped hands, and taste it with his tongue. Great King, would that man, after tasting it, know: 'This is water from the Gaṅgā, this is water from the Yamunā, this is water from the Aciravatī, this is water from the Sarabhū, this is water from the Mahī'?"
"Venerable sir, it would be very difficult to know."
"Even more..."
187:
"...more difficult, Great King, is the task performed by the Blessed One in defining these immaterial mental states—mind and mental factors... as 'this is mind'" (Mi. Pa. 2.7.16).

In the explanation of applied thought (vitakka), it is called takka in the sense of pulling (the object to the mind). The occurrence of that applied thought should be understood in the sense of pulling the object thus: "How much does he think? He thinks of a pot, he thinks of a cart, he thinks for a league (yojana), he thinks for half a league." This is the natural term for takka. It is called vitakka in the sense of pulling various objects to the mind; this is the name for a stronger takka. It is called saṅkappa (intention) in the sense of thinking well. It is called appanā (absorption/fixing) because it fixes the one-pointed mind on the object. The second term (vyappanā) is an expansion by means of a prefix; or else, a stronger appanā is called vyappanā. It is called "directing of the mind" (cetaso abhiniropanā) because it directs and establishes the mind on the object. It is called "right intention" (sammāsaṅkappa) because it is a praised thought that has reached the state of wholesomeness due to its correctness and its nature of leading to liberation.

In the explanation of sustained thought (vicāra), it is called cāra in the sense of roaming and examining the object. This is the natural term for vicāra. It is called vicāra in the sense of roaming all around the object. It is called anuvicāra in the sense of roaming along (the object) repeatedly. It is called upavicāra in the sense of roaming close to (the object). Or else, these terms are expanded by means of prefixes. It is called "connection of the mind" (cittassa anusandhānatā) because of repeatedly binding the mind to the object, like binding an arrow to a bowstring. It is called anupekkhanatā because it remains as if repeatedly observing the object. Or else, it is called anupekkhanatā because of repeatedly observing by way of roaming (on the object).

In the explanation of rapture (pīti), pīti is the natural term. The state of one who is glad is pāmojja (gladness). The mode of intense rejoicing is āmodanā. The mode of rejoicing in various ways is pamodanā. Or, just as the mixing together of medicines, oils, or hot and cold water is called modanā, so too, this rapture is modanā because it unifies the associated states. It is called āmodanā and pamodanā when adorned with prefixes. It is called hāsa (mirth) because it causes cheerfulness. It is called pahāsa because it causes cheerfulness in various ways. These are designations for the modes of being cheerful and very cheerful. Vitta is a name for wealth, but this rapture is called vitti (joy) because it resembles wealth as a cause for happiness (somanassa). For just as a wealthy person experiences happiness depending on wealth, so too, one with rapture experiences happiness depending on rapture; therefore, it is called vitti. This is a name for rapture established in the nature of satisfaction. A person with rapture is called udagga (uplifted) because his body and mind are uplifted and elevated.
188:
The state of a person with an elated body and mind is called odagya (elation). The state of one's own mind is called attamanatā (self-mindedness/gladness). Indeed, the mind of one who is not tranquil (or one who is angry) is not truly one's own mind, because it is the proximate cause of suffering. But the mind of one who is tranquil (or one whose anger has subsided) is truly one's own mind, because it is the proximate cause of happiness. Thus, the state of one's own mind is called attamanatā or sakamanatā (state of one's own mind). It means the state of one who possesses their own mind. Since this attamanatā is not the state of anyone else's mind but is a mental factor (cetasika) that is a property of the mind itself, it is called "the attamanatā of the mind."

## In the Exposition on One-pointedness (Ekaggatā-niddesa)

It is called ṭhiti (steadfastness) because it stands in the object in an unshakeable manner. The two subsequent terms are expanded by the power of the prefixes saṃ and ava. Alternatively, it is called saṇṭhiti (well-steadfastness) because it stands by collecting the associated states (sampayutta-dhamma) together in the object. It is called avaṭṭhiti (stability) because it stands by plunging into the object. Indeed, on the wholesome side, four states—faith (saddhā), mindfulness (sati), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (paññā)—plunge into the object. Because these four states plunge into the object, faith is called okappanā (plunging in), mindfulness is called apilāpanatā (non-drifting), concentration is called avaṭṭhiti (stability), and wisdom is called pariyogāhanā (thorough immersion). On the unwholesome side, however, three states—craving (taṇhā), view (diṭṭhi), and ignorance (avijjā)—plunge into the object. Because these three states plunge into the object, they are called ogha (floods). In this unwholesome side, even if one-pointedness of mind (cittass'ekaggatā) exists, it is not powerful. For example, just as in a dusty place, if water is sprinkled and it is well-leveled, the dust settles only for a short time and rises again as usual when it dries, so too, one-pointedness of mind on the unwholesome side is not powerful. But if, in that same place, water is poured from jars, the ground is dug with a hoe, beaten, kneaded, and plastered so that a reflection appears as if in a mirror, it remains clear even after a hundred years as if it were just done; in the same way, one-pointedness of mind on the wholesome side is powerful.

It is called avisāra (non-distraction) because it is the opposite of visāra (distraction) which occurs by the power of restlessness (uddhacca) and doubt (vicikicchā). The mind that runs away by the power of restlessness and doubt is called vikkhipa (wavering). This concentration is called avikkhepa (non-wavering) because it is not that kind of wavering. By the power of restlessness and doubt, the mind is called visāhaṭa (distracted); it is carried here and there. This concentration is called avisāhaṭamānasatā (the state of a non-distracted mind) because it is the state of a mind that is not so distracted.

Tranquillity (samatha) is of three kinds: tranquillity of mind (citta-samatha), settlement of legal issues (adhikaraṇa-samatha), and the stilling of all formations (sabbasaṅkhāra-samatha). Among these, one-pointedness of mind in the eight attainments is...
189:
Tranquillity of mind (citta-samatha) means: based on that one-pointedness of mind, the movement and agitation of the mind is stilled and quieted; therefore, it is called citta-samatha. The seven kinds of settling, such as 'settling in the presence' (sammukhā-vinaya), are called settling of legal issues (adhikaraṇa-samatha). Based on that samatha, those various legal issues are stilled and quieted; therefore, it is called adhikaraṇa-samatha. Because all formations are stilled and quieted based on Nibbāna, that Nibbāna is called the tranquillity of all formations (sabba-saṅkhāra-samatha). In this sense, citta-samatha is intended here. It is the faculty of concentration (samādhindriya) because it exercises lordship in the characteristic of concentration. It is the power of concentration (samādhibala) because it does not waver due to restlessness (uddhacca). Right concentration (sammā-samādhi) is concentration that is true, concentration that leads out of saṃsāra, and concentration that is wholesome.

In the explanation of the faculty of faith (saddhindriya-niddesa), faith (saddhā) is so called by way of believing in the virtues of the Buddha and others. Or, it is faith because it believes in or trusts the Jewels such as the Buddha. 'Believing' (saddahanā) is the manner of believing. It is 'placing confidence' (okappanā) because it enters into the virtues of the Buddha and others as if breaking through. By this faith, beings are extremely purified in the virtues of the Buddha and others, or it is 'supreme devotion' (abhippasāda) because it is itself extremely pure. Now, because the analysis of terms is carried out by taking the initial word when another method is started by way of compound terms such as 'saddhindriya'—this being the nature of the Abhidhamma—the word 'saddhā' is mentioned again. Or, this is not like the 'female faculty' (itthindriya) being the faculty of a woman. Rather, this is the faculty which is itself faith, thus 'saddhindriya'. The word 'saddhā' is also mentioned again to show this state of being in apposition (samānādhikaraṇa). In this way, the purpose of repeating the initial word in all explanations of terms should be understood. It is the faculty of faith (saddhindriya) because it exercises lordship in the characteristic of decision (adhimokkha). It is the power of faith (saddhābala) because it does not waver due to faithlessness (asaddhiya).

In the explanation of the faculty of energy (vīriyindriya-niddesa), the word 'mental' (cetasiko) is stated to show the mental nature of energy as a rule. For this energy is mentioned in such suttas as: "Monks, that which is bodily energy is the factor of enlightenment of energy; that which is mental energy is also the factor of enlightenment of energy" (Saṃyutta Nikāya, 5.233). Thus, although it is called 'bodily' because it arises in one performing walking meditation and so on, there is no such thing as 'bodily' in the sense of the body-consciousness; the word 'mental' is stated to show that it is indeed only mental. 'Initiative of energy' (vīriyārambho) is the initiative known as energy. By this, other kinds of initiative are excluded. For this word 'ārambha' appears in many senses, such as work, offense, action, energy, injury, and destruction.
190:
To clarify this meaning, it is said, "cetasiko" (mental). "Vīriyārambho" means the initiation that is called energy. By this term "vīriyārambha," other types of initiation (ārambha) apart from energy are excluded. Indeed, this word "ārambha" is used in many senses, such as kamma, offense, action, energy, harm, and destruction.

"Whatever suffering arises, it is all because of initiation (kamma); with the cessation of initiations (kamma), there is no arising of suffering" (Sutta Nipāta 749).

In this Pali passage, kamma is called "ārambha." In the passage, "He commits an offense (ārambhati) and feels remorse," it refers to an offense (āpatti). In the passage, "Great sacrifices with great initiations (ārambha) are not of great fruit," it refers to actions such as the setting up of sacrificial posts. In the passage, "Initiate (ārambhatha), go forth, apply yourselves to the Buddha's teaching," it refers to energy (vīriya). In the passage, "They kill (ārabhandi) living beings for the sake of the ascetic Gotama," it refers to harm (hiṃsā). In the passage, "He is one who abstains from the destruction (samārambha) of seeds and plants," it refers to destruction such as cutting and breaking.

Here, however, only energy is intended. Therefore, it is said, "Vīriyārambho means the initiation (ārambha) known as energy." It is called "ārambha" because of its nature of initiating energy. This is the term describing its inherent nature. It is called "nikkama" (departure) because of its nature of departing from laziness. It is called "parakkama" (advance) because of its nature of advancing to successive stages. It is called "uyyāma" (upward effort) because of its nature of striving upwards. It is called "vāyāma" (special effort) because of its nature of striving particularly. It is called "ussāha" (exertion) because of its nature of being enthusiastic. It is called "ussoḷhī" (intense exertion) because of its nature of striving beyond measure. It is called "thāma" (strength) because of its nature of being firm. It is called "dhiti" (fortitude) because it bears the mind and mental factors, or because it maintains the sequence of wholesome states by occurring without interruption.

Alternatively—this state is called "nikkama" for the sake of dispelling sensual desires; "parakkama" for the sake of cutting bonds; "uyyāma" for the sake of crossing the flood of saṃsāra; "vāyāma" in the sense of reaching the far shore of Nibbāna; "ussāha" in the sense of being a precursor; "ussoḷhī" in the sense of exceeding limits; "thāma" because of its nature of uprooting the door-bolt; and "dhiti" because of its nature of making one stay firm on the object.

When it arises in this way—"Let only skin, sinews, and bones remain"—it is called "asithilaparakkamatā" (unslackening effort) by virtue of unrelaxed exertion. It means firm effort, strong effort. Since this energy does not abandon the desire (chanda) in performing wholesome deeds, does not lay down the burden (dhura), does not discard it, and brings about an undaunted mind, it is called "anikkhittachandatā" (not abandoning desire) and "anikkhittadhuratā" (not laying down the burden). For example, in a place where water and mud are mixed, they say, "Take hold of the draft ox!"
191:
They say, "Take hold of the draft ox!" That ox, even by pressing the ground with its knees, carries the burden and does not let it fall to the ground. In the same way, energy upholds and supports the burden (or the wholesome task to be accomplished, the duty undertaken) in performing wholesome deeds. Therefore, it is called "dhurasamppaggāha" (upholding the burden). It is called "vīriyindriya" (faculty of energy) because it exercises predominance in the characteristic of upholding associated states (or the characteristic of being able to uphold the undertaken task). It is called "vīriyabala" (power of energy) because it is unshakable by laziness. It is called "sammāvāyāma" (right effort) because it is a wholesome exertion that truly leads out of the suffering of the round of rebirths.

In the description of the faculty of mindfulness (satindriya), it is called "sati" (mindfulness) by virtue of recollecting. This is the term for the inherent nature of mindfulness. It is called "anussati" (constant mindfulness) by virtue of repeated recollection. It is called "paṭissati" (confronting mindfulness) by virtue of recollecting as if going towards the object. Alternatively, this term is merely an expansion by virtue of the prefix (upasagga). The mode of recollecting is called "saraṇatā." However, since the name "saraṇatā" is also the name for the Three Refuges, the word "sati" is included again to exclude (distinguish) those Three Refuges. The meaning intended here is that the mode of recollecting known as mindfulness is "saraṇatā." It is called "dhāraṇatā" (bearing) because of its nature of bearing the learned scriptures (pariyatti). The state of not forgetting or not letting the object slip away, in the sense of plunging into the object, is called "apilāpanatā" (non-floating). For example, gourds and such float on water and do not plunge (sink) into the water. Mindfulness is not like that, floating on the object; rather, it plunges into the object. Therefore, it is called "apilāpanatā." It is called "asammussanatā" (non-forgetfulness) because of the state of not forgetting deeds done long ago or words spoken long ago. It is called "indriya" (faculty) because it exercises predominance in the characteristic of making the object appear and the characteristic of illuminating. The faculty known as mindfulness is "satindriya." It is called "satibala" (power of mindfulness) because it is unshakable by negligence (pamāda). It is called "sammāsati" (right mindfulness) because it is true mindfulness, mindfulness that leads out of the round of rebirths, and wholesome mindfulness.

In the description of the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya), it is called "paññā" (wisdom) in the sense of making various meanings (objects) clear. Alternatively, it is called "paññā" because it knows things in various ways, such as impermanence, etc. This is the term for the inherent nature of wisdom. The mode of understanding in various ways is "pajānanā." It is called "vicaya" (investigation) because it investigates impermanence, etc. The term "pavicaya" is an expansion by the prefix. It is called "dhammavicaya" (investigation of states) because it investigates the truths of the Four Noble Truths. It is called "sallakkhaṇā" (discernment) by virtue of well-marking impermanence, etc. That same wisdom is called "upalakkhaṇā" and "paccupalakkhaṇā" due to the difference in prefixes. The state of a wise person is "paṇḍicca" (erudition). The state of a skillful person is "kōsalla" (skillfulness). The state of a subtle wise person is "nēpuñña" (sagacity). It is called "vebhabyā" (elucidation) by virtue of elucidating impermanence, etc. It is called "cintā" (thought) by virtue of thinking about impermanence, etc. Alternatively, wisdom arises in someone and makes that person think about impermanence, etc.; thus it is called "cintā." It is called "upaparikkhā" (examination) because it closely examines impermanence, etc. "Bhūrī" means...
192:
Bhūrī is a name for the earth. This wisdom is also called bhūrī because it has a subtle meaning and because it is vast and extensive like the earth. For that reason, it is said: "The earth is called bhūrī. One who is endowed with wisdom that is vast and extensive like the earth is called bhūripañño (one of vast wisdom)." Alternatively, bhūrī is simply a name for wisdom. It is also called bhūrī because it delights in the true meaning. It is called medhā (sagacity) because it destroys defilements just as a thunderbolt destroys a rocky mountain. Or, it is called medhā in the sense of quick apprehension and retention. It is called pariṇāyikā (guide) because it leads and directs the person in whom it arises towards the practice of their own welfare and towards the penetration of the true characteristics of associated states. It is called vipassanā (insight) because it contemplates phenomena in various ways by way of impermanence and so on. It is called sampajañña (clear comprehension) because it knows impermanence and so on through good modes. It is called patodo (a goad), being like a goad, because it pricks and subdues the crooked mind that runs on the wrong path, in order to set it upon the right path of insight, just as a goad subdues Sindh horses that have taken the wrong path to set them on the right path. It is called indriya (faculty) because it exercises lordship in the characteristic of seeing (knowing). The faculty known as wisdom is paññindriya (the faculty of wisdom). It is called paññābala (the power of wisdom) because it is unshakable by ignorance. Wisdom itself is the weapon (paññāsattha) in the sense of cutting through defilements. Wisdom itself is the palace (paññāpāsāda) in the sense of rising high.

Wisdom itself is the light (paññā-āloka) in the sense of illuminating. Wisdom itself is the radiance (paññā-obhāsa) in the sense of shining. Wisdom itself is the brilliance (paññā-pajjota) in the sense of being a lamp. For a wise person sitting on a single cross-legged seat, the ten-thousandfold world system becomes a single light, a single radiance, a single brilliance; therefore, this is said. Although this meaning is accomplished by even one of these three terms, the Suttas were taught according to the inclinations of beings, such as: "Monks, there are these four lights. Which four? The light of the moon, the light of the sun, the light of fire, and the light of wisdom. Monks, among these four lights, the light of wisdom is supreme." Likewise, "Monks, there are these four radiances... Monks, there are these four brilliances." This teaching is also given here in accordance with those Suttas. Indeed, a meaning that is analyzed in many ways becomes well-analyzed. Furthermore, one person understands in one way, and another in another way.

Wisdom itself is the jewel (paññāratana) because it causes delight, gives delight, produces delight, is highly esteemed, is rare to appear, is incomparable, and is used by noble beings. Beings are not confused by that wisdom, nor does it itself [get confused] regarding the object...
193:
It is called amoha (non-delusion) because it is not confused regarding the object. The term dhammavicaya (investigation of states) has the same meaning as previously stated. Why is this term stated again? It is stated again to show that non-delusion is the opposite of delusion. By stating it again, this meaning is shown: "That which is non-delusion is not merely a state different from delusion, but it is the opposite of delusion; non-delusion, known as the investigation of states, is what is intended here." Sammādiṭṭhi (right view) is the non-perverted, wholesome view that leads out of Saṃsāra.

In the description of the life faculty (jīvitindriya), "the life of those mental states" means life in the sense of the cause of occurrence and the cause of standing of those associated mental states. For only when that life exists do mental states proceed, go, and occur. Therefore, it is called āyu (life). This is its intrinsic term (sabhāva-pada). Since those mental states can only stand, subsist, be maintained, move, occur, and be protected when life exists, the terms such as thiti (standing) and so on are stated. Here, the word-definition (vacanattha) is: It is thiti because they stand by this. It is yapanā because they subsist. Likewise, it is yāpanā. For those who understand thus, the preceding syllable is made short. It is iriyanā because they move by this. It is vattanā because they occur. It is pālanā because they are protected. It is jīvita because they live by this. It is jīvitindriya because it exercises lordship in the characteristic of continuous protection.

In the description of the power of moral shame (hiribala), "which state at that time" means by which state at that time [one is disgusted]. Or, by changing the gender, it should be understood as "which state is [present] at that time." In the term hiriyitabbena, the instrumental case is used in the sense of the accusative (the object). It means one is disgusted with, or loathes, states such as bodily misconduct that ought to be loathed. Pāpakānaṃ means "evil." Akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ means states born of a lack of skill (ignorance). This term samāpattiyā is also the instrumental case used in the sense of the accusative. It means one is disgusted with the attainment, the acquisition, and the possession of those unwholesome states.

In the description of the power of moral dread (ottappabala), the term ottappitabbena is the instrumental case used in the sense of cause (hetu). It means one is afraid of, or dreads, states such as bodily misconduct which are the cause of moral dread and which ought to be dreaded, and also the attainment of unwholesome states as described, which is the cause of moral dread.

In the description of non-greed (alobha), it is called alobha by way of non-attachment. It is also called alobha because it does not lust. This is its intrinsic term. Alubbhanā is the mode of not lusting. A person endowed with greed is called "one who lusts." One who does not lust (alubbhitā) is...
194:
Alubbhito. It is non-attachment. The state of one who is non-attached is called alubbhitatthaṃ. Because it is the opposite of intense passion (sarāga), it is called asārāga (non-passion). Asārajjanā is the manner of the mind being without intense passion. The state of one who is without intense passion is called asārajjitattaṃ. Because one does not plot for the wealth of others, it is called anabhijjhā (non-covetousness). Alobha kusalamūla means the wholesome root known as non-greed. Alobha is called kusalamūla because it assists wholesome states as a root cause (hetu-paccaya). It is called kusalamūla because it is both wholesome (kusala) and a root (mūla) in the sense of being a cause.

In the explanation of adosa (non-hatred), it is called adosa by virtue of non-malice. It is also called adosa because one does not hate. This is the term describing the intrinsic nature of adosa. Adussanā is the manner of the mind being without malice. The state of one who is without malice is called adussitattaṃ. Because it is the opposite of ill-will (byāpāda), it is called abyāpāda (non-ill-will). Because it is the opposite of the suffering caused by anger, it is called abyāpajja (non-affliction). The wholesome root known as adosa is called adosa kusalamūla. The meaning of that term is the same as previously explained.

40-41. In the explanation of kāyapassaddhi (tranquility of the body) and so forth, since the term 'kāya' (body) refers to the three mental aggregates, the Buddha taught 'vedanākkhandha' (the aggregate of feeling) and so on. By this state, those three mental aggregates are tranquilized from the heat of defilements, they become free from distress, and they reach a state of relief; therefore, it is called passaddhi (tranquility). The second term is expanded by the power of a prefix (upasagga). Passambhanā is the manner of the mind being tranquilized. The second term is also expanded by the power of a prefix. The state of the three aggregates that are tranquilized from the heat of defilements because of being endowed with tranquility is called paṭippassambhitattaṃ. By all these terms, only the tranquility of the three aggregates from the heat of defilements is spoken of. By the second method, the tranquility of the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha) from distress is spoken of.

42-43. Lahutā is the manner of lightness. Lahu-pariṇāmatā means that because those states have the quality of changing rapidly, they are called lahu-pariṇāmā; the state of those is lahu-pariṇāmatā. It means the capacity for rapid transformation. Adandhanatā is a term that rejects heaviness, meaning non-heaviness. Avitthanatā is the state of non-rigidity due to the absence of the burden of defilements such as conceit (māna). Thus, by the first method, the manner of lightness of the three aggregates is spoken of. By the second method, the manner of lightness of the aggregate of consciousness is spoken of.

44-45. Mudutā is the state of malleability. In the term maddavatā, maddava means gentleness and smoothness. The state of that gentleness is maddavatā. Akakkhalatā is the state of non-roughness. Akathinatā is the state of non-hardness. Here too, as in the previous method, only the manner of malleability of the three aggregates and, by the latter method, of the aggregate of consciousness is spoken of.
195:
46-47. Kammaññatā means proficiency in action, meaning the state of being fit for application in wholesome deeds. The remaining two terms (kammaññatā, kammaññabhāva) are expanded by the power of phrasing (vyañjana). Indeed, by those two terms, only the manner of proficiency in action of the three mental aggregates according to the first method, and of the aggregate of consciousness according to the second method, is spoken of.

48-49. Paguṇatā means the state of proficiency, meaning the state of being free from illness or free from the sickness [of defilements]. The remaining two terms are expanded by the power of phrasing. Here too, by the first method, only the manner of being free from the sickness of defilements of the three mental aggregates and, by the second method, of the aggregate of consciousness is spoken of.

50-51. Ujukatā means the state of rectitude, meaning the state of proceeding in an upright manner. The state of the three mental aggregates and the aggregate of consciousness being upright is called ujukatā. By the term ajimhatā, the rejection of 'cow-urine crookedness' is meant. By the term avaṅkatā, the rejection of 'moon-crescent crookedness' is meant. By the term akuṭilatā, the rejection of 'ploughshare-tip crookedness' is meant.

One who, having done evil, says "I did not do it," is called 'cow-urine crooked' because of the state of retreating deceit. One who, while doing evil, says "I fear evil," is mostly called 'moon-crescent crooked' because of the state of being curved. One who, while doing evil, says "Who would not fear evil?" is called 'ploughshare-tip crooked' because of the state of not being excessively curved. Alternatively, one whose three doors of action (kammadvara) are all impure is called 'cow-urine crooked.' One whose any two doors are impure is called 'moon-crescent crooked.' One whose any single door is impure is called 'ploughshare-tip crooked.'

However, the teachers who recite the Dīgha Nikāya (Dīgha-bhāṇaka) say this: A certain monk practices twenty-one kinds of wrong livelihood (anesanā) and six kinds of wrong resorts (agocara) throughout all stages of life; this monk is called 'cow-urine crooked.' A certain monk fulfills the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla) in the first stage of life, possesses shame and fear of wrongdoing, and desires training, but in the middle and last stages of life practices like the first monk; this monk is called 'moon-crescent crooked.' A certain monk fulfills the fourfold purification of virtue in the first and middle stages of life, possesses shame and fear of wrongdoing, and desires training, but in the last stage of life practices like the first monk; this monk is called 'ploughshare-tip crooked.'

The state of such a person who is crooked by the power of defilements is called jimhatā, vaṅkatā, and kuṭilatā (crookedness). By the power of rejecting those forms of crookedness, ajimhatā and the others are taught.
196:
This teaching is set forth with the aggregates as the basis (khandhādhiṭṭhāna). For these qualities, such as non-crookedness (ajimhatā) and so on, belong only to the aggregates and not to a person (puggala). Thus, by all these terms, it should be understood that the straightness of the immaterial states (arūpīnaṃ dhammānaṃ) is taught because of their freedom from defilements—referring to the three aggregates in the former method and to the consciousness aggregate (viññāṇakkhandha) in the latter method.

Now, the Appanāvāra (Section on Fixedness) mentioned by the word 'yevāpana' is a summary of the 'yevāpanaka' states (the 'whatever-other' states) shown in the Dhammuddesavāra.

## The Discussion on the Section of Detailed Exposition (Niddesavārakathā) is finished.

By this much, the Dhammavavatthānavāra (Section on the Determination of States), adorned with eight divisions—namely, the four divisions of Question (pucchā), Description of the Occasion (samayaniddesa), Exposition of States (dhammuddesa), and Fixedness (appanā) in the Uddesavāra, and the same four divisions in the Niddesavāra—is completed.

## The Section on Groups (Koṭṭhāsavāra)

58-120. Now, the Saṅgahavāra (Section on Summary) is begun with the words: 'At that time, there are four aggregates,' and so on. This Saṅgahavāra is threefold by way of Brief Exposition (uddesa), Detailed Exposition (niddesa), and Subsequent Detailed Exposition (paṭiniddesa). Therein, the Uddesa is: 'At that time, there are four aggregates,' etc. The Niddesa is: 'Which are the four aggregates at that time?' etc. The Paṭiniddesa is: 'Which is the aggregate of feeling (vedanākhandha) at that time?' etc. This is how it should be understood.

In that Uddesavāra, there are twenty-three groups (koṭṭhāsa) such as 'the four aggregates.' The meaning of these twenty-three groups should be understood as follows: When the first great wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara-paṭhama-mahākusala-citta) arises, there are more than fifty states that have entered the Pali text, excluding the 'yevāpanaka' states, which arise by way of mental factors. When all these states are summarized, they constitute only four aggregates in the sense of a 'group' (rāsa). They are two bases (āyatana) in the sense of 'base' as mentioned below. They are only two elements (dhātu) in the sense of 'intrinsic nature' (sabhāva), 'emptiness' (suññata) being void of self, and 'non-being' (nissatta). Among these fifty-plus states, only three states are called 'nutriments' (āhāra) in the sense of 'nutriment' as a condition. The remaining states are not nutriments.
197:
If it is asked: 'Do those (remaining 53) states not act as conditions for each other or for the matter produced by them?' The answer is: 'It is not that they do not; they certainly do. However, although they are similar in being conditions, these three states are called "nutriments" (āhāra) because they are predominant conditions (atirekapaccaya) in such and such a manner, and also in other manners (such as being supportive).'

How? Among those three, contact-nutriment (phassāhāra) is a condition for those states for which the remaining consciousness and mental factors are conditions, and it also brings the three kinds of feeling. Mental-volition-nutriment (manosañcetanāhāra) is a condition for those states and also brings the three realms of existence. Consciousness-nutriment (viññāṇāhāra) is a condition for those states and also brings rebirth-linking mind and matter (paṭisandhi-nāmarūpa).

If it is said: 'Is not that (consciousness which brings rebirth) only a resultant (vipāka)? But this current consciousness is a wholesome consciousness (kusala-viññāṇa).' Even though it is a wholesome consciousness, it is called 'consciousness-nutriment' because of its similarity to that resultant consciousness. Alternatively, these three are called nutriments in the sense of being supportive (upatthambhaka). These states are supportive conditions for the associated states, just as physical nutriment (kabaḷīkārāhāra) is for the physical body. Therefore, it is said (in the Paṭṭhāna): 'Immaterial nutriments are conditions for the associated states and for the matter produced by them by way of nutriment-condition.'

Another method: Physical nutriment and these three states are called nutriments because they are special conditions in the internal continuity (ajjhattika-santati). Indeed, physical nutriment is the special condition for the physical body of beings who subsist on physical food. In the mental body (nāmakāya), contact is the special condition for feeling; mental volition for consciousness; and consciousness for mind-and-matter. As it is said: 'Monks, just as this body is sustained by nutriment, exists depending on nutriment, and does not exist without nutriment.' Similarly, feeling arises with contact as condition; consciousness with formations as condition; and mind-and-matter with consciousness as condition.

Only eight states are faculties (indriya) in the sense of predominance (adhipatiya), and not the others. Therefore, it is said: 'There are eight faculties.' Only five states are jhāna factors (jhānaṅga) in the sense of close contemplation (upanijjhāyana). Therefore, it is said: 'There is jhāna of five factors.'

Only five states are path factors (maggaṅga) in the sense of leading out (niyyāna) from the round of suffering and in the sense of being a cause (hetu) for reaching Nibbāna. Therefore, it is said: 'There is a path of five factors.' Although the Noble Eightfold Path exists, because the three abstinences (virati) cannot be obtained in a single moment in mundane consciousness, it is called 'a path of five factors.' If it is asked: 'In this sutta, "Monks, this name 'Tathāgata-magga' is a name for the Noble Eightfold Path," just as the supramundane path has eight factors, does not the insight-path (vipassanā-magga) occurring in the preceding stage also have eight factors?' In truth, this suttanta teaching is a figurative teaching (pariyāya-desanā). Therefore, it is said: 'For that yogi, first of all, bodily action is very pure, verbal action is very pure, and livelihood is very pure.'
198:
