In mundane consciousness, however, the three abstinences (virati) are not obtained simultaneously in a single moment; therefore, [the path] is said to be five-factored (pañcaṅgika). One might object: "O Bhikkhu, 'Yathāgata-magga' is a name for this Noble Eightfold Path (S.v.8). Since this meaning is shown by the word 'Yathāgata' in this sutta—that just as the supramundane path is eight-factored, so too the preliminary insight (vipassanā) path is eight-factored—should the mundane path not also be eight-factored?" It should not be so. This sutta teaching is a figurative teaching (pariyāya-desanā). Therefore, He said: "Even before that [insight moment], the bodily action, verbal action, and livelihood of that practitioner are very pure" (M.iii.76). But this Abhidhamma teaching is a literal teaching (nippariyāya-desanā). Since the three abstinences cannot be obtained simultaneously in a single moment in mundane consciousness, it is said to be only "five-factored."

By the meaning of being unshakable, seven states are powers (bala). By the meaning of being a root, three states are roots (hetu). By the meaning of touching, the single state of contact is called contact (phassa). By the meaning of experiencing, the single state of feeling is called feeling (vedanā). By the meaning of perceiving, the single state of perception is called perception (saññā). By the meaning of volition, the single state of volition is called volition (cetanā). By the meaning of cognizing the object, the single state of consciousness is called consciousness (citta). By the meanings of being a group and of experiencing, the single state of feeling is called the aggregate of feeling (vedanā-kkhandha). By the meanings of being a group and of perceiving, the single state of perception is called the aggregate of perception (saññā-kkhandha). By the meanings of being a group and of constructing, the single state of volition is called the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhāra-kkhandha). By the meanings of being a group and of cognizing the object, the single state of consciousness is called the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇa-kkhandha). By the meaning of cognizing and the meaning of 'base' (āyatana) mentioned below, it is the single state of the mind-base (manāyatana). By the meaning of cognizing and the meaning of 'faculty' (indriya), it is the single state of the mind-faculty (manindriya). By the meaning of cognizing and the meanings of being empty of self-nature and not being a living being, it is the single state called the mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇa-dhātu), and not the others. Excluding consciousness, all other remaining states, by the meanings already mentioned, are only the mind-object base (dhammāyatana) and the mind-object element (dhammadhātu).

By the 'Appanā' section (the section on attainment) beginning with "Or whatever other [states there are at that time]," in this Summary Section (Saṅgahavāra) also, only the 'Yevāpanaka' states mentioned below are included. Just as it is here, so it is in all places. After this Summary Section, we will not analyze this much further. In the sections of Brief Exposition (Niddesa) and Detailed Exposition (Paṭiniddesa), the meaning should be understood according to the method mentioned below.

## The Summary Section (Saṅgahavāra) is finished.
## This Summary Section is also named the Section of Groupings (Koṭṭhāsavāra).
199:
## Section on Emptiness (Suññatavāra)
121-145. Now, the Section on Emptiness (Suññatavāra) beginning with "At that time, there are states (dhammā)" is commenced. This Section on Emptiness is distinguished in two ways: by way of brief exposition (uddesa) and detailed exposition (niddesa). Among these two, in the brief exposition, there are twenty-four groupings (koṭṭhāsa) together with the statement "states come to be." In all these groupings, the numerical limitation such as "four, two, three" is not mentioned. Why is it not mentioned? Because it has already been defined in the Summary Section (Saṅgahavāra). Indeed, only those states defined in that Summary Section are also taught here in this Section on Emptiness. In these aforementioned states, neither a being (satta), nor an essence (bhāva), nor a self (atta) is found. These are merely states (dhamma), just phenomena, which are without core and without a controlling leader; they are taught for the purpose of showing this nature of emptiness (suññatā).

Therefore, the meaning in this Section on Emptiness should be understood thus: at whatever time the first great wholesome consciousness (mahākusala-citta) of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) arises, at that time, the more than fifty states that have arisen by way of mental factors are merely states (dhamma) because of their meaning of self-nature (sabhāva). It should be understood that apart from these phenomena (sabhāva-dhamma), no other being, essence, person (posa), or individual (puggala) exists. Likewise, by the meaning of being a group, only aggregates (khandha) come to be. In this way, the application of meaning in all terms should be understood according to the previous method.

Specifically, because there is no jhāna factor other than the jhāna itself, and no path factor other than the path itself, it is therefore stated in this Section on Emptiness only as "jhāna comes to be, the path comes to be." Indeed, by the meaning of closely contemplating the object, only jhāna comes to be; by the meaning of being the cause for reaching Nibbāna, only the path comes to be; no other being or essence exists. In this way, the application of meaning should be made for all terms. The section of detailed exposition (niddesa-vāra) has an obvious meaning.

## The Section on Emptiness (Suññatavāra) is finished.
## The explanation of the meaning of the first consciousness,
## which is shown adorned with the three Great Sections (Mahāvāra), is finished.

## The Second Consciousness
Now, to show the second consciousness and so forth, the passage beginning with "Which are the states?" (katame dhammā) is commenced again. In all those detailed expositions of the second consciousness and so forth, the three Great Sections (Mahāvāra) each should be understood by the same method mentioned for the first consciousness. Not only should the Great Sections be understood, but the meaning of all terms similar to those taught in the first consciousness should also be understood by the method already mentioned. From here on, we will only provide the explanation of terms not yet mentioned. In this detailed exposition of the second consciousness, only this term "sasaṅkhārena" (with prompting) is a term not yet mentioned. Its meaning is: it is called 'sasaṅkhāra' because it occurs together with prompting (saṅkhāra). By that [combination of conditions occurring with prompting]...
200:
The term 'sa-saṅkhārika' (prompted/instigated) means being accompanied by effort (payoga) that instigates a sluggish mind, being accompanied by the means (upāya) for performing wholesome deeds, or being accompanied by a collection of conditions (paccaya-gaṇa). Just as the first great wholesome consciousness arises through a collection of conditions such as the object and wise attention (yoniso manasikāra), this second consciousness arises through that same collection of conditions, accompanied by effort and means.

The arising of this second consciousness should be understood thus: In this Dispensation, a certain monk living on the outskirts of a monastery might think, when the time for sweeping the pagoda courtyard, or the time for attending to the elder monks, or the day for listening to the Dhamma arrives, 'It will be too far for me to go and return; I will not go.' After thinking so, he thinks again, 'It is not proper for one called a monk not to go to the pagoda courtyard, or to attend to the elders, or to listen to the Dhamma; I will go,' and then he goes. The wholesome consciousness that arises in such a monk—whether through his own effort, or through being exhorted by others who point out the disadvantages of not performing duties and the advantages of performing them, or through being compelled by way of censure saying, 'Come, do this work'—is said to have arisen due to a collection of conditions that is prompted (sa-saṅkhārika).

## Dutiya-cittaṃ (The Second Consciousness).

## Tatiya-cittaṃ (The Third Consciousness)

147-148. In the third consciousness, it is called 'ñāṇa-vippayutta' because it is disconnected from knowledge. This consciousness also becomes very joyful and delighted (hattha-pahattha) regarding the object, but the discerning wisdom (paññā-ñāṇa) is not present here. Therefore, this third consciousness should be understood to arise when very young children, upon seeing a monk, bow with the thought, 'This elder is my elder,' and similarly during times such as bowing to a pagoda or listening to the Dhamma.

In the Pali text, however, wisdom is absent in seven places regarding this third consciousness. The rest of the explanation is just as previously stated.

## Tatiya-cittaṃ (The Third Consciousness).

## Catuttha-cittaṃ (The Fourth Consciousness)

In the fourth consciousness, the same method should be understood. However, because this consciousness is described as 'sa-saṅkhārika' (prompted), it should be understood to occur at such times when parents hold young children by their heads and make them bow to pagodas and so on; even though those children have no such desire, they bow with great joy and delight. It is at such times that the fourth consciousness is obtained.

## Catuttha-cittaṃ (The Fourth Consciousness).
201:
## Pañcama-cittaṃ (The Fifth Consciousness)

In the fifth consciousness, 'upekkhā-sahagata' means being associated with the feeling of equanimity. This consciousness is neutral (majjhatta) towards the object. However, discerning wisdom (ñāṇa) does indeed arise in this consciousness. In the Pali text, regarding this fifth consciousness, it is stated in the 'Fourfold Jhāna' section that 'equanimity arises,' and in the 'Eight Faculties' (Indriya-aṭṭhaka) section that 'the equanimity faculty (upekkhindriya) arises.' In the exposition (niddesa) of all terms such as feeling (vedanā), the teaching is given by way of rejecting pleasant, unpleasant, happy, and painful feelings, and then the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (adukkhamasukha-vedanā) is mentioned. The state of the equanimity faculty (upekkhindriya) should be understood by way of its exercising governance in the characteristic of neutrality (majjhatta) of that neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. According to the sequence of terms, zest (pīti) is absent in one place. Therefore, by way of the mental factors (cittanga) included in the Pali text, there are only fifty-five dhammas. By way of these dhammas, the decision should be understood in all groups and in all sections (vāra).

## Pañcama-cittaṃ (The Fifth Consciousness) ends.

## Chaṭṭha-cittādi (The Sixth Consciousness and so on)

156-9. The sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses should be understood in the same manner as described for the second, third, and fourth consciousnesses. In fact, in these consciousnesses, there is only the change of feeling and the absence of zest (pīti). The rest of the sequence of words, along with the manner of arising, is exactly the same as those (the second, third, and fourth). The arising of these consciousnesses during the preliminary practice (parikamma) of compassion (karuṇā) and appreciative joy (muditā) is also permitted in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā. These eight consciousnesses are called Sense-sphere Wholesome Consciousnesses (Kāmāvacara-kusala-citta).

## Puññakiriyavatthu-ādikathā (Discussion on the Bases of Meritorious Action, etc.)

All those sense-sphere wholesome consciousnesses should also be illustrated by the ten bases of meritorious action (puññakiriyavatthu). How? They are: the base of meritorious action consisting in giving (dāna-maya), ...consisting in virtue (sīla-maya), ...consisting in meditation (bhāvanā-maya), ...accompanied by reverence (apaciti-sahagata), ...accompanied by service (veyyāvacca-sahagata), sharing of merit (pattānuppadāna), rejoicing in merit (abbhanumodana), consisting in teaching the Dhamma (desanā-maya), consisting in listening to the Dhamma (savana-maya), and the base of meritorious action of straightening one's views (diṭṭhijukamma). These ten are called the bases of meritorious action. Among them, giving itself is 'dāna-maya'. It is a meritorious action (puññakiriyā) and it is a base (vatthu) for various benefits; therefore, it is called 'puññakiriyavatthu'. In the remaining cases such as 'sīla-maya', the same method should be understood.

Among those ten bases of meritorious action, in the case of the four requisites such as robes, or the six objects such as visible forms, or the ten objects of giving such as food—because of the production of those respective items like robes for the donor...
202:
The volition that occurs during these three periods—in the preliminary stage before giving, at the time of relinquishing and giving, and afterwards when recollecting with a joyful mind—is called 'meritorious action consisting in giving' (dānamaya puññakiriyavatthu).

The volition that occurs for one who undertakes the five precepts, the eight precepts, or the ten precepts; for one who goes to a monastery with the intention "I will ordain"; for one who is ordaining; for one who reflects, "My wish is fulfilled and I have indeed become a monk, excellent, excellent!"; for one who observes the pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla; for one who reflects when using requisites such as robes; for one who restrains the eye-door and so on when forms and so on come into range; and for one who purifies one's livelihood—this is called 'meritorious action consisting in virtue' (sīlamaya puññakiriyavatthu).

The volition that occurs for one who develops [insight] into the eye as impermanent, suffering, and non-self, according to the path of insight mentioned in the Paṭisambhidāmagga... [and similarly for] the mind, forms... mental objects, eye-consciousness... mind-consciousness, eye-contact... mind-contact, feeling born of eye-contact... feeling born of mind-contact... perception of forms... up to old age and death; or all volitions that have not yet reached absorption (appanā) in the thirty-eight objects—this is called 'meritorious action consisting in mental development' (bhāvanāmaya puññakiriyavatthu).

The merit 'associated with reverence' (apaciti-sahagata) should be understood through such acts as going out to meet an elder upon seeing them, taking their bowl and robes, paying homage, and making way for them.

The merit 'associated with service' (veyyāvacca-sahagata) should be understood when performing major or minor duties for elders; or upon seeing a monk entering a village for alms, taking his bowl, arranging for alms in the village, and bringing it back; or upon hearing "Go, bring the monks' bowls," going quickly and bringing the bowls, and so on, while performing bodily services.

'Sharing of merit' (pattānuppadāna) should be understood as the act of one who, after giving a gift and making offerings with incense and so on, shares the portion of merit they have performed, saying, "May so-and-so receive this merit," or "May all beings receive this merit." If it is asked, "Does the merit of one who shares it in this way become exhausted?" the answer is "No." For example, just as when one lamp is lit and from it a thousand lamps are lit, it cannot be said that the first lamp is exhausted; rather, the first light combined with the subsequent lights becomes an even greater light. In the same way, for the one who shares merit, there is no loss; it should be understood that there is only increase.
203:
'Rejoicing in merit' (abbhnumodana) should be understood through the act of rejoicing, saying "Sādhu, Sādhu," in the portion of merit given by others or in any other meritorious deed.

If one teaches with the desire, "Thus they will know me as a Dhamma-teacher," being focused on gain, that teaching is not of great fruit. If one teaches the Dhamma they have mastered to others, not longing for gain or honor, but with the aim of the 'attainment of liberation' (vimuttāyatana), this is called 'meritorious action consisting in teaching' (desanāmaya puññakiriyavatthu).

If one listens [to the Dhamma] with the thought, "Thus they will know me as a person of faith," that listening is not of great fruit. If one listens to the Dhamma with a soft heart suffused with benefit (associated with loving-kindness), thinking, "Thus there will be great fruit for me," this is called 'meritorious action consisting in hearing' (savanamaya puññakiriyavatthu).

The act of one who straightens their view is called 'meritorious action consisting in straightening one's view' (diṭṭhijukamma puññakiriyavatthu). The Dīghabhāṇaka teachers, however, say: "Straightening one's view is the constant defining characteristic for the great fruitfulness of all merits; for whatever merit one performs, it becomes of great fruit only through the straightness of the view."

Among these meritorious actions, 'giving' arises for one who thinks "I will give a gift," for one who is giving a gift, and for one who reflects "I have given." Thus, taking the three volitions together—the preliminary volition (pubbacetanā), the volition at the moment of giving (muñcanacetanā), and the subsequent volition (aparacetanā)—it is called 'meritorious action consisting in giving'. 'Virtue' also arises for one who thinks "I will fulfill virtue," for one who is fulfilling virtue, and for one who reflects "I have fulfilled it." Taking all those together, it is called 'meritorious action consisting in virtue'... [and so on]... 'Straightening one's view' also arises for one who thinks "I will straighten my view," for one who is straightening their view, and for one who reflects "I have straightened my view." Taking all those together, it is called 'meritorious action consisting in straightening one's view'.

In the Suttas, however, only three meritorious actions are mentioned. Among those three, the inclusion of the other meritorious actions should be understood. Reverence (apaciti) and service (veyyāvacca) are included in 'virtue'. Sharing of merit (pattānuppadāna) and rejoicing in merit (abbhnumodana) are included in 'giving'. Teaching, hearing, and straightening one's view are included in 'mental development'. In the view of the teachers who say "Straightening one's view is the constant defining characteristic of all merits," that straightening of view is included in all three. Thus, these are three in brief and ten in detail.
204:
Among those ten bases of meritorious action, one who thinks, "I will give a gift," thinks with any one of the eight types of sense-sphere wholesome consciousness. One who is giving also gives with any one of those eight types of consciousness. One who reflects, "A gift has been given by me," also reflects with any one of those eight types of consciousness. One who thinks, "I will fulfill virtue," also thinks with any one of those eight types of consciousness. One who is fulfilling virtue also fulfills it with any one of those eight types of consciousness. One who reflects, "Virtue has been fulfilled by me," also reflects with any one of those eight types of consciousness. One who thinks, "I will develop meditation," also thinks with any one of those eight types of consciousness. One who is developing it also develops it with any one of those eight types of consciousness. One who reflects, "Meditation has been developed by me," also reflects with any one of those eight types of consciousness.

One who thinks, "I will perform the act of paying respect to elders," also thinks with any one of those eight types of consciousness. One who is performing it also performs it with any one of those eight types of consciousness. One who reflects, "It has been done by me," also reflects with any one of those eight types of consciousness. One who thinks, "I will perform the act of service with my body," or one who is performing it, or one who reflects, "It has been done by me," also reflects with any one of those eight types of consciousness. One who thinks, "I will share merit," or one who is sharing it, or one who reflects, "It has been shared by me," or one who thinks, "I will rejoice in the sharing of merit or in other wholesome deeds," also thinks with any one of those eight types of consciousness. One who is rejoicing also rejoices with any one of those eight types of consciousness. One who reflects, "I have rejoiced," also reflects with any one of those eight types of consciousness. One who thinks, "I will teach the Dhamma," also thinks with any one of those eight types of consciousness. One who is teaching also teaches with any one of those eight types of consciousness. One who reflects, "It has been taught by me," also reflects with any one of those eight types of consciousness. One who thinks, "I will listen to the Dhamma," also thinks with any one of those eight types of consciousness. One who is listening also listens with any one of those eight types of consciousness. One who reflects, "It has been heard by me," also reflects with any one of those eight types of consciousness. One who thinks, "I will straighten my view," also thinks with any one of those eight types of consciousness. However, one who is straightening the view does so with any one of the four types of consciousness associated with knowledge. One who reflects, "My view has been straightened," reflects with any one of the eight types of consciousness.

In this context, the four infinites are to be understood. The four infinites are: space is infinite, world systems are infinite, the world of beings is infinite, ...
205:
The Buddha's knowledge is infinite. Indeed, in the eastern direction of space, or in the west, north, or south, there is no limit such as "this many hundreds of yojanas" or "this many thousands of yojanas." Just as an iron rod the size of Mount Sineru, if dropped into the earth after splitting it in two, would keep falling and find no standing ground, so space is called infinite. World systems, too, have no limit by hundreds or thousands. Even if four Great Brahmas born in the Akaniṭṭha realm—possessed of a speed capable of crossing a hundred thousand world systems in the time it takes a light arrow from a strong archer to cross the shadow of a palm tree transversely—were to run with that speed, thinking, "We will see the end of the world systems," they would pass away in the middle of their journey without seeing the end of the world systems. Thus, world systems are called infinite. In these many world systems, there is no measure of beings living in water or on land. Thus, the world of beings is called infinite. Even beyond these three, the Buddha's knowledge is truly infinite.

In this way, in the immeasurable world systems, for immeasurable beings, many sense-sphere unprompted wholesome consciousnesses accompanied by joy and associated with knowledge arise for a single individual; they also arise in great numbers for many individuals. All these, in the sense of being sense-sphere, accompanied by joy, associated with knowledge, and unprompted, reach unity. They become a single great consciousness that is accompanied by joy, associated with three roots, and unprompted. Likewise, the prompted great consciousness... and so on... likewise, the prompted consciousness accompanied by equanimity, dissociated from knowledge, and associated with two roots. Thus, all the sense-sphere wholesome consciousnesses arising in immeasurable beings in immeasurable world systems, the Fully Enlightened One—as if weighing them with a great scale, or as if measuring them by putting them into a bushel—defined them with his omniscience and showed them by dividing them into eight categories based on their similarity, saying, "These are only eight."

Furthermore, in this context, the accumulation of merit is taken in six ways. For merit is: self-initiated (sayaṅkāra), initiated by others (paraṅkāra), done by one's own hand (sāhattika), done by command (āṇattika), done with understanding (sampajanakata), and done without understanding (asampajanakata). Among these, that which is done according to one's own nature is called "sayaṅkāra." That which is done after seeing another doing it is called "paraṅkāra." That which is done with one's own hand is called "sāhattika." That which is done by commanding another...
206:
Wholesome action instigated by others is called 'āṇattika'. Wholesome action done with faith in kamma and its result is called 'sampajānakata'. Wholesome action done without knowing kamma or its result is called 'asampajānakata'. Among those (actions done by oneself, etc.), the person who performs the action by himself does so with one of these eight wholesome consciousnesses. Likewise, one who causes others to perform it, one who performs it with his own hands, or one who performs it by giving a command, does so with one of these eight wholesome consciousnesses. Specifically, wholesome action done with knowledge (sampajānakaraṇa) occurs through the four consciousnesses associated with knowledge (ñāṇasampayutta). Wholesome action done without knowledge (asampajānakaraṇa) occurs through the four consciousnesses dissociated from knowledge (ñāṇavippayutta).

In this context, the four other purities of the offering (dakkhiṇāvisuddhi) should also be taken. They are: the righteousness of the requisites (dhammikatā), the greatness of volition (cetanāmahatta), the perfection of the basis—the recipient (vatthusampatti), and the excellence of qualities (guṇātirekatā). Among these four, requisites obtained in accordance with the Dhamma are called 'dhammika'. The volition of a donor who gives with faith and conviction is called 'cetanāmahatta'. The state of being an Arahant is called 'vatthusampatti'. The state of an Arahant having just emerged from the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) is called 'guṇātirekatā'. The sense-sphere wholesome kamma of one who can give by combining these four factors brings results in this very life, as in the cases of the treasurer Puṇṇa, Kāḷavaliya, and the florist Sumana.

In brief, if all these sense-sphere wholesome consciousnesses are considered as 'mind' (citta), there is only one, in the sense of being varied. By way of feeling, there are two: that accompanied by joy (somanassa-sahagata) and that accompanied by equanimity (upekkhā-sahagata). By way of the teaching that analyzes knowledge, there are four. The great consciousness accompanied by joy, associated with knowledge, and unprompted (asaṅkhārika), and the great consciousness accompanied by equanimity, associated with knowledge, and unprompted, are one and the same in terms of being associated with knowledge and being unprompted. Similarly, there are (one each of) associated with knowledge and prompted (sasaṅkhārika), dissociated from knowledge and unprompted, and dissociated from knowledge and prompted. Thus, in those consciousnesses which are fourfold by way of the teaching that analyzes knowledge, there are eight wholesome consciousnesses: four unprompted and four prompted, by way of analyzing unprompted and prompted states. Having known these consciousnesses according to their true nature, the Blessed One—who is omniscient, the supreme leader of groups, and the most excellent among sages—declares, teaches, prescribes, establishes, opens, analyzes, and makes them clear.

## In the Commentary on the Dhammasaṅgaṇī named Atthasālinī,
## The Exposition of Sense-Sphere Wholesome is finished.
207:
## Description of Fine-Material Sphere Wholesome

## The First Jhāna: The Fourfold Method

Now, to show the fine-material sphere wholesome, the text beginning with "Katame dhammā kusalā" is undertaken. In that context, in the phrase "rūpūpappattiyā maggaṃ bhāveti," fine-material existence (rūpabhava) is called "rūpa." "Upappatti" means arising, rebirth, or manifestation. "Magga" means the cause (upāya). The word-definition of this term 'magga' is: it seeks, searches for, generates, or produces that rebirth; therefore, it is called "magga." This means that by whatever cause rebirth, manifestation, or arising in the fine-material realm occurs, one develops the cause for that rebirth in the fine-material realm.

An objection may be raised: Does rebirth in the fine-material realm always occur by means of this cause called jhāna? It does not. For by the jhāna which is a cause leading to penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya), as stated in: "Monks, develop concentration; one who is concentrated knows and sees things as they truly are," there is also the transcending of fine-material existence. However, since there is no other cause for rebirth in the fine-material realm besides this jhāna, it is said, "He develops the path for rebirth in the fine-material sphere."

In terms of ultimate reality, this so-called path (magga) is volition (cetanā), and it is also the states associated with volition (cetanā-sampayutta-dhamma), or both. For in the passage, "Sāriputta, I know hell, and I know the path (magga) leading to hell," volition is called "magga."

In the passage, "Faith, shame, wholesome giving, and volition—these are the qualities followed by the virtuous. This is called the divine path (magga); by this, one goes to the celestial world," the states associated with volition are called "magga." In the Saṅkhāruppatti Sutta and others, in the phrase, "Monks, this is the path (magga), this is the practice (paṭipada)," both volition and the states associated with volition are called "magga."

However, in this context of the fine-material sphere wholesome, because it is taught as "jhāna," the states associated with volition are intended. Nevertheless, since the volition associated with jhāna is primary, it is appropriate to call both volition and the states associated with it "magga," grouping them under the term "jhāna" as the cause for rebirth in the fine-material realm.

"Bhāveti" means he generates, produces, or increases. This is the meaning of "bhāvanā" here. In other contexts, however, by the power of prefixes, there are other meanings such as esteem (sambhāvanā), permeation (paribhāvanā), and manifestation (vibhāvanā). Among them, in the case of sambhāvanā: "Udāyī, here my disciples esteem (sambhāventi) me in the higher virtue, thinking, 'The ascetic Gotama is virtuous, endowed with the highest mass of virtue.'..."
208:
In the word 'samannāgato' (Majjhima Nikāya, 2, 243), the term 'bhāvanā' refers to 'sambhāvanā', meaning conviction (okappanā). In the passage, 'Concentration saturated with virtue is of great fruit and great benefit; wisdom saturated with concentration is of great fruit and great benefit; the mind saturated with wisdom is well-freed from the taints (āsavas)' (Dīgha Nikāya, 2, 186), 'bhāvanā' here refers to 'paribhāvanā', meaning saturation or impression (vāsanā). In the passage, 'Make the form disappear, make the feeling... perception... mental formations... consciousness disappear,' 'bhāvanā' here refers to 'vibhāvanā', meaning making disappear or vanishing (antaradhāpanā). However, in the passage, 'Again, Udāyi, I have taught the path to my disciples, practicing which my disciples develop (bhāventi) the four foundations of mindfulness' (Majjhima Nikāya, 2, 247), 'bhāvanā' here refers to producing and increasing. In this context (of Abhidhamma) as well, this meaning of 'increasing/developing' is intended. Therefore, it is said: 'Bhāveti means it generates, it produces, it increases.'

Why is the teaching here presented with the person as the forerunner (puggala-pubbaṅgama), unlike the exposition of the sense-sphere wholesome (kāmāvacara-kusala) where the dhamma is the forerunner? It is because it is accomplished through the path (paṭipadā). This (fine-material sphere wholesome) must be accomplished through one of the four paths; it cannot arise without a path like the sense-sphere wholesome. Since the path exists only when there is a practitioner (person), to show this meaning, the teaching is presented with the person as the forerunner, saying: 'He develops the path for the sake of rebirth in the fine-material realm.'

'Vivicceva kāmehi' means being secluded from, free from, and departed from sensual pleasures. The word 'eva' here should be understood as having the sense of restriction (niyama). Because it has the sense of restriction, it shows that even though sensual pleasures are absent at the time of attaining and dwelling in the first jhāna, those sensual pleasures are the opposite of the first jhāna, and that this jhāna can only be attained by abandoning sensual pleasures. How is this shown? When the restriction is made as 'vivicceva kāmehi', it becomes clear: 'Surely, these sensual pleasures are the opposites, in the presence of which this (jhāna) does not occur, just as the light of a lamp does not occur in the presence of darkness.' Just as one can reach the opposite shore only by leaving this shore, this jhāna is attained only by abandoning those sensual pleasures. Therefore, the restriction (niyama) is made.

Here, one might ask: 'Why is this (eva) mentioned only in the first phrase and not in the subsequent phrase? Could one attain and dwell in jhāna without being secluded from unwholesome states?' It should not be regarded in this way. It is mentioned in the first phrase because it is the escape (nissaraṇa) from those sensual pleasures.
209:
Because of transcending the sense-sphere and because of being the opposite of sensual lust, this jhāna is indeed the escape from sensual pleasures. Thus it was said: 'This renunciation (nekkhamma) is the escape from sensual pleasures' (Itivuttaka and Dīgha Nikāya). In the subsequent phrase as well, just as in the teaching, 'Monks, only here is there a recluse, here a second recluse' (Majjhima Nikāya, 1, 139; Aṅguttara Nikāya, 4, 241), where the word 'eva' is brought in and spoken, it should be spoken here as well. Since it is impossible to attain and dwell in jhāna without being secluded from unwholesome states known as the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) other than this sensual desire, the word 'eva' should be understood in both phrases as: 'secluded only from sensual pleasures, secluded only from unwholesome states.'

In both phrases, although the general term 'vivicca' (secluded) includes all types of seclusion such as momentary seclusion (tadaṅga-viveka) and physical seclusion (kāya-viveka), here only three types should be understood: physical seclusion (kāya-viveka), mental seclusion (citta-viveka), and seclusion by suppression (vikkhambhana-viveka).

By the word 'kāmehi' (from sensual pleasures), it should be understood that all 'objective sensuality' (vatthukāma) mentioned in the Niddesa as 'What are objective sensualities? Pleasing forms...' etc., and all 'defilement-based sensuality' (kilesakāma) mentioned in that same Mahāniddesa and Vibhaṅga as 'Desire is sensuality, lust is sensuality, desire and lust are sensuality, thought (saṅkappa) is sensuality, lust is sensuality, thought and lust are sensuality; these are called sensualities,' are included. Only then will the meaning 'secluded only from sensual pleasures' be appropriate in the sense of being secluded from objective sensuality. By saying this, physical seclusion (kāya-viveka) is expressed.

In the phrase 'secluded from unwholesome states', the meaning of being secluded from defilement-based sensuality or from all unwholesome states is appropriate. By saying this, mental seclusion (citta-viveka) is expressed. Here, by the first phrase expressing seclusion from objective sensuality, the abandoning of sensual happiness is shown; by the second phrase expressing seclusion from defilement-based sensuality, the acquisition of the happiness of renunciation (nekkhamma) is clarified. Thus, by expressing seclusion from both objective and defilement-based sensuality, it should be understood that: the first phrase clarifies the abandoning of the basis of defilement, the second clarifies the abandoning of the defilement itself; the first clarifies the abandoning of the cause of frivolity, the second clarifies the cause of foolishness; the first clarifies the purity of effort (payoga-suddhi), and the second clarifies the nurturing of the disposition (āsaya-posana). This is the method regarding the side of objective sensuality among the sensualities mentioned in 'kāmehi'.

On the side of defilement-based sensuality, however, only sensual desire (kāmacchanda), which has many divisions such as 'desire' and 'lust', is intended as sensuality. And that (sensual desire)...
210:
Although sensual desire (kāmacchanda) is included among unwholesome states, it is taught separately in the Vibhaṅga because it is the opposite of jhāna, in such ways as: "Among those states, what is sensual desire? Sensuality..." and so on. Alternatively, it is taught in the first phrase (vivicceva kāmehi) because it is the defilement of sensuality (kilesakāma), and in the second phrase (vivicca akusalehi dhammehi) because it is included in the unwholesome. Because of its various forms, that sensuality is taught in the plural as "kāmehi" rather than in the singular as "kāmato". Although other states are also unwholesome, only the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) are taught in the Vibhaṅga in such ways as: "Among those states, what are the unwholesome states? Sensual desire..." because of the desire to show they are the direct opposites of the jhāna factors mentioned above. Indeed, the hindrances are the opposites of the jhāna factors. It means that only these jhāna factors are the opposing states that can abandon, destroy, and crush the hindrances. Therefore, it is stated in the Peṭaka (Nettippakaraṇa): "Concentration (samādhi) is the opposite of sensual desire (kāmacchanda), rapture (pīti) of ill-will (byāpāda), initial application (vitakka) of sloth and torpor (thina-middha), happiness (sukha) of restlessness and remorse (uddhacca-kukkucca), and sustained application (vicāra) of doubt (vicikicchā)."

Thus, here, by the phrase "vivicceva kāmehi", seclusion by suppression (vikkhambhanaviveka) of sensual desire is taught. By the phrase "vivicca akusalehi dhammehi", [seclusion] of all five hindrances is taught. Alternatively, by way of "taking what has not been taken" (aggahitaggahaṇa), the first phrase teaches [seclusion from] sensual desire, and the second phrase teaches the remaining hindrances. Similarly, by the first phrase, greed (lobha) which has the five cords of sensual pleasure as its object among the three unwholesome roots is taught; by the second phrase, hatred (dosa) and delusion (moha) which have objects such as the bases of resentment (āghātavatthu) are taught. Or, among states such as the floods (ogha), the first phrase teaches the flood of sensuality (kāmogha), the bond of sensuality (kāmayoga), the taint of sensuality (kāmāsava), the clinging to sensuality (kāmupādāna), the bodily tie of covetousness (abhijjhākāyagantha), and the fetter of sensual lust (kāmarāgasaṃyojana); the second phrase teaches the remaining floods, bonds, taints, clingings, ties, and fetters. By the first phrase, craving (taṇhā) and its associated states are taught; by the second phrase, ignorance (avijjā) and its associated states are taught. Furthermore, it should be understood that by the first phrase, the suppression-seclusion (vikkhambhanaviveka) of the eight consciousnesses rooted in greed is taught, and by the second phrase, that of the remaining four unwholesome consciousnesses. This is the explanation of the meaning of "vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi".

Having thus shown the factor of abandoning (pahānaṅga) of the first jhāna, the phrase "savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ" etc., is now stated to show the factors of association (sampayogaṅga). Therein, by distinguishing the characteristics etc. mentioned below, it exists together with initial application (vitakka) and sustained application (vicāra) which have reached the state of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) due to association with absorption (appanā). Like a tree endowed with flowers and fruit, this jhāna is called "jhāna with initial application and sustained application". In the Vibhaṅga, however, "Endowed with this initial application and this sustained application, well-endowed..."
211:
"...is endowed, well-endowed" and so on, the teaching is given in terms of a person (puggalādhiṭṭhāna) in the Vibhaṅga. However, the meaning therein should be understood in the same way as stated in this commentary.

In the word "vivekaja": Seclusion (viveka) means being secluded from the hindrances. It means the disappearance of the hindrances. Alternatively, seclusion (viveka) is the group of mental states associated with jhāna that is secluded from the hindrances. Because it is born from that seclusion from hindrances, or because it arises in that group of states secluded from hindrances, it is called "vivekaja" (born of seclusion).

In the word "pītisukha": Rapture (pīti) and happiness (sukha) have already been explained below. Among those five kinds of rapture, the "pervading rapture" (pharaṇāpīti) which, having become the root of absorption concentration (appanāsamādhi), grows and reaches association with concentration, is the rapture intended in this context. Because this rapture and this happiness exist in this jhāna, or because they are in this jhāna, this jhāna is called "pītisukha" (jhāna having rapture and happiness). Alternatively, rapture and happiness are combined as "pītisukha" (like Dhamma-Vinaya). Because the rapture and happiness born of seclusion exist in this jhāna, it is also called "vivekajapītisukha". In truth, just as the jhāna is born of seclusion, so too the rapture and happiness in this jhāna are born of seclusion. And they exist in it. Therefore, it is appropriate to say "vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ" as a single compound. In the Vibhaṅga, however, it is stated in such ways as: "This happiness is accompanied by this rapture" and so on. The meaning therein should also be understood in this same way.

In the term "First Jhāna": It is called "first" because it is the first in numerical order. It is called "first" because it is attained first. It is also called "first" because it is to be entered first. However, this "being entered first" is not an absolute characteristic. For one who has attained the eight attainments and has mastery (vasībhāva) can enter them starting from the beginning to the end, or from the end to the beginning, or by skipping in between. Nevertheless, it is called "first" in the sense of arising first.

"Jhāna" is of two kinds: meditation on an object (ārammaṇūpanijjhāna) and meditation on characteristics (lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna). Therein, the eight attainments are reckoned as "meditation on an object" because they closely meditate on objects such as the earth kasiṇa. Insight (vipassanā), the Path (magga), and the Fruit (phala) are called "meditation on characteristics". Therein, insight is "meditation on characteristics" because it closely meditates on characteristics such as impermanence (anicca). The Path is "meditation on characteristics" because the task to be performed by insight is accomplished by the Path. The Fruit is called "meditation on characteristics" because it closely meditates on the Truth of Cessation (nirodhasacca) which has the characteristic of reality (tatha). Among these two kinds, "meditation on an object" is intended in this context. Therefore, it should be understood as "jhāna" because it closely meditates on the object, or because it burns up opposing states.
212:
"Upasampajja" means having reached, having attained. Or it means having fulfilled, having accomplished. In the Vibhaṅga, however, it is said: "'Upasampajja' means the acquisition, the re-acquisition, the attainment, the arrival, the touching, the realization, the fulfillment of the first jhāna." The meaning of the words in that Vibhaṅga should be understood in this same way. "Viharati" (dwells) means that by dwelling in a posture suitable for that jhāna, one becomes endowed with the jhāna of the kind described, and brings about the activity, the maintenance, the protection, the sustenance, the keeping going, the movement, and the dwelling of the personality (attabhāva). For it is said in the Vibhaṅga: "'Viharati' means one carries on, proceeds, protects, sustains, keeps going, moves, dwells; therefore it is called 'viharati'."

In the term "pathavīkasiṇa," the earth-disk itself is called "pathavīkasiṇa" because of its sense of being a totality. The counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta) obtained depending on that earth-disk is also called "pathavīkasiṇa." The jhāna obtained in that earth-kasina counterpart sign is also called "pathavīkasiṇa." Among these—the earth-disk, the sign, and the jhāna—in this context, the jhāna should be understood as "pathavīkasiṇa." "Having attained and dwelling in the jhāna known as the earth-kasina" is the summary meaning here.

If it is asked what should be done by a clansman (kulaputta) who, having performed the preliminary work (parikamma) in this earth-kasina and produced the fourfold or fivefold jhānas, wishes to reach the fruit of Arahantship by developing insight (vipassanā) which has jhāna as its proximate cause: First, he should purify the four kinds of virtue (sīla)—namely, virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha, virtue of restraint of the sense faculties, virtue of purification of livelihood, and virtue concerning the use of requisites. Standing on well-purified virtue, he should cut off whichever of the ten obstacles (palibodha), such as dwelling-place and so on, he may have. Then, having approached a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitta) who gives a meditation subject, and while investigating a meditation subject suitable for his own temperament among the thirty-eight meditation subjects mentioned in the Pāli, if this earth-kasina is suitable for that clansman, he should take up this very meditation subject. Abandoning a dwelling-place unsuitable for the development of jhāna and dwelling in a suitable one, having cut off minor obstacles, he should practice for the sake of attaining jhāna without neglecting any of the meditation procedures, including the protection of the kasina preliminary sign, the avoidance of the seven unsuitable things, the cultivation of the seven suitable things, and the ten kinds of skill in absorption (appanā-kosalla). This is the summary here. The detailed explanation should be understood according to the method stated in the Visuddhimagga. Just as in this case, so also in the subsequent second jhāna and so on, the details should be understood according to the method stated in the Visuddhimagga. Indeed, the entire meditation procedure for all meditation subjects has been expanded in detail in the Visuddhimagga according to the method of the Commentaries.
213:
It has already been explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga. What is the use of repeating it in various places? Therefore, we shall not expand on that meditation procedure again. However, without omitting the meaning that has not yet appeared below the Pāli text, we will provide a continuous word-by-word commentary.

"Tasmiṃ samaye" (at that time) means at the time when one dwells having attained the first jhāna. "Contact occurs... etc... non-distraction occurs"—thus, in this first wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere, fifty-six states occur according to the sequence of words already taught. However, those are sense-sphere states, whereas these are fine-material sphere states that are "exalted" (mahaggata) by way of the difference in planes; this is the distinction here. The remaining terms are just the same as in that first wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere. In this first jhāna, only the four "yevāpanaka" (or-whatever) states, starting with desire (chanda), are obtained. The section on groupings (koṭṭhāsavāra) and the section on emptiness (suññatavāra) are just as usual.

## The First [Jhāna].

## The Second Jhāna

161-162. In the description of the second jhāna, "vitakka-vicārānaṃ vūpasamā" (with the stilling of initial and sustained thought) means because of the stilling, the transcending, and the non-appearance of these two states—initial thought and sustained thought—at the moment of the second jhāna. In that second jhāna, although all the states of the first jhāna are absent (for indeed, the contact and so on that occur in the first jhāna are different, and those that occur in this second jhāna are different), it should be understood that this is said—"with the stilling of initial and sustained thought"—to show that the attainment of the second jhāna and so on, which are subsequent to the first jhāna, occurs through the transcending of the gross factors. "Ajjhattaṃ" (internally) here means one's own internal state is intended. In the Vibhaṅga, however, only "ajjhattaṃ paccattaṃ" (internally, individually) is said. Since one's own internal state is intended, the meaning here is "arisen within oneself" or "produced in one's own continuity."

"Sampasādanaṃ" (tranquillizing) refers to faith (saddhā). Because of its association with faith, the jhāna is also called "sampasādana," just as a cloth is called "blue" because of its association with the color blue. Or else, because that jhāna is endowed with faith and tranquillizes the mind by the stilling of the disturbance of initial and sustained thought, it is also called "sampasādana." In this second alternative meaning, the word connection should be understood as "sampasādanaṃ cetaso" (tranquillizing of the mind). In the first alternative meaning, however, the word "cetaso" (of the mind) should be joined with "ekodibhāvaṃ" (unification). In that case, the meaning is construed thus: it is called "ekodi" because it arises as single (being eminent); the meaning is that it arises as eminent and noble because it is not overridden by initial and sustained thought.
214:
In the world, a noble person is also called 'eka' (one/single). Alternatively, it is appropriate to say 'ekodi' because it arises without a companion, being devoid of initial thought (vitakka) and sustained thought (vicāra). In another way, it is called 'udi' because it arouses (udāyati) the associated states; the meaning is that it raises them up. Being 'eka' in the sense of noble and being that 'udi', it is called 'ekodi'. This is a synonym for concentration (samādhi). Thus, because it develops or increases this concentration called ekodi, this second jhāna is called 'ekodibhāva' (the state of unification of mind). Since this ekodi belongs only to the mind (citta), and not to a being or a soul (jīva), this state is called 'cetaso ekodibhāva' (unification of mind).

One might ask: "Does this faith (saddhā) not also exist in the first jhāna? And does this concentration named ekodi not also exist there? If so, why is only this second jhāna called 'sampasādana' (internal confidence) and 'cetaso ekodibhāva'?" To that question, it is answered—that first jhāna is not perfectly clear, like water troubled by waves, due to the disturbance of initial and sustained thought. Therefore, even though faith exists, it is not called 'sampasādana'. Furthermore, because it is not perfectly clear and due to the disturbance of initial and sustained thought, concentration is not clearly manifest in that first jhāna. Therefore, it is also not called 'ekodibhāva'.

In this second jhāna, however, because of the absence of the disturbances of initial and sustained thought, faith gains the opportunity and becomes strong. Due to the acquisition of the companion of strong faith, concentration also becomes manifest. Therefore, it should be understood that only this second jhāna is called 'sampasādanaṃ cetaso ekodibhāvaṃ'. In the Vibhaṅga, it is stated only this much: "Sampasādana means faith, believing, confidence, and internal clarity. Cetaso ekodibhāva means the stability of the mind... right concentration." It should be understood that this explanatory commentary does not contradict the Vibhaṅga as stated, but rather correlates and agrees with it.

It is called 'avitakka' (without initial thought) because initial thought is absent in this jhāna, having been abandoned through meditation. In the same way, it is called 'avicāra' (without sustained thought). In the Vibhaṅga, it is also taught: "Thus, this initial thought and this sustained thought are stilled, quieted, calmed, ceased, vanished, extinguished, dried up, withered, and made to disappear. Therefore, it is called 'avitakka avicāra'."

Here, one might ask: "Since this meaning is already established by the phrase 'vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā' (with the stilling of initial and sustained thought), why is 'avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ' said again?" It is answered—this is indeed so; although the meaning is established, this phrase does not merely indicate that meaning. Have we not said that by transcending the gross factors, the attainment of the subsequent jhānas after the first jhāna...
215:
...is achieved; thus it is said 'with the stilling of initial and sustained thought' to show this.

Furthermore, because of the stilling of initial and sustained thought, this second jhāna clarifies the mind; it is not clear because of the stilling of the taints of defilements. Because of the stilling of initial and sustained thought, this second jhāna reaches the state of noble concentration; it is not 'ekodibhāva' because of the abandoning of the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) like access concentration (upacāra-jhāna), nor is it 'ekodibhāva' because of the manifestation of the jhāna factors like the first jhāna. Thus, the phrase 'with the stilling of initial and sustained thought' is a statement that shows the cause of 'sampasādana' and 'ekodibhāva'. Similarly, because of the stilling of initial and sustained thought, this second jhāna is without initial and sustained thought. It is not that they are absent by nature as in the third and fourth jhānas, or as in eye-consciousness and so on. Thus, it also shows the cause of the state of being without initial and sustained thought, and does not merely show the absence of initial and sustained thought. However, the phrase 'avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ' (without initial and sustained thought) shows only the mere absence of initial and sustained thought. Therefore, even though the previous phrase was said, the latter should be said again.

'Samādhija' means born from the concentration of the first jhāna or born from associated concentration. Between those two, although the first jhāna is also born from associated concentration, only this second jhāna concentration deserves to be called 'samādhi'. The reason is that it is exceedingly stable and perfectly clear due to the absence of the disturbance of initial and sustained thought. Therefore, to praise the quality of this second jhāna, only this second jhāna is called 'samādhija' (born of concentration). The term 'pītisukhaṃ' (joy and happiness) is to be understood in the same way as previously explained.

'Dutiya' (second) is called second because of the numerical order. It is also called second because it is attained for the second time. In the fivefold jhāna classification, starting with "At that time contact occurs," the terms for initial thought and sustained thought are omitted, and in the fivefold path, the term for right intention (sammā-saṅkappa) is omitted. Through the power of those omitted terms, the decision regarding terms with and without grammatical inflections should be understood. In the section on portions (koṭṭhāsavāra), it is also stated: "The jhāna has three factors, the path has four factors." The remaining explanation is the same as that of the first jhāna.

## The Second Jhāna is finished.

## The Third Jhāna

In explaining the third jhāna, 'pītiyā ca virāgā' (with the fading away of joy) means that 'virāga' is the disgust for or the transcending of the aforementioned joy (pīti). The word 'ca' (and) between those two terms has the sense of connecting. That 'ca' connects either the stilling or the stilling of initial and sustained thought. Between those two, when it connects only the stilling, then the construction should be understood as: "due to the disgust for joy and, further, due to the stilling of joy." In this construction, 'virāga' has the meaning of disgust. Therefore, due to the disgust for joy...
216: In the phrase 'and by the stilling' (vūpasamā ca), this meaning should be understood: When the stilling of vitakka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought) is taken together, the construction should be understood as 'due to the fading away of pīti (rapture) and, furthermore, due to the stilling of vitakka and vicāra.' In this construction, the word 'virāga' (fading away) has the sense of 'transcending.' Therefore, the meaning should be understood as 'due to the transcending of pīti and due to the stilling of vitakka and vicāra.'## Although these vitakka and vicāra have indeed already been stilled in the second jhāna, this is stated here to show the path to attaining this third jhāna and to praise its virtues. When it is said, 'and by the stilling of vitakka and vicāra,' it is made clear: 'Is not the stilling of vitakka and vicāra the path to this jhāna?' For example, in the third noble path (Anāgāmi-magga), although sakkāyadiṭṭhi (personality belief) and others have not yet been fully abandoned, stating their abandonment as 'due to the abandoning of the five lower fetters' is a form of praise, and it serves to inspire those who are striving to attain that path. Similarly, here, stating the stilling of vitakka and vicāra, which have already been stilled, is a form of praise. Therefore, this meaning is stated: 'due to the transcending of pīti and due to the stilling of vitakka and vicāra.'## In the phrase 'he dwells equanimous' (upekkhako ca viherati), it is called 'upekkhā' because it looks on (ikkhati) appropriately (upapattito). The meaning is that it looks on evenly; it looks on without partiality. Because he is endowed with that equanimity which is clear, abundant, and firm, the person possessed of the third jhāna is called 'upekkhako' (one who is equanimous).## Equanimity (upekkhā) is of ten kinds: chaḷaṅgupekkhā (six-limbed equanimity), brahmavihārupekkhā (equanimity as a divine abiding), bojjhaṅgupekkhā (equanimity as a factor of enlightenment), vīriyupekkhā (equanimity of energy), saṅkhārupekkhā (equanimity towards formations), vedanupekkhā (equanimity as feeling), vipassanupekkhā (equanimity of insight), tatramajjhattupekkhā (specific neutrality), jhānupekkhā (equanimity of jhāna), and pārisuddhupekkhā (equanimity of purification).## Among those ten, that which is mentioned as: 'Here, monks, a monk, having seen a form with the eye, is neither elated nor depressed, but dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending'—this equanimity, which is the state of not abandoning the pure natural disposition when the six desirable or undesirable objects come into range at the six doors of an Arahant (khīṇāsava), is called 'chaḷaṅgupekkhā'.
217: That which is mentioned as: 'He dwells pervading one direction with a mind imbued with equanimity'—this equanimity, which is a state of neutrality towards beings, is called 'brahmavihārupekkhā'.## That which is mentioned as: 'He develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity based on seclusion'—this equanimity, which is a state of neutrality towards conascent states, is called 'bojjhaṅgupekkhā'.## That which is mentioned as: 'From time to time, he attends to the sign of equanimity'—this equanimity, described as energy that is neither overly exerted nor overly lax, is called 'vīriyupekkhā'.## That which is mentioned as: 'How many equanimities towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhā) arise by the power of serenity (samatha)? How many equanimities towards formations arise by the power of insight (vipassanā)? Eight equanimities towards formations arise by the power of serenity; ten equanimities towards formations arise by the power of insight'—this equanimity, which is the state of neutrality in standing still after reflecting on the abandonment of hindrances (nīvaraṇa) etc., and in the taking of those as objects, is called 'saṅkhārupekkhā'.## That which is mentioned as: 'At whatever time a wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere has arisen accompanied by equanimity'—this equanimity, described as neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, is called 'vedanupekkhā'.## That which is mentioned as: 'Whatever there is, whatever has come to be, that he abandons and acquires equanimity'—this equanimity, which is a state of neutrality in investigation, is called 'vipassanupekkhā'.## That which is mentioned among the 'yevāpanaka' (or-whatever-else) states such as chanda (desire) etc., which is the state of carrying conascent states evenly, is called 'tatramajjhattupekkhā'.## That which is mentioned as: 'He dwells equanimous'—this equanimity, which produces impartiality even towards that sublime happiness (of the third jhāna), is called 'jhānupekkhā'.## That which is mentioned as: 'The fourth jhāna which has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity'—this equanimity, which is purified from all opposition and is unconcerned even with the stilling of opposition, is called 'pārisuddhupekkhā'.## Among these ten types of equanimity, chaḷaṅgupekkhā, brahmavihārupekkhā, bojjhaṅgupekkhā, tatramajjhattupekkhā, jhānupekkhā, and pārisuddhupekkhā are, in their ultimate sense, only the single mental factor of tatramajjhattupekkhā. However, according to the difference of this or that state and occasion, this (tatramajjhattupekkhā)...
218:
Although they are the same in essence, they differ according to various moments and transitions. Just as a single being is differentiated by the stages of child, youth, elder, general, king, and so on. Therefore, among those types of equanimity, it should be understood that in whichever consciousness six-factored equanimity (chaḷaṅgupekkhā) arises, enlightenment-factor equanimity (bojjhaṅgupekkhā) and others do not arise; or conversely, where enlightenment-factor equanimity arises, six-factored equanimity and others do not arise.

Just as these are one in essence, so too are equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhā) and insight equanimity (vipassanūpekkhā). In truth, these are wisdom (paññā) itself, but are divided into two according to function. To explain in detail: just as a man who enters his house in the evening and searches for a snake with a forked stick, seeing it lying in the granary, looks at it to see 'Is it a snake or not?' and seeing the three marks on its neck, becomes free of doubt and becomes neutral (majjhattatā) in the investigation of 'Is it a snake or not?'; even so, when the three characteristics are seen by the insight knowledge of a yogi who has begun insight, the neutrality that arises in the investigation of the impermanence, etc., of formations is called 'insight equanimity' (vipassanūpekkhā).

Furthermore, just as that snake-catcher, having firmly grasped the snake with the forked stick, searches only for the means of release, thinking 'How can I release this snake without harming it and without being bitten by it myself?' and becomes neutral in the grasping; even so, when the three characteristics have been seen, for the yogi who sees the three realms of existence like houses ablaze with fire, the neutrality that exists in the grasping of formations through craving and views is called 'equanimity towards formations' (saṅkhārupekkhā). Thus, when insight equanimity is accomplished, equanimity towards formations is also accomplished. However, this wisdom is divided into two by the functions called neutrality in investigation and in grasping. Energy-equanimity (vīriyupekkhā) and feeling-equanimity (vedanupekkhā) are also different in essence from each other and from the remaining types of equanimity.

Among these ten types of equanimity, 'jhāna equanimity' (jhānupekkhā) is intended here. That jhāna equanimity has the characteristic of neutrality; its function is non-attention (anābhoga) even towards the sublime happiness of the third jhāna; it manifests to knowledge by causing the absence of activity (abyāpāra) in that happiness for the associated states; and it has the revulsion towards rapture (pīti) as its proximate cause. Here, an objector says: 'Is this jhāna equanimity not essentially the same as specific neutrality (tatramajjhattatupekkhā)? And that specific neutrality exists in the first and second jhānas as well. Therefore, in those jhānas too, it should be said that "he dwells equanimous." Why is it not said?' It is not said because its function is not distinct. Indeed, in the first and second jhānas, the function of that specific neutrality is not distinct because it is overwhelmed by initial application (vitakka), sustained application, and rapture. But in this third jhāna, because it is not overwhelmed by initial application, sustained application, and rapture, it becomes like one with an uplifted head and its function becomes distinct; therefore, it is mentioned.

## The complete explanation of the meaning of the sentence
## 'He dwells equanimous' is finished.
219:
Now, in the phrase 'mindful and clearly comprehending' (sato ca sampajāno): he is 'mindful' (sato) because he remembers. He is 'clearly comprehending' (sampajāno) because he understands in all ways and diversely. Thus, mindfulness and clear comprehension are stated in terms of the person. Among these two, mindfulness has the characteristic of remembering, the function of non-forgetting (which is the opposite of mindfulness-loss), and the manifestation of guarding (from defilements). Clear comprehension has the characteristic of non-delusion, the function of investigating (to the end of the task), and the manifestation of scrutiny.

In these jhanas, this mindfulness and clear comprehension certainly exist in the preceding ones (the first and second jhanas) as well. Indeed, for one who is forgetful and lacks clear comprehension, even access concentration (upacāra) cannot be fulfilled, let alone absorption (appanā). However, because those earlier jhanas are gross, the mind's progress is easy, like a man walking on the ground; the function of mindfulness and clear comprehension is unmanifest there. But because this third jhana is subtle due to the abandoning of gross factors, the mind's progress must be desired only as one maintained by the function of mindfulness and clear comprehension, like a man walking on the edge of a razor. Therefore, this phrase is stated only in this third jhana.

What more is there to say? Just as a young calf not yet weaned from its mother, even if separated from the mother cow, will return to her again if not guarded, so too this third jhana bliss, though separated from joy (pīti), might return to joy again if not guarded by the protection of mindfulness and clear comprehension; it would become associated with joy once more. Furthermore, beings are greatly attached to bliss. And this third jhana bliss is an exceedingly excellent bliss, for there is no bliss superior to this third jhana bliss. However, only through the power of mindfulness and clear comprehension does non-attachment to this third jhana bliss occur, and not otherwise. It should be understood that this phrase is stated only in this third jhana to show this special meaning.

Now, in the phrase 'experiences happiness with the body' (sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṃvedeti): although for one possessed of the third jhana there is no conscious advertence (ābhoga) such as 'I shall experience bliss,' nevertheless, because there is bliss associated with his mental body (nāmakāya), or because his physical body (rūpakāya) is suffused with the very sublime (mind-born) matter produced by that bliss associated with the mental body, he can experience bliss even after emerging from the jhana because the physical body is so suffused. Therefore, to show this meaning, He said: 'experiences happiness with the body.'

Now, in the phrase 'of which the Noble Ones declare: "He dwells in equanimity, mindful, and happy"' (yaṃ taṃ ariယာ ācikkhanti upekkhako satimā sukhavihārīti): it means that because of which third jhana, the Noble Ones such as the Buddhas 'declare, teach, describe, establish, open, analyze, make plain, and reveal' in praise of the person possessed of that third jhana. How do they praise him? As 'one who dwells in equanimity, mindful, and happy.' The construction here should be understood as: he dwells having attained that third jhana.
220:
Why do those Noble Ones praise that person in this way? It is because he is worthy of praise. For this person is equanimous even in the Third Jhana, which has extremely sweet bliss and has reached the pinnacle of bliss; he is not pulled by attachment to bliss therein. He is mindful because of the presence of mindfulness in such a way that 'joy does not arise.' He experiences with the mental body (nāmakāya) that unblemished bliss which is liked by the Noble Ones and cultivated only by the Noble Ones. Therefore, he is worthy of praise. Thus, wishing to reveal the qualities that are the cause for praise, it should be understood that the Noble Ones praise him, saying, 'He is equanimous, mindful, and dwells in bliss.'

It is called 'Third' (tatiya) because of the numerical order. It is also called 'Third' because one attains this Jhana for the third time. In the group of five Jhana factors, such as 'at that time there is contact,' the term 'joy' (pīti) is also diminished. By the power of that term 'joy,' the decision regarding terms with and without inflections should be understood. In the Koṭṭhāsavāra, it is also stated that 'it is a Jhana with two factors.' The rest is just like the Second Jhana.

## Tatiyaṃ.

## Catutthajjhānaṃ

In the explanation of the Fourth Jhana, 'due to the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain' means due to the abandoning of physical pleasure (kāyika-sukha) and physical pain (kāyika-dukkha). 'Beforehand' (pubbeva) means that such abandoning occurred beforehand and not at the moment of the Fourth Jhana. 'Due to the disappearance of joy and grief' means that because these two—mental pleasure (cetasika-sukha) and mental pain (cetasika-dukkha)—disappeared beforehand, it is meant as 'due to abandoning.' When are they abandoned? They are abandoned at the moment of access (upacāra) to the four Jhanas. Indeed, joy (somanassa) is abandoned at the moment of access to the Fourth Jhana. Pain, grief, and pleasure are abandoned at the moments of access to the First, Second, and Third Jhanas respectively. Although not stated in this order of abandoning, the abandoning of pleasure, pain, joy, and grief mentioned here should be understood according to the order in which the faculties (indriya) are pointed out in the Indriya-vibhaṅga.

If these are abandoned at the moment of access to each respective Jhana, then why is it said: 'Where does the arisen faculty of pain (dukkhindriya) cease without remainder? Here, monks, a monk...'
221:
'...quite secluded from sensual pleasures... enters and dwells in the First Jhana; here the arisen faculty of pain ceases without remainder. Where does the arisen faculty of grief... faculty of pleasure... faculty of joy cease without remainder? Here, monks, a monk, due to the abandoning of pleasure... enters and dwells in the Fourth Jhana. Here the arisen faculty of joy (somanassindriya) ceases without remainder' (Saṃyutta Nikāya). Why is cessation stated only in the Jhanas in this way? It is because of surpassing cessation (atisaya-nirodha). For in the First Jhana and so on, there is surpassing cessation of those faculties, not merely cessation. At the moment of access, however, there is merely cessation, not surpassing cessation.

This is because, in the access to the First Jhana with various advertings (āvajjana), although the faculty of pain has ceased, it might arise due to the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, and so on, or due to the discomfort and heat of an uneven seat; but it cannot arise within absorption (appanā). Or else, although it has ceased in access, this pain has not well ceased because it has not been destroyed by its opposite. Within absorption, however, the entire body is suffused with bliss due to the pervading of joy (pīti-pharaṇa). For one whose body is suffused with bliss, the faculty of pain is well ceased because it has been destroyed by its opposite.

In the access to the Second Jhana, which has advertings different from the absorption process, although the faculty of grief (domanassindriya) has been abandoned, it can arise. This is because this faculty of grief arises when there is physical exhaustion and mental distress based on initial and sustained thought (vitakka-vicāra). It does not arise when initial and sustained thought are absent. In whatever mind the faculty of grief arises, it arises because initial and sustained thought exist in that mind. Since initial and sustained thought are not yet abandoned in the access to the Second Jhana, grief might arise there. In the Second Jhana, however, it cannot arise because its causes, initial and sustained thought, have been destroyed.

Similarly, although the faculty of pleasure (sukhindriya) has been abandoned in the access to the Third Jhana, it might arise for one whose body is touched by refined matter originated by joy. In the Third Jhana, however, it cannot arise. This is because in the Third Jhana, joy (pīti), which is the cause of pleasure, has completely ceased. Similarly, although the faculty of joy (somanassindriya) has been abandoned in the access to the Fourth Jhana, it might arise because of its proximity, because of the absence of equanimity that has reached absorption, and because it has not been properly transcended. In the Fourth Jhana, however, it cannot arise. For that very reason, the word 'without remainder' (aparisesa) is included in those respective places, saying, 'the arisen faculty of pain ceases without remainder.'

Here it may be asked: 'If these feelings were already abandoned in the access to each respective Jhana, why are they brought together and mentioned here in the Fourth Jhana?' The answer is: 'For the purpose of easy comprehension.' For the 'neither-pain-nor-pleasure' feeling mentioned in the phrase 'neither-pain-nor-pleasure' (adukkham-asukha) is subtle and difficult to understand; it cannot be easily grasped by knowledge. Therefore, just as a cowherd, in order to catch a cow that is difficult to tame and cannot be caught no matter how one approaches it, herds all the cows into a single pen, and then, as he brings them out one by one in order...'
222:
Just as one might say, "This is the very cow to be caught, catch it," and thus have even the stray cow caught, in the same way, the Blessed One, for the sake of easy grasping of the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, brought together all these feelings and showed them. By showing these feelings thus brought together, it is possible to grasp with wisdom: "This state is neither pleasure nor pain, neither joy nor grief; this state is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling."

Alternatively, it should be understood that these feelings were mentioned to show the cause for the liberation of mind (cetovimutti) that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant. The abandoning of pleasure and pain, etc., are the causes for that liberation of mind. As it was said: "Friends, there are four causes for the attainment of the liberation of mind that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant. Here, friends, a bhikkhu, with the abandoning of pleasure... enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna. Friends, these are the four causes for the attainment of the liberation of mind that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant." Or, just as self-identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) and so on, though already abandoned by other paths, are said to be abandoned in the third path to praise the virtue of that third path, so too it should be understood that these feelings are mentioned here to praise the virtue of this fourth jhāna. Or, it should be understood that these are mentioned to show the extreme remoteness of lust (rāga) and hatred (dosa) in this fourth jhāna through the destruction of their causes. For among these feelings, pleasure is a cause for joy (somanassa), and joy is a cause for lust; pain is a cause for grief (domanassa), and grief is a cause for hatred. By destroying pleasure and the rest, lust and hatred, along with their causes, are abandoned and thus become extremely remote.

"Neither-painful-nor-pleasant" (adukkhamasukha) means "not-painful" due to the absence of pain, and "not-pleasant" due to the absence of pleasure. By this expression which excludes pain and pleasure, the third feeling which is the opposite of pain and pleasure is shown, not merely the absence of pain and pleasure. The third feeling is called neither-painful-nor-pleasant. It is also called equanimity (upekkhā). It should be understood as having the characteristic of experiencing the neutral state which is the opposite of the desirable and undesirable; its function is being indifferent; its manifestation is unapparent; and its proximate cause is the cessation of pleasure.

"Purity of mindfulness through equanimity" (upekkhā-sati-pārisuddhi) means the jhāna that has purity of mindfulness produced by equanimity. For in this fourth jhāna, mindfulness is extremely pure. That purity of mindfulness is made by equanimity, not by anything else. Therefore, this is called purity of mindfulness through equanimity. In the Vibhaṅga also it is said: "This mindfulness is clarified, purified, and cleansed by this equanimity; therefore it is called purity of mindfulness through equanimity." And the equanimity by which mindfulness becomes pure in this jhāna should be understood as specific neutrality (tatramajjhattatā) in its essence. Not only is mindfulness purified by that equanimity here, but indeed all associated states are also purified. However, the teaching is given with mindfulness as the head.
223:
In this regard, although this equanimity (tatramajjhattatā) exists in the lower three jhānas as well, it is like the crescent moon during the day. Just as the crescent moon, though present during the day, is not pure or radiant because it is overcome by the sun's light and because it lacks the night which is its compatible companion that assists it with a pleasant or cool nature; so too, this crescent moon of specific neutrality (tatramajjhattatā-upekkhā) is not pure in the three jhānas starting from the first, because it is overcome by the power of opposing states such as initial application (vitakka) and because it does not obtain the "night" of compatible equanimity-feeling (upekkhā-vedanā). Because that equanimity is not pure, the mindfulness and other states that arise together with it are also not pure, like the light of the impure crescent moon during the day. Therefore, not even one of those jhānas is called "purity of mindfulness through equanimity."

But in this fourth jhāna, because there is no overcoming by the power of opposing states such as initial application, and because it obtains the "night" of compatible equanimity-feeling, this crescent moon of specific neutrality is exceedingly pure. Because that equanimity is pure, the mindfulness and other states that arise together with it are also pure and radiant, like the light of the pure crescent moon. Therefore, it should be understood that this fourth jhāna alone is called "purity of mindfulness through equanimity."

"Fourth" (catuttha) is so called because it is the fourth in numerical order. It is also called the fourth because one attains this fourth jhāna.
