In the section beginning with "contact occurs" (phassa hoṭi), within the contact-pentad, upekkhā-vedanā should first be understood as "feeling." However, in the jhāna-pentad and the eight faculties, it is indeed stated as "equanimity occurs, the equanimity faculty occurs." The terms that were diminished in the third jhāna are likewise diminished here. In the section on portions (koṭṭhāsa-vāra), it should be understood as a jhāna with two factors by way of equanimity and one-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā). All the rest is exactly the same as the third jhāna.

## The Fourfold Method is Finished.

## The Fivefold Method

Now, the fivefold method is commenced with "Which states are wholesome?" (katame dhammā kusalā). Why is it commenced? It is commenced both by way of the inclination of the individuals and by way of the elegance of the teaching. It is said that in the assembly of devas who were seated together, to some devas, initial application (vitakka) alone appeared as gross, while sustained application (vicāra), rapture (pīti), pleasure (sukha), and one-pointedness of mind appeared as peaceful. For their benefit, the Teacher analyzed the second jhāna as having four factors, consisting of sustained application only, without initial application.
224:
To some, sustained thought (vicāra) appears gross, while rapture (pīti), bliss (sukha), and one-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā) appear peaceful. For their suitability, He analyzed it as the third jhāna with three factors. To some, rapture appears gross, while bliss and one-pointedness of mind appear peaceful. For their suitability, He analyzed it as the fourth jhāna with two factors. To some, bliss appears gross, while equanimity (upekkhā) and one-pointedness of mind appear peaceful. For their suitability, He analyzed it as the fifth jhāna with two factors. This is first the analysis by way of the 'disposition of the person' (puggalajjhāsaya).

Because He has perfectly penetrated the element of truth (dhamma-dhātu), He is said to have attained the elegance of teaching (desanāvilāsa); the Blessed One has indeed perfectly penetrated that element of truth. Therefore, being a Teacher who is skilled in the methods of instruction due to the greatness of His knowledge and who has attained the elegance of teaching, He determines the teaching as He wishes according to the factors that can be obtained. In doing so, He analyzed here the first jhāna with five factors, the second jhāna with four factors which is without applied thought (vitakka) and has only sustained thought (vicāra), the third jhāna with three factors, the fourth jhāna with two factors, and the fifth jhāna with two factors. This is called the 'elegance of teaching' (desanāvilāsa).

Furthermore, the Blessed One taught three kinds of concentration in the Suttanta: 'Bhikkhus, there are these three concentrations—concentration with applied and sustained thought (savitakka-savicāra), concentration without applied thought but with sustained thought only (avitakka-vicāramatta), and concentration without applied or sustained thought (avitakka-avicāra).' Among these concentrations, although the concentration with applied and sustained thought and the concentration without applied or sustained thought were analyzed and shown below, the concentration without applied thought but with sustained thought only has not yet been shown. It should be understood that this five-fold method (pañcaka-naya) was undertaken to show that concentration without applied thought but with sustained thought only.

In showing the second jhāna of that five-fold method, among the states such as contact (phassa), only applied thought (vitakka) is omitted. In the section of classification (koṭṭhāsavāra), only this point is distinct: 'There is the jhāna with four factors, there is the path (magga) with four factors.' All the rest is exactly the same as the first jhāna. Those states which are the second, third, and fourth jhānas in the four-fold method (catukka-naya) are themselves the third, fourth, and fifth jhānas in this five-fold method. This method should be understood to illustrate the sequence of attaining those jhānas—

It is heard that a minister's son came from the countryside to the city to serve the King. Having seen the King for only one day, he destroyed all his wealth through the ruinous habit of drinking. One day, (he was taken out of the tavern and placed on a refuse heap), being intoxicated and without clothes.
225:
They covered him with a mere old mat and took him out of the tavern. When an expert in the science of body marks (aṅgavijjā) saw him sleeping on a refuse heap, he made a decision: "This man will be a refuge for many people; he should be looked after." He then bathed him with fine clay, dressed him in a pair of thick cloths, bathed him again with scented water, dressed him in a pair of fine silk (dukūla) garments, took him up to a palace, fed him with excellent food, and after entrusting him to attendants saying, "Serve him in this manner," he departed.

Then the attendants placed him on a bed. To prevent him from going to the tavern, four strong men stood pressing his four limbs (hands and feet). One person massaged his feet. One person held a palmyra fan and fanned him. One person sat playing the lute and singing.

Having reached the bed, his exhaustion vanished, and after sleeping for a short while, he woke up. Unable to bear the pressing of his hands and feet, he rebuked them, "Who is pressing my hands and feet? Go away!" They departed at his single word. Then, after sleeping again for a short while, he woke up and, unable to bear the massaging of his feet, said, "Who is massaging my feet? Go away!" He too departed at his single word. Again, after sleeping for a short while, he woke up and, unable to bear the wind from the fan which felt like a storm, said, "Who is this? Let him go away!" He too departed at his single word. Once more, after sleeping for a short while, he woke up and, unable to bear the sound of singing and music which felt like an earache, he rebuked the lute player. He too departed at his single word. In this way, as the disturbances of exhaustion, pressing, massaging, fanning, and the sound of singing and music gradually vanished, he slept comfortably, and upon waking, went to the King. The King also granted him great authority and a retinue. He became a refuge for many people.

In that story, the son of a good family living in a household who has reached ruin through many misfortunes should be seen as the minister's son who reached ruin through the habit of drinking. The Tathāgata should be seen as the man expert in the science of body marks. The Buddha's decision, "This son of good family will be a refuge for many people; he is worthy of ordination (pabbajjā)," should be seen as that man's decision, "This man will be a refuge for many people; he is worthy of being looked after."
226:
Just as the bathing of that minister's son with fine clay, so should the noble son's obtaining of the monkhood (pabbajjā) be understood. Just as the dressing of that minister's son in thick cloth, so should the noble son's wearing of the garment of virtue consisting of the ten precepts (dasa-sikkhāpada) be understood. Again, just as the bathing of that minister's son with scented water, so should this noble son's bathing with the scented water of virtue such as the restraint of the Pātimokkha (pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla) be understood. Again, just as the clothing of that minister's son in a pair of fine white silk garments, so should this noble son's wearing of the fine white silk of the aforementioned perfection of purity of virtue (sīla-visuddhi) be understood.

Just as the taking up of that minister's son, who is clothed in fine white silk, to the palace, so should this noble son's ascending to the palace of the development of concentration (samādhi-bhāvanā), while clothed in the fine white silk of purity of virtue, be understood. Furthermore, just as that minister's son enjoys fine food, so should this noble son's consuming of the ambrosia of the Dhamma, such as mindfulness (sati) and clear comprehension (sampajañña) which are beneficial to concentration, be understood.

Just as the attendants carry that minister's son, who has finished his meal, to his bed, so should this noble son's being carried to access concentration (upacāra-jhāna) by means of factors such as initial thought (vitakka) be understood. Again, just as the group of four men who massage the hands and feet of that minister's son to prevent him from going to a tavern, so should the renunciation thought (nekkhamma-vitakka) that presses the mind upon the object to prevent it from moving towards sensual perception (kāma-saññā) be understood. Just as the man who massages the feet of that minister's son, so should the sustained thought (vicāra) that repeatedly examines the mind upon the object be understood. Just as the man who fans that minister's son with a palm-leaf fan, so should rapture (pīti) which provides coolness to the mind of this noble son be understood.

Just as the musician who pleases the ears of that minister's son, so should the feeling of joy (somanassa) that pleases the mind of this noble son be understood. Just as that minister's son, whose fatigue is gone by going to bed, falls asleep for a moment, so should this noble son's attainment of the first jhāna (paṭhama-jjhāna), whose fatigue of the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) is gone by means of the support of access concentration, be understood. Alternatively, just as that minister's son, who has woken up and risen from bed, cannot bear the massaging of his hands and feet and thus scolds the massagers, and upon their departure falls asleep again for a moment, so should this noble son, who has emerged from the first jhāna, be understood as seeing the fault of initial thought (vitakka) because he cannot bear it as it oppresses the mind; and by abandoning initial thought, he attains the second jhāna (dutiya-jjhāna) which has no initial thought but only sustained thought (vicāra). Furthermore, just as that minister's son, who repeatedly sleeps and wakes, cannot bear the foot-massaging and so forth in the aforementioned order and thus scolds the foot-massagers and so forth, and upon their departure repeatedly falls asleep for a moment, so should this noble son, who repeatedly emerges from the second jhāna and so forth, be understood as seeing the faults of sustained thought (vicāra) and so forth...
227:
...because of being unable to bear sustained thought (vicāra) and so forth, he sees the faults of sustained thought and so forth in due order; and by abandoning those various faults that have been seen, he should be understood as attaining the third jhāna (tatiya-jjhāna) which is without initial and sustained thought, the fourth jhāna (catuttha-jjhāna) which is without rapture (nippīti), and the fifth jhāna (pañcama-jjhāna) where joy (somanassa) has been abandoned.

Just as the minister's son, rising from his bed and going to the presence of the King, attains high office, so should this person's attainment of Arahantship (arahatta) be understood when he emerges from the fifth jhāna and enters the path of insight (vipassanā). Just as that minister's son who has attained high office becomes a refuge for many people, so should this person who has attained Arahantship be understood as being a refuge for many. By this much, this person is called an unsurpassed and noble field of merit (puññakkhetta).

## The Fivefold Method is finished.

By this much, the ninefold classification of purity (suddhikana-vaka) consisting of the two methods, the fourfold and the fivefold, has been explained. In terms of essence, however, this ninefold classification of purity should be understood as only the fivefold jhāna (pañcaka-naya), because the fourfold method is included within the fivefold method.

## The Four Modes of Progress

176-180. Now, since this jhāna is accomplished through the sequence of progress (paṭipadā), the section beginning with "Again, which things are wholesome?" (puna katame dhammā kusalā) is undertaken to show the different modes of progress of that jhāna. Therein, because the practice leading to jhāna involves pain and difficulty, it is called "painful progress" (dukkha-paṭipadā). Because the higher knowledge (prajñā) is slow, it is called "sluggish intuition" (dandhābhiññā). Thus, "painful progress," "sluggish intuition," and "earth kasina" (pathavī-kasiṇa) are all three merely names for the jhāna. The same method applies to "painful progress with quick intuition" (dukkha-paṭipadā khippābhiññā) and so forth.

Among those modes of progress, the development of jhāna that occurs from the first initial attention until the access concentration (upacāra) of that particular jhāna arises is called "progress" (paṭipadā). The wisdom (paññā) that occurs from access concentration until absorption (appanā) is called "intuition" (abhiññā). That progress is painful (dukkha) for some because it is difficult and unpleasant to practice due to the abundance of opposing states such as the hindrances (nīvaraṇa). For others, it is pleasant (sukha) due to the absence of those hindrances. Intuition (abhiññā) is also sluggish (dandhā) for some because it is dull and does not occur quickly. For others, it is quick (khippā) because it is not dull and occurs rapidly. Therefore, the person who, from the beginning, is weary with painful effort and exertion (sasaṅkhāra) while suppressing the defilements...
228:
If one abandons (defilements) through painful effort and formations, it is called painful progress (dukkha paṭipadā) for that person. Having abandoned the defilements, if the manifestation of the factors of absorption (jhānaṅga), such as initial application (vitakka), occurs only after a long time while dwelling in the perfume of attainment (appanā), it is called sluggish direct knowledge (dandhābhiññā) for that person. If the factors of absorption manifest quickly, it is called quick direct knowledge (khippābhiññā) for that person. When abandoning defilements, if one can do so easily and without hardship, it is called pleasant progress (sukha paṭipadā) for that person.

In that (practice of absorption), among the preliminary duties such as cutting off impediments (palibodha) and suitability or unsuitability, and skill in attainment (appanākosalla) as described in the "Description of the Development of Mind" (Cittabhāvanāniddesa) of the Visuddhimagga, for one who resorts to what is unsuitable, there is painful progress and sluggish direct knowledge. For one who resorts to what is suitable, there is pleasant progress and quick direct knowledge. For one who resorts to what is unsuitable in the beginning and suitable later, or suitable in the beginning and unsuitable later, it should be understood as a mixed practice. Likewise, for one who practices meditation without performing preliminary duties such as cutting off impediments, there is painful progress; for one who performs them, there is pleasant progress. For one who does not perfect skill in attainment, there is sluggish direct knowledge; for one who perfects it, there is quick direct knowledge.

Furthermore, the distinction between these (progress and direct knowledge) should be understood by way of craving (taṇhā) and ignorance (avijjā), and by way of previous practice (adhikāra) in serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā). For one overcome by craving, there is painful progress; for one not overcome, there is pleasant progress. For one overcome by ignorance, there is sluggish direct knowledge; for one not overcome, there is quick direct knowledge. For one who has no previous practice in serenity, there is painful progress; for one who has previous practice, there is pleasant progress. For one who has no previous practice in insight, there is sluggish direct knowledge; for one who has previous practice, there is quick direct knowledge.

The distinction between these should also be understood by way of defilements and faculties (indriya). For one with intense defilements and dull faculties, there is painful progress and sluggish direct knowledge. For one with sharp faculties, however, there is quick direct knowledge. For one with weak defilements and dull faculties, there is pleasant progress and sluggish direct knowledge. For one with sharp faculties, however, there is quick direct knowledge.

Thus, among these modes of progress and direct knowledge, when a person reaches absorption (jhāna) through painful progress and sluggish direct knowledge, that absorption is called "painful progress and sluggish direct knowledge" (dukkha-paṭipadā dandhābhiññā). The same method applies to the remaining absorptions.
229:
In those second absorptions and so on, progress (paṭipadā) should be understood in the sense of the mindfulness described as: "Mindfulness of a nature suitable to that first absorption and so on shall be well-established; wisdom shall be of a nature to remain without declining," or in the sense of abandoning the attachment (nikanti) to those respective absorptions. Direct knowledge (abhiññā) should be understood as the bringing about of attainment absorption (appanā) for a person who has reached the access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) of those respective second absorptions and so on. Progress and direct knowledge also occur by way of the source of arrival (āgamana). The second absorption that arises after reaching the first absorption of painful progress and sluggish direct knowledge is also of the same nature. The same method should be understood for the third and fourth absorptions. Just as the fourfold distinction is understood by way of progress in the fourfold method (catukkanaya), it is also understood by way of progress in the fivefold method (pañcakanaya). Thus, four sets of nine are taught by way of progress. In those four sets of nine, there are 36 states of consciousness according to the text; however, in terms of essence, there are only 20, because the fourfold method is included within the fivefold method.

## The Tetrad on Progress (Paṭipadā-catukka).

## The Tetrad on Objects (Ārammaṇa-catukka)

Now, just as this absorption is fourfold by way of the distinction of progress, it is also fourfold by way of the distinction of objects. Therefore, to show that distinction, the passage beginning with "Which states are wholesome?" is begun again. In those passages such as "limited, with a limited object," if an absorption is not well-practiced and is unable to be a condition for a higher absorption, this absorption is called "limited" (paritta) (meaning it has small power). If an absorption occurs with an object that is not expanded, or is only the size of a pot lid, it is called "having a limited object" (parittārammaṇa) because its object is narrow. If an absorption is well-practiced and well-developed, being able to be a condition for a higher absorption, this absorption is called "immeasurable" (appamāṇa) (meaning it has great power). If an absorption occurs with an extensive object, it is called "having an immeasurable object" (appamāṇārammaṇa) because its object has an expanded measure. The mixed method should be understood by way of the mixing of the aforementioned characteristics. Thus, four sets of nine are also taught by way of objects. The counting of consciousness here is exactly the same as in the previous tetrad on progress.

## The Tetrad on Objects (Ārammaṇa-catukka).

## The Mixed Tetrad on Objects and Progress (Ārammaṇa-paṭipadā-missaka)

Now, to show the sixteenfold method of mixing objects and progress, the passage beginning with "Which states are wholesome?" is begun again. In that first method, the absorption taught is inferior due to four reasons: because of being of painful progress, because of being of sluggish direct knowledge, because of being of limited power, and because of having a limited object. The absorption taught in the sixteenth method is superior because of being of pleasant progress, because of being of quick direct knowledge, because of being of immeasurable power...
230:
The jhāna taught is inferior due to four reasons: because it is of painful practice (dukkha-paṭipadā), because it is of sluggish direct knowledge (dandhābhiññā), because it is of limited power (parittattā), and because it is of limited object (parittārammaṇattā). The jhāna taught in the sixteenth method is superior due to four reasons: because it is of pleasant practice (sukha-paṭipadā), because it is of swift direct knowledge (khippābhiññā), because it is of immeasurable power (appamāṇattā), and because it is of immeasurable object (appamāṇārammaṇattā). In the remaining fourteen methods, the state of being inferior or superior should be understood by one, two, or three reasons.

Why is this method taught? It is taught because it is the cause for the arising of jhāna. Indeed, the Blessed One has shown pure jhāna (suddhika-jhāna) in the earth kasina (pathavī-kasiṇa) by way of the fourfold method and the fivefold method; likewise, pure practice (suddhika-paṭipadā) and pure object (suddhika-ārammaṇa). Among those methods, for those deities who are able to understand pure jhāna in the earth kasina while it is being taught by way of the fourfold method, the fourfold method in pure jhāna was taught according to their suitability. For those who are able to understand while it is being taught by way of the fivefold method, the fivefold method was taught according to their suitability. For those who are able to understand pure practice and pure object while they are being taught by way of the fourfold method, the fourfold method in pure practice and pure object was taught according to their suitability. For those who are able to understand while it is being taught by way of the fivefold method, the fivefold method was taught according to their suitability. Thus, the teaching was given below according to the inclinations of the individuals.

Furthermore, because the Blessed One has attained the elegance of teaching, possesses the fourfold analytical knowledge (paṭisambhidā), has knowledge purified by the ten powers (dasabala) and the fourfold intrepidity (vesārajja), and has well-penetrated the true nature and characteristics of phenomena, He is skilled in the designation of dhammas (dhamma-paññatti) and is able to determine the teaching according to whichever method is obtained. Therefore, because of this attainment of elegance in teaching, the Blessed One taught this discourse in the earth kasina by way of the pure fourfold method and so on.

Again, because whoever produces jhāna cannot do so without the object and the practice, this sixteenfold method was taught as the fixed cause for the arising of jhāna.

By this sequence of words, the ninefold pure (suddhika-navaka), the four ninefold practices (paṭipadā-navaka), and the four ninefold objects (ārammaṇa-navaka)—these sixteen ninefold sets—making twenty-five ninefold sets in total, are taught. Among those twenty-five ninefold sets, since there are two methods (fourfold and fivefold) in each ninefold set, there are fifty methods. Among those methods, according to the Pali text: "In the twenty-five fourfold methods, there are one hundred (jhāna consciousnesses), and in the twenty-five fivefold methods, there are one hundred and twenty-five," there are two hundred and twenty-five (225) jhāna consciousnesses. However, because the fourfold method is included within the fivefold method, in terms of actual essence, there are only one hundred and twenty-five...
231:
...there are one hundred consciousnesses. In the Pali text, there are two hundred and twenty-five consciousnesses. In the explanation (niddesa) of each of these consciousnesses, there are three Great Chapters (Mahāvāra) such as the Definition of Phenomena (Dhamma-vavatthāna). The teachers of the Council (Saṅgāyanā) have summarized those Great Chapters by showing only the method in the explanation of each consciousness.

## Earth Kasina (Pathavī-kasiṇa)

Now, since these jhānas also arise in the water kasina (āpo-kasiṇa) and so on, the Pali text beginning with "Which dhammas are wholesome?" (katame dhammā kusalā) is started again to show those. In those [kasinas] such as the water kasina, the entire Pali method, the clarification of meaning, the counting of consciousness, and the summary of chapters should be understood exactly as taught in the earth kasina. As for the method of meditation (bhāvanā-naya), everything from the preliminary work (parikamma) of the kasina has already been explained in the Visuddhimagga. In the Mahāsakuludāyi Sutta, however, ten kasinas are taught. Among those kasinas, the consciousness kasina (viññāṇa-kasiṇa) is both the lofty consciousness (mahaggata-viññāṇa) produced in the concept of space and the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana-samāpatti) arising from preliminary work on that lofty consciousness. Since it belongs entirely to the immaterial teaching (āruppa-desanā) in every way, it is not taught here in the context of the fine-material sphere teaching (rūpāvacara-desanā).

The space kasina (ākāsa-kasiṇa) refers to the concept of space obtained by removing the kasina, the aggregates (khandha) occurring with that space concept as an object, the delimited space (paricchedākāsa) taken as a sign in one of the openings such as a wall-hole, and the fourfold and fivefold jhānas arising with that delimited space as an object. Among these two methods, the former belongs to the immaterial teaching, and the latter belongs to the fine-material sphere teaching. Because of this mixture, this space kasina is not included in the fine-material sphere teaching. However, the jhāna arising in delimited space is a path for rebirth in the fine-material realm (rūpūpapatti), so that delimited space should be taken. In that delimited space, only the fourfold and fivefold jhānas arise; immaterial jhānas do not arise. Why? Because the removal of the kasina (kasiṇugghāṭana) is not obtained. Indeed, even if that delimited space is removed again and again, it remains only space, so the removal of the kasina is not possible there. Therefore, the jhāna arising in that delimited space leads to a happy dwelling in the present life (diṭṭhadhamma-sukhavihāra), serves as a basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā), and serves as a basis for insight (vipassanā), but it does not serve as a basis for the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti). However, in this delimited space, successive cessation (anupubba-nirodha) is obtained up to the fifth jhāna, and it is also a basis for the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa). Just as the jhāna arising in this delimited space is a basis for direct knowledge, so too is the jhāna arising in the previous kasinas. However, being a basis for the attainment of cessation is the unique feature here. All other things that should be said regarding this space kasina have already been stated in the Visuddhimagga.
232:
A yogi who desires to perform special psychic transformations (iddhi-vikubbana) in such ways as "Being one, he becomes many," and so forth, must first develop the eight attainments (samāpatti) in the first eight kasiṇas. Then, he must tame his mind through these fourteen modes: (1) in the forward order of kasiṇas (from earth to white), (2) in the reverse order of kasiṇas (from white to earth), (3) in the forward and reverse order of kasiṇas, (4) in the forward order of jhānas, (5) in the reverse order of jhānas, (6) in the forward and reverse order of jhānas, (7) by skipping jhānas (entering jhānas by skipping one level), (8) by skipping kasiṇas (entering kasiṇas by skipping one level), (9) by skipping both jhānas and kasiṇas, (10) by shifting the factors (changing the jhāna factors), (11) by shifting the objects (changing the kasiṇa objects), (12) by shifting both factors and objects, (13) by defining the factors, and (14) by defining the objects. The detailed explanation of these fourteen modes has already been stated in the Visuddhimagga.

Without taming the mind through these fourteen modes, it is impossible for a beginner (ādikammika) yogi, who has not previously developed such meditation, to accomplish special psychic transformations. Indeed, for a beginner, even performing the preliminary work (parikamma) for a kasiṇa is a heavy burden; only one in a hundred or a thousand can perform the preliminary work for a kasiṇa. For one who has performed the preliminary work, the arising of the sign (nimitta) is a heavy burden; only one in a hundred or a thousand can produce the sign. When the sign has arisen, developing that sign and reaching absorption (appanā) is a heavy burden; only one in a hundred or a thousand can attain absorption. For one who has attained absorption, taming the mind through the fourteen modes is a heavy burden; only one in a hundred or a thousand can tame the mind. For one whose mind is tamed through the fourteen modes, performing special psychic transformations is a heavy burden; only one in a hundred or a thousand can reach the stage of psychic transformation. For one who has reached psychic transformation, having the power of quick reviewing (khippanisanti) is a heavy burden; only one in a hundred or a thousand is capable of quick reviewing. This is like the Elder Rakkhita, who had eight years of seniority (vassa) since his higher ordination, among the thirty thousand possessors of psychic power who came to attend to the illness of the Elder Mahārohaṇagutta at Ambatthala in Sri Lanka. That entire story has been detailed in the Visuddhimagga.

## Discussion on Kasiṇa.

## Discussion on the Bases of Mastery (Abhibhāyatana)

Having thus explained the wholesome states of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara-kusala) in the eight kasiṇas, now, because there are other wholesome states of the fine-material sphere called the Bases of Mastery (abhibhāyatana) which occur in these same eight kasiṇas—though the object is the same, the development (bhāvanā) is different—the text continues:
233:
Therefore, to show that wholesome state of the fine-material sphere called the Bases of Mastery, the text begins with "Which are the states that are wholesome?" and so forth. In that context of the Bases of Mastery, "perceiving no form internally" (ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī) refers to one who is devoid of the perception of preliminary work (parikamma-saññā) regarding the forms within his own continuity, either because of not having attained it or because of not desiring it. "He sees forms externally" means that, having performed the preliminary work on the eight external kasiṇas, he sees those forms in the eight external kasiṇas by the power of preliminary work and by the power of absorption. "Limited (non-expanded) objects" refers to objects that have not been expanded.

Regarding the phrase "having mastered" (abhibhuyya) those objects: for example, just as a man with good digestion, upon receiving a mere spoonful of rice, might gather it together and make it into a single mouthful, thinking, "What is there here to be eaten?", even so, a person of superior wisdom and clear knowledge, thinking, "What is there to be attained in this limited object? This is no burden for me," masters those forms and enters absorption. The meaning is that he produces absorption here simultaneously with the arising of the counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta). By the words "I know, I see," the preceding stage of his attention (manasikāra) is described. However, in the Āgama Commentaries (Sutta Commentaries), it is said that by these words, his advertence (ābhoga) is described; and that occurs for one who has emerged from the attainment, not within the attainment.

"Immeasurable (expanded) objects" refers to objects that have been expanded in size. Here, "having mastered" means: for example, just as a gluttonous man, upon receiving a tray full of rice, does not see it as very much, thinking, "Let there be more; what can this much do for me?", even so, a person of superior wisdom and clear knowledge, thinking, "What is there to be attained here? This is not immeasurable; it is no burden for me in producing one-pointedness of mind," masters those objects and enters absorption. The meaning is that he produces absorption here simultaneously with the arising of the counterpart sign.

In the phrases "a limited object that is limited, a limited object that is immeasurable," because the word "limited" appears here, the state of having an immeasurable object is not taken; and because the word "immeasurable" appears later, the state of having a limited object (is not taken). In the Commentary, however, it is said: "In this place, instead of taking four objects each, only two each are taken. For what reason? If four were taken, the teaching would occur sixteen times. The Teacher has already taught the sixteen-fold teaching below in detail, like one spreading sesame seeds on a mat. In this place, His intention (ajjhāsaya) is to give the teaching only eight times. Therefore, it should be understood that only two each are taken."
234:
"Suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇāni" refers to objects with pure and impure colors. Indeed, in this context, pure kasinas such as blue (nīla) and so forth are intended as "suvaṇṇa" (beautiful), and impure ones as "dubbaṇṇa" (ugly). However, in the Āgama Commentaries, it is said: "Whether they are beautiful or ugly, these bases of mastery (abhibhāyatana) are taught only by way of the limited (paritta) and the immeasurable (appamāṇa)." Among these four bases of mastery, the limited comes by way of the speculative temperament (vitakkacarita), the immeasurable by way of the deluded temperament (mohacarita), the beautiful by way of the hating temperament (dosacarita), and the ugly by way of the lustful temperament (rāgacarita). Indeed, these objects are suitable for those of such temperaments. This suitability is explained in detail in the Description of Temperaments (Cariyāniddesa) of the Visuddhimagga.

Why is it that in the Suttas it is taught as "One who is percipient of forms internally sees forms externally that are limited," and so forth, but here in the Abhidhamma, in the four bases of mastery, it is taught only as being non-percipient of forms internally? It is because internal forms are not to be mastered (overcome). Indeed, whether in the Suttas or in this Abhidhamma, only external forms are to be mastered. Therefore, those external forms are mentioned as a rule in both the Suttas and this Abhidhamma. The phrase "non-percipient of forms internally" is merely for the elegance of the Teacher's (the Buddha's) teaching. What has been said so far is the explanation of new terms in the four bases of mastery. As for the pure method (suddhikanaya) and the varieties of progress (paṭipadā), they should be understood in each basis of mastery in the same way as explained in the earth kasina (pathavīkasiṇa).

The distinction in these bases of mastery is that the fourfold object (ārammaṇacatukka) becomes a twofold object (ārammaṇaduka). The sixteenfold method also becomes an eightfold method. All the rest is the same as what was said in the earth kasina. Thus, in each of these bases of mastery, there are fifteen groups of nine (navaka): one pure group of nine, four progress groups of nine, two object groups of nine, and eight mixed object-progress groups of nine. Therefore, in the four bases of mastery, a total of sixty groups of nine should be understood.

## In the Fifth Base of Mastery and so forth

The word "nīlāni" is taught by way of including all blue kasinas. The word "nīlavaṇṇāni" is taught by way of the blue color, and "nīlanidassanāni" by way of appearance. This means they appear as a solid blue, with no visible gaps and no mixture of other colors. The word "nīlanibhāsāni" is taught by way of radiance. It means having a blue radiance or being endowed with blue light. By this, the extreme purity of these bases of mastery is shown. Indeed, these four bases of mastery are taught by way of extremely pure color. In the case of "pītāni" (yellow) and so forth, the meaning should be understood in this same way. One who develops the blue kasina takes the sign (nimitta) in a flower, or a cloth, or a color element...
235:
...and so forth. The creation of the kasina, the preliminary work (parikamma), and the procedure for absorption (appanā) are all explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga. Just as twenty-five groups of nine were understood in the earth kasina, twenty-five groups of nine should be understood in each of these bases of mastery.

## Discussion on the Bases of Mastery (Abhibhāyatanakathā)
## Discussion on the Liberations (Vimokkhakathā)

Now, this fine-material sphere wholesome [consciousness] (rūpāvacarakusala) does not arise only by way of the bases of mastery (abhibhāyatana) because of mastering the bases known as objects; rather, it also arises by way of the liberations (vimokkha). Therefore, to show that method of liberation as well, the teaching begins again with "Which states are wholesome?" and so forth.

In what sense is it known as "liberation" (vimokkha)? In the sense of resolving (adhimuccana). What is this sense of resolving? It is the sense of being well-released from opposing states, and the sense of being well-immersed in the object by way of delight. It means occurring in the object without hesitation and with a state of non-restraint, like the sleeping of a child who has let go of his limbs in his father's lap. This method is begun to show the fine-material sphere wholesome [consciousness] that has reached the state of liberation with such characteristics.

In that text, "rūpီ" (one having form) means: the fine-material jhāna produced in one's own internal (ajjhatta) hair and so forth is "form" (rūpa); because one has that form, one is "rūpī". One who performs the preliminary work (parikamma) for the blue kasina internally does so in the hair, or the bile, or the pupil of the eye. One who performs the preliminary work for the yellow kasina does so in the fat, or the skin, or the yellow part of the eyes. One who performs the preliminary work for the red kasina does so in the flesh, or the blood, or the tongue, or the palms of the hands and soles of the feet, or the red part of the eyes. One who performs the preliminary work for the white kasina does so in the bones, or the teeth, or the nails, or the white part of the eyes. This is said with reference to a person endowed with jhāna that has arisen after performing the preliminary work in this way. "Sees forms" (rūpāni passati) means seeing external forms such as the blue kasina with the jhāna-eye. By this, the attainment of jhāna in internal and external objects is shown.
236:
"Ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī" means not perceiving form internally (having no perception of form). It means one who has not produced fine-material sphere jhāna in one's own hair, and so forth. By this, it is shown that the jhāna is obtained only externally after performing the preliminary work (parikamma) externally.

By the word "subhaṃ" (beautiful), the jhānas occurring in the very pure color kasinas such as blue (nīla), etc., are shown. In those color kasina jhānas, although there is actually no attention (ābhoga) as "beautiful" within the absorption (appanā), because one dwells having made a very pure and beautiful kasina the object, and because that person dwells having attained the first jhāna as "beautiful" ... etc., and likewise the second jhāna, etc., the teaching is given in this way.

In the Paṭisambhidāmagga, however, it is said: "How is the liberation (vimokkha) of one who is resolved (adhimutta) on the beautiful? Here, a bhikkhu dwells pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness (mettā) ... etc. Because of the development of loving-kindness, beings are not repulsive. ... Dwells pervading one direction with a mind imbued with compassion (karuṇā) ... empathetic joy (muditā) ... equanimity (upekkhā) ... etc. Because of the development of equanimity, beings are not repulsive. Thus, the resolution on the beautiful is liberation."

In this Abhidhamma, however, since the divine abodes (brahmavihāras) will appear later in the text, that method is set aside, and the liberation of the beautiful (subhavimokkha) is allowed only by way of the very blue, very yellow, very red, very white, and the completely pure blue, completely pure yellow, completely pure red, and completely pure white. Thus, the states called kasina, abhibhāyatana (base of mastery), and vimokkha (liberation) are only fine-material sphere jhānas. That jhāna is called 'kasina' in the sense of the entirety of the object; it is called 'abhibhāyatana' in the sense of mastering the object; and it is called 'vimokkha' in the sense of being resolved on the object and being liberated from opposing states. Among those three, it should be understood that the teaching on kasina is by way of the Abhidhamma method, while the remaining teachings are by way of the Suttanta method. This is the explanation of the terms not yet mentioned here. In each liberation, seventy-five groups of nine (navakas) should be understood, making twenty-five for each as in the earth kasina.

## Discussion on Liberations (Vimokkhakathā)

## Discussion on Divine Abodes (Brahmavihārakathā)

Now, in order to show the fine-material sphere wholesome states arising by way of the divine abodes such as loving-kindness, etc., the text begins with "Again, which states are wholesome?" and so on. In that (text)...
237:
"Mettāsahagata" means accompanied by loving-kindness. The same method should be understood for "accompanied by compassion" and so forth that follow. The entire procedure for the development of loving-kindness and so forth, by which a person practicing dwells having attained Jhānas accompanied by loving-kindness and so forth, has already been explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga. The meaning of the remaining Pali text should be understood in the same way as the method stated for the earth kasina.

Specifically, in the earth kasina, there are twenty-five groups of nine (navakas). In these Divine Abodes, in the first three—loving-kindness, compassion, and appreciative joy—there are twenty-five groups of seven (sattakas) by way of the three-fold and four-fold Jhānas. In equanimity, there are twenty-five groups of one (ekakas) by way of the fourth Jhāna. In compassion and appreciative joy, these yevāpanaka states are also obtained along with the four states such as desire (chanda) and so forth. The state of "painful practice" (dukkhapaṭipadā) and so forth in these Divine Abodes should be understood: in loving-kindness by way of removing ill-will (byāpāda), in compassion by way of removing cruelty (vihiṃsā), in appreciative joy by way of removing aversion (arati), and in equanimity by way of removing lust (rāga) and resentment (paṭigha). Furthermore, being "of limited object" (parittārammaṇa) occurs by way of not having many beings as the object, and being "of immeasurable object" (appamāṇārammaṇa) occurs by way of having many beings as the object; this is the distinction. The rest is exactly the same as the method stated for the earth kasina.

Thus, first, by way of the Pali text (it should be understood)—

Having known these Divine Abodes in the manner stated,
Which were taught by the Buddha, the Supreme Brahma,
This miscellaneous discussion (pakiṇṇakakathā) regarding them should also be understood further.

Among these aforementioned loving-kindness, compassion, appreciative joy, and equanimity, in terms of word-meaning: it is called 'Mettā' because it loves (mejjati); the meaning is that it loves with the aspect of desiring welfare. Or, it is called 'Mettā' because it occurs in a loved person, or because it occurs for the benefit of a loved person. It is called 'Karuṇā' because it causes the hearts of good people to tremble when others are in suffering. Or, it is called 'Karuṇā' because it oppresses and destroys the suffering of others. Or, it is called 'Karuṇā' because it occurs by way of spreading over those who are suffering. It is called 'Muditā' because those endowed with that state rejoice by it, or because it rejoices itself, or because it is merely the act of rejoicing. It is called 'Upekkha' because it looks on appropriately by abandoning ill-will such as "May they be free from enmity" and so forth, and by arriving at a state of neutrality.

In terms of characteristics and so forth: Mettā has the characteristic of occurring as the aspect of desiring the welfare of beings; its function (rasa) is the providing of welfare to beings; its manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna) is the removal of resentment; its proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) is seeing the lovableness of beings. The stilling of ill-will is the success (sampatti) of that Mettā; the arising of (selfish) affection is its failure (vipatti). Karuṇā has the characteristic of occurring as the aspect of wanting to remove the suffering of beings; its function (rasa) is the inability to bear the suffering of others;
238:
It is manifested in knowledge as the characteristic of non-harming (avihimsā) towards beings. It has the proximate cause of seeing the helplessness of beings who are oppressed by suffering. The subsiding of harming (vihimsā) is its success (sampatti), while the arising of sorrow (soka) is its failure (vipatti).

That which has the characteristic of gladness towards beings is called 'appreciative joy' (muditā). It has the function of non-envy (anissāyana). It is manifested in knowledge as the mode of removing discontent (arati). It has the proximate cause of seeing the success and prosperity of beings. The subsiding of discontent is the success of muditā, while the arising of worldly merriment (pahāsa) based on worldly gain is its failure.

That which has the characteristic of proceeding in a neutral mode towards beings is called 'equanimity' (upekkhā). It has the function of seeing equality in beings. It has the manifestation of the subsiding of resentment (paṭigha) and attachment (anunaya). It has the proximate cause of seeing through the knowledge of ownership of kamma (kammassakatā) thus: 'Beings are the owners of their own kamma; by whose will shall they become happy, or be released from suffering, or not decline from the prosperity they have attained?' The subsiding of resentment and attachment is the success of equanimity, while the arising of ignorant equanimity (aññāṇupekkhā) based on the household life is its failure.

For all four of these divine abidings (Brahmavihāras), the happiness of insight (vipassanā) and the attainment of existence (bhavasampatti—attaining a good destination) are common benefits. However, the removal of ill-will and so forth are specific benefits. Among these Brahmavihāras, mettā has the benefit of removing ill-will (byāpāda). The remaining karuṇā, muditā, and upekkhā have the benefits of removing harming (vihimsā), discontent (arati), and lust (rāga) respectively. It has also been stated thus:

'Friends, this liberation of the mind through loving-kindness (mettā-cetovimutti) is the escape from ill-will. Friends, this liberation of the mind through compassion (karuṇā-cetovimutti) is the escape from harming. Friends, this liberation of the mind through appreciative joy (muditā-cetovimutti) is the escape from discontent. Friends, this liberation of the mind through equanimity (upekkhā-cetovimutti) is the escape from lust.'

In each of these Brahmavihāras, there are two kinds of enemies: the near enemy and the far enemy. The near enemy of the divine abiding of mettā is lust (rāga), because it is similar in seeing the qualities of beings. Like an enemy living nearby, it easily finds an opportunity. Therefore, mettā must be well-guarded against lust. Ill-will (byāpāda) is called the far enemy because its nature is dissimilar to mettā. Therefore, one should develop mettā without fear of ill-will. It is impossible for one who is developing mettā to become angry.

The near enemy of the divine abiding of compassion (karuṇā) is the grief that arises from not obtaining, or from reflecting on the past loss, cessation, or change of pleasant, desirable, lovely, and charming forms cognizable by the eye, which are associated with worldly gain...
239:
...reflecting repeatedly on that which was previously obtained but has now passed away, ceased, or changed, grief (domanassa) arises. Such grief is called household-based grief. Household-based grief, which comes in this manner, is the near enemy of compassion because it is similar in seeing failure (vipatti). Cruelty (vihesā) is the far enemy because its nature is dissimilar. Therefore, one should practice compassion without fear of that cruelty. It is impossible for one to practice compassion and yet harm others with hands or other means.

In the divine abiding of appreciative joy (muditā) as well: 'Joy (somanassa) arises in one who repeatedly reflects on the obtaining of, or on the past obtaining of, pleasant, desirable, lovely, and charming forms cognizable by the eye, which are associated with worldly gain. Such joy is called household-based joy.' Household-based joy, which comes in this manner, is the near enemy of muditā because it is similar in seeing success (sampatti). Discontent (arati) is the far enemy because its nature is dissimilar. Therefore, one should develop muditā without fear of that discontent. It is impossible for one to be joyful and yet be discontented in a secluded dwelling or in the most noble wholesome states.

In the divine abiding of equanimity (upekkhā): 'On seeing a form with the eye, equanimity (upekkhā) arises in the foolish, deluded worldling, who has not overcome limitations, who has not overcome the results of kamma, who does not see the danger, the unlearned worldling. Such equanimity does not transcend the form. Therefore, that equanimity is called household-based equanimity.' Ignorant equanimity (aññāṇupekkhā), which comes in this manner, is the near enemy of equanimity because it is similar in the sense of not reflecting on faults and virtues. Lust (rāga) and resentment (paṭigha) are the far enemies because their natures are dissimilar. Therefore, one should practice equanimity without fear of those lust and resentment. It is impossible for one to practice equanimity and yet be lustful or resentful.

In all these Brahmavihāras, the desire to act (kattukāmyatā-chanda) is the beginning, the suppression of hindrances (nīvaraṇa) and so forth is the middle, and the attainment of absorption (appanā) is the end. By the power of the concept (paññatti), a single being or many beings are the object. When access concentration (upacāra) or absorption (appanā) is reached, the object should be expanded.

The sequence of expanding the object is as follows: Just as a skilled farmer plows after defining the area to be plowed, so too, one should first define a single dwelling (āvāsa) and develop mettā towards the beings in that dwelling thus: 'May the beings in this dwelling be free from enmity.' Having made the mind soft and workable in that dwelling, then two dwellings...
240:
They should be delimited in this way. Beyond that, one should progressively delimit three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, or ten monasteries; then a single street, a half-village, a village, a district, a kingdom, a single direction, and so on, up to a single world system (Cakkavāḷa), or even beyond that, and develop loving-kindness (Mettā) towards the beings in those respective places. The same applies to compassion (Karuṇā) and the others. This is the method of expanding the object (ārammaṇavaḍḍhanakkama) in these divine abidings (Brahmavihāra).

Just as the outcome of the kasiṇas is the immaterial attainments (āruppa), the outcome of the concentrations is the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the outcome of insight (vipassanā) is the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti), and the outcome of both serenity (samatha) and insight is the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti); likewise, the outcome of the three preceding divine abidings is this divine abiding of equanimity (Upekkhā-brahmavihāra). To illustrate: just as it is impossible to set up a pinnacle and rafters in the air without first erecting pillars and mounting the beams, so too it is impossible to develop the fourth jhāna in the preceding divine abidings without having attained the third jhāna. However, this divine abiding of equanimity does not arise based on the third jhāna produced through the kasiṇas, because the objects are of a different nature.

Here, it may be asked: "Why are these—loving-kindness, compassion, appreciative joy, and equanimity—called divine abidings (Brahmavihāra)? Why are there only four? What is their order? And why are they called immeasurables (Appamaññā) in the Vibhaṅga?" The answer is: Firstly, they should be understood as divine abidings in the sense of being noble (seṭṭha) and because of their faultless nature. These abidings are noble because they constitute the right conduct toward beings. Just as the Brahmas dwell with faultless minds, so too the practitioners associated with these qualities dwell like the Brahmas; thus, they are called divine abidings in the sense of being noble and faultless.

As for the questions such as "Why are there only four?", the answer is as follows:

They are four by way of being the path of purification (Visuddhimagga) and so on.
Their order is established by way of the modes of bringing welfare and so on.
They are called immeasurables (Appamaññā) because they occur toward an immeasurable object.

Indeed, among these, loving-kindness is the path of purification for one who is full of ill-will (byāpāda); compassion for one full of cruelty (vihiṃsā); appreciative joy for one full of discontent (arati); and equanimity for one full of lust (rāga). Furthermore, there are only four ways of mental attention toward beings: bringing welfare, removing harm, rejoicing in success, and neutrality. Just as a mother...
241:
...among four sons—a young child, a sick son, an adolescent son, and a son busy with his own affairs—the mother wishes for the young child to grow, wishes for the sick son to be cured of his illness, wishes for the adolescent son to long maintain his youthful success, and is unconcerned (neutral) toward the son busy with his own affairs. In the same way, one who dwells in the divine abidings should act toward all beings through the power of loving-kindness and the rest. Therefore, by way of being the path of purification and so on, the immeasurables are only four.

Since one who wishes to develop these four immeasurables must first act toward beings by way of the mode of bringing welfare, and loving-kindness is characterized by the mode of bringing welfare; then, seeing, hearing, or considering the suffering and oppression of those beings for whom welfare was thus desired, one should act by way of the mode of removing suffering, and compassion is characterized by the mode of removing suffering; then, seeing the success of those beings for whom welfare and the removal of suffering were desired, one should act by way of rejoicing in their success, and appreciative joy is characterized by the mode of rejoicing; thereafter, since there is nothing more to be done, one should act with the mode of neutrality, known as the state of looking on, and equanimity is characterized by the mode of neutrality. Therefore, by way of these modes of welfare and so on, loving-kindness is mentioned first. After that, this order of compassion, appreciative joy, and equanimity should be understood.

Because all these occur toward an immeasurable object, they are called immeasurables (Appamaññā). Immeasurable beings are the objects of these qualities. Even if practiced toward a single being, they occur by way of pervading entirely without taking a limit such as "loving-kindness and so on should be developed in only this much of an area." Therefore, it is said:

They are four by way of being the path of purification and so on,
By way of the modes of welfare and so on,
And because they occur toward an immeasurable object,
These qualities are called immeasurables.

Although they share the single characteristic of having an immeasurable object, among these, the first three belong only to the third and fourth jhānas. Why? Because they are not dissociated from joy (somanassa). Why are they not dissociated from joy?
242:
Because they are the means of escape from ill-will and other such states arising from displeasure, (the first three—loving-kindness, compassion, and appreciative joy—are conjoined with joy). However, the last one (equanimity as a divine abiding) is conjoined only with one of the remaining (fourth or fifth) jhānas. Why? Because it is conjoined with neutral feeling. This is because equanimity as a divine abiding, which occurs as a mode of neutrality toward beings, cannot exist without neutral feeling.

## Discussion on the Divine Abidings (Brahmavihārakathā)

## Discussion on Foulness (Asubhakathā)

Now, in order to show the wholesome states of the fine-material sphere which are absolutely beneficial for beings of lustful temperament, and which occur by way of individual jhānas upon various objects, the passage beginning with "Which states are wholesome?" (Katame dhammā kusalā) is once again undertaken.

In the phrases such as "associated with the perception of a bloated corpse" (uddhumātakasaññāsahagata), it is called "bloated" (uddhumāta) because it is swollen like a bag full of air, due to the state of being puffed up by the gradual rise of bloating after the end of life. The bloated itself is the "bloated corpse" (uddhumātaka). Alternatively, it is called "uddhumātaka" because it is a loathsome, bloated body, being disgusting. This is a designation for a corpse of such a nature. A body that is discolored and has a patchy dark-blue color is called "livid" (vinīla). The livid itself is the "livid corpse" (vinīlaka). Alternatively, it is called "vinīlaka" because it is a loathsome, livid body, being disgusting. This is a designation for a corpse that has a red color in fleshy parts, a white color in places where pus has accumulated, and is generally dark-blue in color, appearing like a dark-blue cloth draped over the dark parts. A corpse that has pus trickling from broken places is called "festering" (vipubba). The festering itself is the "festering corpse" (vipubbaka). Alternatively, it is called "vipubbaka" because it is a loathsome, festering body, being disgusting. This is a designation for a corpse of such a nature. A body that is split by being cut into two parts is called "cut-up" (vicchidda). The cut-up itself is the "cut-up corpse" (vicchiddaka). Alternatively, it is called "vicchiddaka" because it is a loathsome, cut-up body, being disgusting. This is a designation for a corpse cut in the middle. A corpse that has been gnawed by dogs, jackals, etc., in various ways here and there is called "gnawed" (vikkhāyita). The gnawed itself is the "gnawed corpse" (vikkhāyitaka). Alternatively, it is called "vikkhāyitaka" because it is a loathsome, gnawed body, being disgusting. This is a designation for a corpse of such a nature. A corpse that has been thrown in various directions is called "scattered" (vikkhitta). The scattered itself is the "scattered corpse" (vikkhittaka). Alternatively, it is called "vikkhittaka" because it is a loathsome, scattered body, being disgusting. This is a designation for a corpse whose hands are in one place, feet in another, and head in another, having been thrown here and there. That which is both hacked in the previously mentioned manner and scattered is called "hacked and scattered" (hatavikkhittaka). This refers to a corpse that has been hacked on its limbs with a weapon in the shape of a crow's foot and then scattered in the manner already described...
243:
This name (hatavikkhittaka) is a designation for such a corpse. It is called "bleeding" (lohitaka) because it scatters, spreads, and trickles blood here and there. This is a designation for a corpse smeared with blood trickling from itself. Worms are called "puḷava." It is called "worm-infested" (puḷavaka) because it causes worms to be shed. This is a designation for a corpse full of worms. A bone itself is called "aṭṭhika." Alternatively, it is called "aṭṭhika" because it is a loathsome bone, being disgusting. This name (aṭṭhika) is used for both a skeleton and a single bone. Furthermore, these same names apply to the signs (nimitta) that arise based on these bloated corpses, etc., and to the jhānas obtained through those signs.

Among those (foulness objects), the perception that arises by way of absorption (appanā) in the sign of a bloated corpse is called "perception of a bloated corpse" (uddhumātakasaññā). That which is associated with that perception of a bloated corpse in the sense of being conjoined is called "associated with the perception of a bloated corpse" (uddhumātakasaññāsahagata). The same method applies to "associated with the perception of a livid corpse," and so on. Whatever procedure of meditation should be stated here has already been stated in every way in the Visuddhimagga. The remaining commentary on the Pali text should be understood in the same manner as previously mentioned. However, the distinction here is that, just as in the equanimity divine abiding by way of the fourth jhāna, in this foulness meditation, there are twenty-five individual factors (ekaka) in each by way of the first jhāna. Since the foulness object should not be expanded, the sign as an object arising in a small bloated area is to be understood as a "limited object" (parittārammaṇa). The sign as an object in a large bloated area is to be understood as an "immeasurable object" (appamāṇārammaṇa). The same method applies to the remaining types of foulness.

Thus, the Ten-Powered One (the Buddha), whose fame is praised by the Thousand-Eyed One (Sakka), has taught these ten kinds of foulness, which are the causes for each individual jhāna. Having thus understood all those kinds of foulness according to the method of the Pali, this further miscellaneous discussion (pakiṇṇakakathā) regarding them should also be understood.

Among these ten kinds of foulness, a person who has attained jhāna in any one of them becomes one whose conduct is free from greed, like one who is free from lust, because lust has been well suppressed. Even though this is so, the reason why this classification of foulness is taught is to be understood as being by way of the natural occurrence of the body and by way of the different types of lustful temperament.

For a corpse, when reaching a state of loathsomeness, may reach the state of being bloated, or it may reach one of the other states such as being livid. In whatever way...
244:
In such a corpse, the bloated (uddhumātaka) foulness is repulsive, the livid (vinīlaka) foulness is repulsive—by attending in this way, the learning sign (uggaha-nimitta) is to be grasped. Therefore, it should be understood that the ten types of foulness are taught according to the natural state of the corpse.

Specifically, among these ten types of foulness, the bloated (uddhumātaka) foulness is a suitable remedy for one who is lustful of the body's shape, as it manifests the ruin of the body's form. The livid (vinīlaka) foulness is suitable for one who is lustful of the body's complexion, as it manifests the corruption of the skin's color. The festering (vipubbaka) foulness is suitable for one who is lustful of the body's scent produced by flowers, perfumes, and so on, as it manifests the foul-smelling nature connected to the body's sores. The cut-up (vicchiddaka) foulness is suitable for one who is lustful of the body's solidity (perceiving it as without holes or cavities), as it manifests the hollow nature within. The gnawed (vikkhāyitaka) foulness is suitable for one who is lustful of the fullness of flesh in body parts such as the breasts, as it manifests the destruction of the excellence of the accumulation of flesh. The scattered (vikkhittaka) foulness is suitable for one who is lustful of the graceful movement of the limbs, as it manifests the scattering of the major and minor limbs. The hacked and scattered (hatavikkhittaka) foulness is suitable for one who is lustful of the perfection of the body's joints, as it manifests the alteration and destruction of the body's joints. The bleeding (lohitaka) foulness is suitable for one who is lustful of the beauty produced by ornaments, as it manifests the repulsiveness of being smeared with blood. The worm-infested (puḷavaka) foulness is suitable for one who is lustful of the attachment to 'my body,' as it manifests the body's commonality with many families of worms. The skeleton (aṭṭhika) foulness is suitable for one who is lustful of the perfection and beauty of the teeth, as it manifests the repulsiveness of the bones in the body. Thus, it should be understood that the ten types of foulness are also taught according to the varieties of lustful temperament.

Because in these ten types of foulness, just as a boat in a river with a swift current and unstable water can only stay by the power of the oar and cannot stay without it, so too, because the object is weak, the mind can only become concentrated and stay by the power of initial application (vitakka); it cannot stay without initial application. Therefore, only the first absorption (paṭhama-jhāna) occurs here, not the second and so on. Even in this repulsive object, rapture and happiness (pīti-somanassa) arise because of seeing the benefits, thinking, 'Surely by this practice I shall be liberated from aging and death,' and because of abandoning the fever of the hindrances (nīvaraṇa). This is like the joy of a flower-scavenger at a dung heap who sees the benefit, thinking, 'Now I shall receive many wages,' or like the joy of a patient suffering from a severe illness when vomiting or purging occurs.

These ten types of foulness are one and the same by way of characteristic. For the characteristic of all these ten is simply the state of being impure, foul-smelling, disgusting, and repulsive. This aforementioned foulness is not only apparent in a dead body by this characteristic, but it is also apparent in the body of a living person. For example, it appeared to Elder Mahā Tissa residing at Cetiya Mountain upon seeing the teeth of a laughing woman, and it appeared to the attendant novice of Elder Saṃgharakkhita who looked up at the king on the back of an elephant. Indeed, just as a dead body is foul, so too is a living body purely foul.
245:
By this characteristic, [foulness] appears not only in a dead body, but also in a living body, just as it appeared to Elder Mahā Tissa residing at Cetiya Mountain upon seeing the [teeth] bones [of a laughing woman], and as it appeared to the attendant novice of Elder Saṃgharakkhita who looked up at the king on the back of an elephant. For indeed, just as a dead body is foul, so too is a living body purely foul. However, in this living body, the characteristic of foulness is not apparent [to most people] because it is hidden by external ornaments.

## Talk on Foulness.

Is this fine-material absorption (rūpāvacara-appanā), starting from the earth kasiṇa and ending with the perception of the skeleton, the only one, or are there other fine-material absorptions? There are others. The absorption of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna-jhāna) and the development of mindfulness of the body (kāyagatāsati) were not mentioned here. Although they were not mentioned, when the air kasiṇa is taken, the mindfulness of breathing absorption is already included. When the color kasiṇas are taken, mindfulness of the body occurring by way of the fourfold and fivefold jhānas in parts such as the hair is already included. When the ten types of foulness are taken, mindfulness of the body occurring by way of the absorption on the repulsiveness of the thirty-two parts, and by way of the absorption on the color of the nine charnel ground (sivathika) stages, is already included. Therefore, all fine-material absorptions are indeed mentioned here.

## The Talk on Fine-material Wholesome States is Finished.

## Description of Immaterial Wholesome States

## The Sphere of Infinite Space

Now, to show the immaterial wholesome states, the text begins again with 'Which states are wholesome?' and so on. Therein, 'arūpūpapattiyā' means: the immaterial existence is 'arūpa'; rebirth in the immaterial existence is 'arūpūpapatti'; [for the sake of] that rebirth in the immaterial existence. 'Maggaṃ bhāveti' means: one produces and develops the means, the root, the cause. 'Sabbaso' means: in every way, or all [perceptions of form] without remainder. 'Rūpasaññānaṃ' refers to the fine-material jhānas, which are spoken of by way of perception (saññā) as the head, and also to their objects (the kasiṇa forms). For even the fine-material jhāna is called 'rūpa' in such passages as 'Possessing form, he sees forms' (rūpī rūpāni passati). Its object is also [called form] in such passages as 'Externally he sees forms, beautiful and ugly.' Therefore, here, the perception occurring in the fine-material jhāna is 'rūpasaññā'; in this way...
246:
This name "rūpasaññā" (perception of form) is a designation for the fine-material sphere jhāna (rūpāvacara jhāna), spoken of by way of its predominant perception. Because the object of that jhāna is named "kasina-form," that object is called "rūpasaññā." It means that the object is designated as "form." In this way, it should be understood that the objects of that rūpa-jhāna, such as the earth-kasina and so on, are also called "rūpasaññā."

"Samatikkamā" (by surpassing) occurs through detachment (virāga) and cessation (nirodha). What is meant is this: by way of the fifteen rūpasaññās known as jhānas—consisting of the wholesome, the resultant, and the functional—and by way of the eight rūpasaññās known as objects—consisting of the earth-kasina and so on—one enters and dwells in the base of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana) through the total detachment from and cessation of these, and because of the causes of detachment and cessation. This is because one who has not completely surpassed perceptions of form in every way is unable to enter and dwell in this base of infinite space.

Among those objects and perceptions, for one who is not detached from the object, the surpassing of perception cannot occur; and when perceptions are well surpassed, the object is also well surpassed. Therefore, without directly mentioning the surpassing of the object, the Vibhaṅga states: "Among those rūpasaññās, what is rūpasaññā? For one who has attained a fine-material sphere attainment, or for one who has been reborn there, or for one who dwells in happiness in this very life, there is perception, perceiving, and the state of perceiving; these are called rūpasaññās. One has surpassed, specially surpassed, and well surpassed these rūpasaññās. Therefore, it is said: 'by surpassing perceptions of form in every way'" (Vibh. 602). Thus, only the surpassing of perceptions is taught. However, since these attainments must be reached by surpassing the object—unlike the first jhāna and so on which occur on a single object—it should be understood that this commentary is also made by way of surpassing the object.

"Paṭighasaññānam atthaṅgamā" (with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance) means that perception which arises from the impingement of the bases such as the eye and the objects such as visible forms is called perception of resistance (paṭighasaññā). This is a designation for perceptions of form (sights) and so on. As it is said in the Vibhaṅga: "Among those, what is paṭighasaññā? Perception of form, perception of sound, perception of smell, perception of taste, and perception of touch; these are called perceptions of resistance" (Vibh. 603). By the disappearance of all ten of these perceptions of resistance—the five wholesome resultants and the five unwholesome resultants—it means they are ceased by way of abandoning and by not letting them arise again through non-occurrence.

In fact, these perceptions of resistance do not exist even for one who has attained the first jhāna and so on, because at that time, the mind does not occur by way of the five doors. Even though this is so, [they are mentioned here as] having been abandoned in other jhānas...
247:
Just as pleasure and pain are mentioned in the fourth jhāna, and self-identity view (sakkāya-diṭṭhi) and so on are mentioned in the third path (anāgāmi-magga), it should be understood that the cessation of these perceptions of resistance is mentioned in this first formless discourse by way of praising this jhāna to inspire effort in those who practice it.

Alternatively, it is true that those perceptions of resistance do not exist for one who has attained a fine-material sphere jhāna; however, they do not 'not exist' because of having been abandoned (they simply lack the conditions to arise). This is because the development of fine-material sphere jhāna does not lead to detachment from form, and the occurrence of those perceptions of resistance is connected to form. This formless meditation (arūpa-bhāvanā), however, does lead to detachment from form. Therefore, it is appropriate to say that those perceptions of resistance have been abandoned in this formless jhāna. Not only is it appropriate to say so, but it is also appropriate to definitely maintain that they are abandoned in this way.

Indeed, it was because those perceptions of resistance were not yet abandoned prior to this formless jhāna that the Blessed One said, "Sound is a thorn" to one who has attained the first jhāna. In this formless jhāna, however, because they have been abandoned, the imperturbability (āneñjata) and the peaceful liberation (santavimokkha) of the formless attainments are taught. While the ascetic Āḷāra of the Kālāma clan was in a formless attainment, he not only failed to see five hundred carts passing right by him, but he did not even hear the sound of the carts.

"Nānattasaññānam amanasikārā" (through non-attention to perceptions of diversity) refers either to perceptions occurring in diverse objects or to perceptions that have diverse natures. Because the Vibhaṅga defines them thus: "Among those, what are perceptions of diversity? For one who has not attained [jhāna], there is perception, perceiving, and the state of perceiving associated with the mind-element (manodhātu) or associated with the mind-consciousness-element (manoviññāṇadhātu); these are called perceptions of diversity" (Vibh. 604). Thus, by this classification, those very perceptions are intended here. The perceptions included in the mind-element and mind-consciousness-element of one not in attainment occur in diverse objects of different natures, such as visible forms, sounds, and so on. Furthermore, these forty-four perceptions—namely, 8 sense-sphere wholesome perceptions, 12 unwholesome perceptions, 11 sense-sphere wholesome resultant perceptions, 2 unwholesome resultant perceptions, and 11 sense-sphere functional perceptions—are called perceptions of diversity because they are unlike one another and have diverse natures. "Amanasikārā" means through the total non-attention, non-advertence, non-engagement, and non-reflection upon those perceptions of diversity. It means this because one does not advert to, does not attend to, and does not reflect upon those perceptions.

This is because, among these three types of perceptions, the previously mentioned perceptions of form and perceptions of resistance do not exist even in the realm of existence produced by this first formless jhāna, let alone at the time of dwelling in this attainment within that realm. Therefore, the absence of those perceptions of form and resistance is taught in both ways as "surpassing" (samatikkamā) and "disappearance" (atthaṅgamā). Regarding perceptions of diversity, however, the 8 sense-sphere wholesome perceptions...
248:
The nine functional perceptions (kiriya-saññā), the ten unwholesome perceptions (akusala-saññā), [and the eight great wholesome perceptions (mahākusala-saññā)]—these twenty-seven perceptions exist in the state of existence brought about by this jhāna. Therefore, it should be understood that [the attainment of the base of infinite space] is said to occur because of non-attention to those perceptions. Indeed, even in that realm, one who dwells having attained this first immaterial jhāna dwells only through non-attention to those twenty-seven perceptions. If one attends to those perceptions, one is not an attainer of the jhāna.

In this context, briefly, by the phrase 'with the transcending of perceptions of form' (rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamā), the abandoning of all fine-material sphere states (rūpāvacara-dhamma) is expressed. It should be understood that by the two phrases 'with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact' (paṭighasaññānaṃ atthangamā) and 'with non-attention to perceptions of diversity' (nānattasaññānaṃ amanasikārā), the abandoning and non-attention to all sense-sphere consciousness and mental factors (kāmāvacara-citta-cetasika) are expressed.

Thus, the Blessed One, by means of these three phrases—'with the transcending of the fifteen perceptions of form, with the disappearance of the ten perceptions of sensory impact, and with non-attention to the forty-four perceptions of diversity'—spoke in praise of the attainment of the base of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana-samāpatti). For what reason did He speak thus? He spoke for the purpose of generating intense effort and for the purpose of enticement in those who listen. For if some foolish people should say, 'The Teacher says, "Produce the attainment of the base of infinite space"; what indeed is the benefit of this produced attainment? What is its advantage?', He spoke in praise of the attainment in these ways so that they might not be able to speak thus. Upon hearing that praise, they will think: 'This attainment is indeed so peaceful, so sublime; we shall produce this attainment.' Then, they will make an effort to bring about that attainment.

He also spoke in praise of this attainment for the purpose of enticing them, like the Visakaṇṭaka merchant. The Visakaṇṭaka merchant refers to a molasses merchant. It is said that he took solid molasses, soft molasses, molasses pieces, sugar, and so on, in a cart to a border village and proclaimed, 'Buy Visakaṇṭaka! Buy Visakaṇṭaka!' Hearing this, the villagers said, 'What is called poison (visa) is very harsh; he who eats it dies. A thorn (kaṇṭaka) also kills by piercing. Both of these are harsh; what benefit is there in this?' and they closed their house doors and made their children run away. Seeing this, the merchant thought, 'These villagers are not skilled in terminology; now I will make them buy by means of a device.' He then proclaimed, 'Buy the very sweet delicacy! Buy the very delicious delicacy! Solid molasses, soft molasses, and sugar can be obtained at a cheap price; they can even be obtained for counterfeit coins and counterfeit small change.' Hearing this, the villagers were greatly delighted, came out, and bought them by giving a high price.

In that simile, the merchant's proclamation 'Buy Visakaṇṭaka' is like the Blessed One's words 'Produce the attainment of the base of infinite space.' 'Both of these...
249:
It should be understood that the villagers' thought, 'Both of these are harsh; what advantage is there in this?' is like the listeners' thought, 'The Blessed One said, "Produce the base of infinite space"; what advantage is there in this? We do not know the benefit of that base of infinite space.'
