Then, the merchant's words such as 'Buy the very sweet' are like the Blessed One's declaration of the advantages of the base of infinite space, such as the transcending of perceptions of form. Just as those villagers, upon hearing of the advantages, gave a high price and took the molasses, so too, it should be understood that the Blessed One spoke for the purpose of generating effort and for the purpose of enticement, thinking that those with minds enticed by these advantages would make great effort and produce this attainment.

In the phrase 'associated with the perception of the base of infinite space' (ākāsānañcāyatana-saññā-sahagataṃ): because that space has no end, it is called 'infinite' (ananta). Infinite space is 'ākāsānanta'. 'Ākāsānanta' itself is 'ākāsānañca'. That 'ākāsānañca' is the 'base' (āyatana) for this jhāna along with its associated states, in the sense of being a support, like the 'abode of the gods' (devāyatana) is for the gods; thus it is 'ākāsānañcāyatana'. Thus, because it is both 'ākāsānañca' and an 'āyatana', it is called 'ākāsānañcāyatana'. This is a designation for the space from which the kasiṇa has been removed. That which is associated with the perception that has reached absorption (appanā) in that object of the base of infinite space is called 'associated with the perception of the base of infinite space'.

Just as in other Suttas it is taught as 'infinite space', in this Abhidhamma, it should not be taken as either 'infinite' (ananta) or 'limited' (paritta). Why? Because if 'infinite' is taken, 'limited' is not included; if 'limited' is taken, 'infinite' is not included. If that were the case, the fourfold classification of objects (ārammaṇa-catukka) would not be complete, and the teaching would not occur sixteen times. The Fully Enlightened One, in this context, had the intention to make the teaching occur sixteen times. Therefore, without saying 'infinite' or 'limited', He said 'associated with the perception of the base of infinite space'. Only by saying this are both 'infinite' and 'limited' included, the fourfold classification of objects is completed, and the teaching is completed sixteen times. The remaining meaning of the Pali should be understood in the same manner as described below. Here, because of the difficulty in exhausting the attachment to the fine-material sphere fourth jhāna, it is called 'painful progress' (dukkha-paṭipadā). For one whose attachment is exhausted, because the occurrence of absorption is slow, it is called 'slow intuition' (dandhābhiññā). Conversely, 'pleasant progress' (sukha-paṭipadā) and 'quick intuition' (khippābhiññā) should be understood. The jhāna occurring in the space from which a small kasiṇa has been removed is called 'having a limited object' (parittārammaṇa). The jhāna occurring in the space from which a vast kasiṇa has been removed is called 'having an immeasurable object' (appamāṇārammaṇa). As in the case of the divine abiding of equanimity (upekkhā-brahmavihāra), here too, by way of the fourth jhāna, twenty-five single items (ekaka) occur.
250:
They occur. Just as they occur in this sphere of infinite space, so too they occur in the sphere of infinite consciousness and the others that follow (25 each). However, I will explain only the specific differences in those spheres.

## Viññāṇañcāyatana
In the phrase "transcending the sphere of infinite space" (ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma), according to the method previously mentioned, the jhāna is called the "sphere of infinite space" because it has infinite space as its base (adhiṭṭhāna) along with its associated states. By the same method, the object is also called the "sphere of infinite space." Thus, by transcending both this jhāna and its object through non-occurrence and non-attention, one attains and dwells in this jhāna of the sphere of infinite consciousness. Therefore, it should be understood that the Buddha taught "transcending the sphere of infinite space" by taking both the jhāna and the object together.

In the phrase "accompanied by the perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness" (viññāṇañcāyatana-saññā-sahagataṃ), it is called "infinite" (ananta) because that first formless consciousness has no end by way of being attended to as "infinite." Infinity itself is "ānañca." Instead of saying "viññāṇānañca," it is said as "viññāṇañca." This term "viññāṇañca" is a conventional usage (ruḷhī-sadda) here. That very infinite first formless consciousness is called the "sphere" (āyatana) because it is the base for this perception; thus, it is the "sphere of infinite consciousness." Because it is accompanied by the perception occurring in that base of the sphere of infinite consciousness, it is called "accompanied by the perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness." This is a designation for the jhāna that has the first formless consciousness occurring in space as its object. In this jhāna of the sphere of infinite consciousness, it is "painful progress" (dukkha paṭipadā) due to the difficulty of exhausting the attachment to the attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness. For one who has exhausted attachment, it is "slow intuition" (dandhābhiññā) because the attainment of absorption (appanā) is slow. Conversely, "pleasant progress" (sukha paṭipadā) and "quick intuition" (khippābhiññā) should also be understood. It should be understood as having a "limited object" (parittārammaṇa) when it occurs by taking as its object the attainment of space from which a limited kasina has been removed. Conversely, it should be understood as having an "immeasurable object" (appamāṇārammaṇa). The remaining explanation is the same as what was said before.

## Ākiñcaññāyatana
In the phrase "transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness" (viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma) as well, by the method previously mentioned, the jhāna is called the "sphere of infinite consciousness" because it has the infinite first formless consciousness as its base. By the same method, the object is also called the "sphere of infinite consciousness." Thus, by transcending both this jhāna and its object through non-occurrence and non-attention, one attains and dwells in this jhāna of the sphere of nothingness. Therefore, it should be understood that the Buddha taught "transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness" by taking both the jhāna and the object together.
251:
In the phrase "accompanied by the perception of the sphere of nothingness" (ākiñcaññāyatana-saññā-sahagata), "nothingness" (akiñcana) means that there is not even a slight residue of that first formless consciousness; it means there is not even a trace of its dissolution (bhaṅga) remaining. The state of having no residue is "ākiñcañña." This is a designation for the departure or disappearance of the consciousness of the sphere of infinite space from knowledge. That nothingness is called the "sphere" (āyatana) because it is the base for this perception; thus, it is the "sphere of nothingness." Because it is accompanied by the perception occurring in that sphere of nothingness, it is called "accompanied by the perception of the sphere of nothingness." This is a designation for the jhāna that has the departure of the consciousness occurring in space as its object.

In this jhāna of the sphere of nothingness, it is "painful progress" (dukkha paṭipadā) due to the difficulty of exhausting the attachment to the attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness. For one who has exhausted attachment, it is "slow intuition" (dandhābhiññā) because the attainment of absorption (appanā) is slow. Conversely, it is "pleasant progress" (sukha paṭipadā) and "quick intuition" (khippābhiññā). It should be understood that if it takes as its object the departure of the consciousness occurring in space from which a small kasina has been removed, it is "limited object" (parittārammaṇa), and conversely, it is "immeasurable object" (appamāṇārammaṇa). The remaining words are the same as what was said before.

## Nevasaññānāsaññāyatana
In the phrase "transcending the sphere of nothingness" (ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ samatikkamma) as well, by the method previously mentioned, the jhāna is called the "sphere of nothingness" because it has nothingness as its base. By the same method, the object is also called the "sphere of nothingness." Thus, by transcending both the jhāna and the object through non-occurrence and non-attention, one attains and dwells in this sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Therefore, it should be understood that the Buddha taught "transcending the sphere of nothingness" by taking both together.

In the phrase "accompanied by the perception of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana-saññā-sahagata), as to why it is called "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" due to the state of which perception, and how that perception occurs to the practitioner, the Vibhaṅga Pāḷi explains by extracting the term "neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient" (nevasaññīnāsaññī): "He attends to that very sphere of nothingness as peaceful; he develops the attainment with a remainder of formations; therefore, he is called neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient." In that context, "attends to as peaceful" means he attends to it as "peaceful" because it has a peaceful object, thinking, "This attainment is indeed peaceful, for it can remain even by taking non-existence (natthibhāva) as its object." If he attends to it as peaceful, how does transcendence occur? It occurs because of the desire not to attend to it. Even if that yogi...
252:
That meditator adverts to the attainment of the sphere of nothingness as peaceful. However, for that meditator, such adverting, repeated adverting, and attention as "I shall advert to this jhāna, I shall attain it, I shall resolve upon it, I shall emerge from it, I shall review it" do not occur. Why? Because the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is more peaceful and more sublime than the sphere of nothingness.

For example, a king endowed with great royal majesty, while traveling through the city streets on the back of an elephant, sees ivory carvers and other craftsmen, dressed firmly in a single cloth, with their heads wrapped in another, their bodies covered in ivory dust, making various ivory carvings and so on. Seeing them, he is pleased with their skill, thinking, "Oh, how skilled these masters are, that they can perform such delicate arts!" However, it does not occur to the king to think, "Oh, if only I could give up my kingship and become such a craftsman!" Why is that? Because the benefits of kingship are so great. He simply passes those craftsmen by. 

In the same way, although this meditator adverts to that attainment as peaceful, such adverting, repeated adverting, and attention as "I shall advert to this attainment, I shall attain it, I shall resolve upon it, I shall emerge from it, I shall review it" do not occur. As he adverts to that attainment as peaceful, he reaches that extremely subtle perception which has attained absorption, of which it is said, "He is one with neither-perception-nor-non-perception; he develops the attainment with a remainder of formations." "Attainment with a remainder of formations" refers to the fourth formless attainment, which has formations that have reached an extremely subtle state.

Now, to show the meaning of that which is called "sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" by virtue of the perception thus attained, it is said (in the Vibhaṅga): "The sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception refers to the states of consciousness and mental factors of one who has attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, or of one who has been reborn there, or of one who dwells in happiness in this very life." Among these, the states of consciousness and mental factors of one who has attained it are intended here.

As for the meaning of the words here: because of the absence of gross perception and the presence of subtle perception, the jhāna together with its associated states has neither perception nor non-perception, thus it is "neither-perception-nor-non-perception." That which is neither-perception-nor-non-perception is also an "ayatana" (sphere) because it is included within the mind-base and the mental-object base; thus it is the "sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception." Alternatively, because the perception here is incapable of performing the function of distinct perception...
253:
Because it is incapable of performing the function of distinct perception, it cannot be called perception; yet, because it exists as a remainder of subtle formations, it is not non-perception; thus it is "neither-perception-nor-non-perception." That neither-perception-nor-non-perception is also an "ayatana" (sphere) in the sense of being a support for the remaining states; thus it is the "sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception."

Not only is perception like this here, but in fact, feeling is also neither-feeling-nor-non-feeling, consciousness is neither-consciousness-nor-non-consciousness, and contact is neither-contact-nor-non-contact. This method applies to the remaining associated states as well. However, it should be understood that this teaching is given with perception as the head. This meaning should be illustrated by the similes of the oil-smeared bowl and so on. It is said that a novice smeared a bowl with oil and set it aside. At the time of drinking rice gruel, the Elder said, "Bring the bowl." The novice said, "Venerable sir, there is oil in the bowl" (referring to its unsuitability). Then, when told, "Bring it, novice, I will fill the oil tube," he said, "Venerable sir, there is no oil" (referring to there not being enough to fill the tube). In that simile, just as there is said to be oil in the sense of it being unsuitable for gruel because it is smeared inside, and there is said to be no oil because of the absence of enough to fill a tube, so too, that perception is "neither-perception" because it is incapable of performing the function of distinct perception, and "non-non-perception" because it exists as a remainder of subtle formations.

What is the function of perception here? It is the perceiving of an object and the producing of disenchantment by becoming an object of insight. Just as the fire element in hot water is unable to perform the function of burning, so this perception is unable to perform the function of perceiving distinctly. It is also unable to produce disenchantment by becoming an object of insight like the perception in the other attainments. A monk who has not previously practiced insight on other aggregates is not capable of reaching disenchantment by comprehending the aggregates of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Indeed, only a great wise person who is a natural insight-worker like the Venerable Sāriputta would be able to. Even such a person can only do so by way of comprehension in groups (kalāpasammasana), thinking, "Thus indeed these states, having not been, come to be; having been, they disappear," and not by way of insight into states one by one (anupadadhamma-vipassanā). Thus this attainment has reached such subtlety.

And just as with the simile of the oil-smeared bowl, this meaning should also be illustrated by the simile of water on the road. It is said that a novice walking ahead of an Elder who was traveling saw a little water and said, "Venerable sir, there is water; remove your sandals." Then, when the Elder said, "If there is water, bring the bathing cloth, I will bathe," the novice replied, "Venerable sir, there is no water." In that simile, just as there is said to be water because there is enough to wet the sandals, but there is no water for the purpose of bathing...
254:
When it is said, "I will bathe," he says, "Venerable sir, there is no [water]." In that analogy, although it could be said "there is water" in the sense that there is just enough to wet one's sandals, for the purpose of bathing, it must be said "there is no water." Similarly, this perception (of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception) is not "perception" because it is incapable of performing the function of distinct perception; yet it is not "non-perception" because it exists in a subtle state as a remainder of formations (saṅkhāra). This meaning should be clarified not only by these analogies but also by other suitable ones. Thus, it is called "associated with the perception of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana-saññā-sahagata) because it occurs with the perception in this sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, or because it occurs with the perception that is the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. This is a designation for the jhāna that has the attainment of the sphere of nothingness as its object.

Here, in this (sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception), it is "painful practice" (dukkhā paṭipadā) because it is difficult to exhaust the attachment to the attainment of the sphere of nothingness. It is "slow intuition" (dandhābhiññā) because for one whose attachment is exhausted, the arrival at absorption (appanā) is slow. If the opposite is the case, it is "pleasant practice" (sukhā paṭipadā) and "quick intuition" (khippābhiññā). It should be understood as having a "limited object" (parittārammaṇa) because it occurs by taking as its object the disappearance of the consciousness that occurred in the space from which a limited kasina has been removed; if the opposite is the case, it has an "immeasurable object" (appamāṇārammaṇa). The remaining points are the same as those mentioned previously.

## Asadisurūpo nātho, āruppaṃ yaṃ catubbidhaṃ āha;
## Taṃ iti ñatvā tasmiṃ, pakiṇṇakakathāpi viññeyyā.

The Protector (the Buddha), who possesses an incomparable form (or nature), taught the fourfold formless states. Having known those formless states in this way, the miscellaneous discussion regarding those jhānas should also be understood.

Arūpasamāpattiyo hi—
## Ārammaṇātikkamato, catassopi bhavantimā;
## Aṅgātikkamamētāsaṃ, na icchanti vibhāvino.

These four formless attainments exist only by the transcending of the object. Wise men do not desire the transcending of factors for these formless attainments.

Among those formless attainments, the first occurs by transcending the sign of form (rūpa-nimitta); the second by transcending space (ākāsa); the third by transcending the consciousness that occurred in space; and the fourth by transcending the disappearance (non-existence) of the consciousness that occurred in space. Thus, in every way, it should be understood that "these four formless attainments exist by the transcending of the object." The wise do not desire the transcending of factors for these. This is because, unlike in the fine-material sphere attainments (rūpāvacara-samāpatti), there is no transcending of factors in these formless attainments. For in all these, there are only two jhāna factors: equanimity (upekkhā) and one-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā). Even though there is no transcending of factors—

## Supaṇītarā honti, pacchimā pacchimā idha;
## Upamā tattha viññeyyā, pāsādatalasāṭikā.

In these formless attainments, each subsequent attainment is more refined. In this regard, the analogies of the palace floors and the cloths should be understood.
255:
For example, on the lowest floor of a four-storied palace, there might be present the five refined cords of sensual pleasure in the form of divine dancing, singing, music, fragrant scents, flowers, delicious drinks, food, couches, and clothing. On the second floor, there would be more refined ones; on the third floor, even more refined; and on the fourth floor, the most refined of all. In that analogy, although those four floors are just palace floors and there is no difference between them as palace floors, yet because of the difference in the excellence of the five cords of sensual pleasure, each upper floor is more refined than the one below it.

And just as there might be four cloths of four, three, two, and one pala weight, made of coarse thread, fine thread, more refined thread, and most refined thread respectively, spun by a certain woman, all being equal in length and breadth. In that analogy, although those four cloths are equal in length and breadth and there is no difference between them in size, yet because of their pleasant touch, fineness, and great value, each subsequent cloth is more refined than the preceding one. In the same way, although there are only these two factors—equanimity and one-pointedness of mind—in all these four formless attainments, yet because of the excellence of development (bhāvanā), each subsequent attainment in these formless states should be understood as being more and more refined through the increasingly refined nature of those factors. These attainments, which are thus refined in succession, [are explained as follows]:

One man stands clinging to a pavilion situated in a dirty place,
Another stands leaning on that one who is clinging.
Another stands outside without leaning on him,
And another stands leaning on the one who stands outside.
By the similarity with these four men in order,
The four attainments should be understood by the wise.

In those verses, the explanation of the meaning is as follows: There is a pavilion in a dirty place. Then a man comes and, loathing that filth, stands as if clinging to that pavilion, holding it with his hands. Then another man comes and stands leaning on the man who is clinging to the pavilion. Then another man comes and thinks: "Both this one who clings to the pavilion and the one who stands leaning on him are badly situated; they will surely fall when the pavilion collapses. Let me stand outside." Having thought so, he stands outside without leaning on the one who was leaning on the man clinging to the pavilion. Then another man comes...
256:
Thinking of the insecurity of the man hanging from the pavilion and the man leaning on him, and considering the one standing outside as "well-situated," he stood depending on that person.

In that analogy, the space produced by the removal of the kasina (kasiṇugghāṭimākāsa) should be seen as the pavilion in an impure place. The sphere of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana), which takes space as its object due to disgust for material signs, should be seen as the man hanging from the pavilion due to disgust for the impurity. The sphere of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana), which arises by taking the sphere of infinite space as its object, should be seen as the man who stands depending on the man hanging from the pavilion. Thinking of the insecurity of both of them, like the one standing outside without depending on the man hanging from the pavilion, the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana), which does not take the sphere of infinite space as its object but takes the non-existence of that consciousness (the concept of non-existence) as its object, should be seen. Thinking of the insecurity of the one hanging from the pavilion and the one leaning on him, and considering the one standing outside as "well-situated," like the one who stands depending on that person, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana), which arises by taking the sphere of nothingness situated in the external region—known as the non-existence of consciousness (the concept of non-existence)—as its object, should be noted. And in its occurrence:

It indeed takes that as its object, because of the absence of any other;
Just as a person, for the sake of livelihood, depends on a king even though seeing his faults.

Indeed, this sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, even though seeing the fault in that sphere of nothingness as "this attainment has the sphere of infinite consciousness as its near enemy," it still takes that very sphere of nothingness as its object because of the absence of any other suitable object. How? "Just as a person, for the sake of livelihood, serves a king even though seeing his faults." For instance, a person who cannot find a livelihood elsewhere, for the sake of livelihood, lives depending on a king who is a ruler of all directions but has unrestrained and harsh conduct of body, speech, and mind, even though seeing his faults as "this king has harsh conduct." In the same way, this sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, being unable to obtain any object other than that sphere of nothingness, takes that very sphere of nothingness as its object even though seeing its faults. And in taking the object in this way:

Just as one climbing a long ladder holds the ladder rails,
Or as one climbing a mountain peak holds the summit itself,
Or as one climbing a mountain leans on his own knee,
Even so, this jhāna occurs depending on the (ākiñcaññāyatana) jhāna.

## The Discussion on the Wholesome of the Formless Sphere is finished.
257:
## Explanation of the Wholesome of the Three Planes
Now, since all these wholesome states of the three planes exist in various divisions such as "low" and so forth, the text begins again with "Which states are wholesome?" etc., in order to show those divisions. In that context, "hīna" means low or inferior. It should be understood by way of striving (āyūhana). That which exists in the middle of the low and the excellent is called "majjhima" (medium). That which is brought to a state of prominence is called "paṇīta" (superior), meaning excellent. Those medium and superior wholesome states should also be understood only by way of striving. For if, at the moment of striving, the desire (chanda), or energy (viriya), or consciousness (citta), or investigation (vīmaṃsā) is low, that wholesome state is called "hīna." For one in whom those states are medium, it is "majjhima," and if they are superior, it is "paṇīta." The wholesome state that is performed by making the desire to act (kattukamyatā-chanda) the lead, the chief, the head, and the precursor, is called "chandādhipateyya" (predominance of desire) because it comes from the predominance of desire. The same method applies to the predominance of energy (viriyādhipateyya) and so forth.

Standing at this point, the methods (naya) should be counted. First of all, there is one method as analyzed, one as low, one as medium, one as superior, and one as predominance of desire. These are first the five methods in the predominance of desire. In the same way, there are twenty methods, being four groups of five, for the predominance of energy and so forth. Alternatively, there are twenty methods as follows: one pure (suddhika) method, three starting with low, four starting with predominance of desire, and twelve starting with predominance of desire-low.

Where are these twenty great methods analyzed? They are analyzed in the "Triad of the Low" (Hīna-ttika) of the Great Treatise (the Paṭṭhāna). However, at this point, taking the medium group from the Triad of the Low, three portions should be made by way of low, medium, and superior. Then, setting aside the medium group and taking the low and superior, nine portions each should be made. For in the low itself, there are low, medium, and superior. In the superior also, there are low, medium, and superior. Thus, in the low-low, there is low; in the low-low, there is medium; in the low-low, there is superior. In the low-medium, there is low; in the low-medium, there is medium; in the low-medium, there is superior. In the low-superior, there is low; in the low-medium, there is medium; in the low-superior, there is superior—this is one group of nine (navaka). In the superior-low also, there is low, medium, and superior. Likewise, in the superior-medium, there is low, medium, and superior; in the superior-superior, there is low, medium, and superior—this is the second group of nine. Thus, the two groups of nine make eighteen. These eighteen are called the doors of action (kammadvāra).
258:
Because they are produced by these eighteen doors of action (kamma-dvāra), and by the power of these doors of action, the eighteen [types of] Khattiyas, eighteen Brāhmaṇas, eighteen Vessas, eighteen Suddas, and forty-eight lineages (gotta) and conducts (caraṇa) should be understood.

Among these wholesome states (kusala) occurring in the three planes (tebhūmaka), sense-sphere wholesome (kāmāvacara-kusala) is either tri-root (tihetuka) or bi-root (duhetuka) by way of being associated with knowledge (ñāṇa-sampayutta) or dissociated from knowledge (ñāṇa-vippayutta). Fine-material-sphere (rūpāvacara) and immaterial-sphere (arūpāvacara) wholesome states, however, are only tri-root and only associated with knowledge. Among these wholesome states, sense-sphere wholesome arises both with predominance (adhipati) and without predominance. Fine-material-sphere and immaterial-sphere wholesome states arise only as endowed with predominance. In this sense-sphere wholesome, both types of predominance—object-predominance (ārammaṇādhipati) and conascent-predominance (sahajātādhipati)—are obtained. In fine-material-sphere and immaterial-sphere wholesome states, object-predominance is not obtained; only conascent-predominance is obtained.

In that [Pali] text, the state of consciousness as the predominance of consciousness (cittādhipati) is stated by way of the associated states (sampayutta-dhamma). Since two consciousnesses cannot arise together at the same time, there is no such thing as the predominance of consciousness for the associated consciousness. Likewise, for states such as desire (chanda), there are no such things as the predominance of desire (chandādhipati) and so on. Some teachers, however, desire [to explain] predominance by way of the manner of its arrival, thus: "If wholesome arises for one who has consciousness, it will arise for me"; in this way, whichever consciousness is made the lead and made the chief, and another wholesome consciousness is exerted, for that person, that preceding consciousness is called the predominance of consciousness; because it comes from that [preceding consciousness], this [subsequent] consciousness is called 'having the predominance of consciousness'. This method, however, is seen neither in the Pali nor in the Commentaries. Therefore, the state of predominance should be understood only by the method already stated.

Among these nineteen great methods, in the first 'pure' method (suddhika-naya), there are consciousnesses, groups of nine (navaka), and textual sections (pāṭhavāra) of the stated magnitude. Therefore, in the consciousnesses associated with knowledge, the divisions of consciousness, navaka, and vāra multiplied by twenty should be understood according to the stated magnitude; in the four consciousnesses dissociated from knowledge, they should be understood as multiplied by sixteen. This is called the Miscellaneous Discussion (Pakiṇṇaka-kathā) on wholesome states in the three planes.

## Tebhūmaka-kusala

## Lokuttara-kusala-vaṇṇanā

Having thus shown the wholesome that produces the attainments of the three planes of existence, now, in order to show the supramundane wholesome (lokuttara-kusala) for the sake of transcending all planes of existence, the words beginning with "Again, which states are wholesome?" are commenced. In that passage, for what reason is it called 'supramundane' (lokuttara)?
259:
It is called 'supramundane' (lokuttara) because it crosses over the world, because it transcends the world, and because it stands having overcome the world (Paṭisambhidāmagga II, 43). "Develops jhana" means it produces, generates, and increases absorption jhana (appanā-jhāna) of a single thought-moment.

It is called 'leading out' (niyyānika) because it leads out from the world, because it leads out from the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa). Or, it is called 'leading out' because the person leads out by means of that [jhana]. Indeed, the person endowed with that [jhana] leads out while fully understanding the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca), leads out while abandoning the truth of origin (samudaya-sacca), leads out while realizing the truth of cessation (nirodha-sacca), and leads out while developing the truth of the path (magga-sacca). Just as wholesome states of the three planes are called 'leading to accumulation' (ācayagāmī) because they build up and increase death and rebirth in the round, this supramundane jhana is not like that. This supramundane jhana is called 'leading to reduction' (apacayagāmī) because it goes along destroying and making deficient the causes of death and rebirth that were built up by the wholesome of the three planes, just as when one man is building an eighteen-cubit wall, another man takes a large sledgehammer and goes along destroying and dismantling the places that were built.

In the phrase "for the abandoning of wrong views (diṭṭhigata)," the wrong views themselves are called 'diṭṭhigata', similar to [the usage in] 'excrement' (gūthagata) or 'urine' (muttagata). Or, they are called 'diṭṭhigata' because they are included within the sixty-two types of wrong views. Or, they are called 'diṭṭhigata' because they have the same course as wrong views. The meaning is: states that have a movement similar to wrong views, or a procedure similar to wrong views. What are those states? They are the unwholesome states of self-view (sakkāya-diṭṭhi), doubt (vicikicchā), attachment to rites and rituals (sīlabbata-parāmāsa), and the greed, hatred, and delusion that lead to the lower realms, together with their associated states. Indeed, as long as the first path (pathama-magga) is not developed, they are called 'states having a movement similar to wrong views' because of their continued existence. Thus, both the wrong views and the states similar to wrong views are called 'diṭṭhigata'. "For the abandoning of those diṭṭhigata" means for the sake of abandoning them by way of eradication (samuccheda-pahāna). "First" (pathama) means first by way of counting and first by way of initial arising. "Stage" (bhūmi): in passages such as "on the ground (bhūmi) free from obstructions," this great earth is called 'bhūmi'. In passages such as "in the sense-sphere happy stage (bhūmi)," the arising of consciousness (cittuppāda) is called 'bhūmi'. Here, however, the fruit of recluseship (sāmaññaphala) is intended. That fruit of recluseship is called 'bhūmi' because it is the support for associated states, and those states arise in it. Or, it is called 'bhūmi' because, although it is equal in being supramundane, it itself becomes or arises, unlike Nibbāna which does not [arise as a conditioned state]. "For the attainment of that first stage" means for the sake of reaching or obtaining the first fruit of recluseship known as the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala); thus the meaning should be understood.
260:
The meaning here should be understood as: for the sake of attaining, for the sake of acquiring the first fruit of recluseship, known as the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). 'Vivicca' means secluded or detached by way of seclusion by eradication (samuccheda-viveka). (In the context of 'by way of seclusion by eradication,' it should be understood as the absolute cutting off of defilements that lead to the lower realms, and the cutting off of other defilements just as a flash of lightning dispels a mass of darkness.)

Now, although even mundane jhāna cannot be accomplished without a mode of progress (paṭipadā), even so, in this supramundane state, wishing to teach by setting aside the 'pure' (suddhika) method and emphasizing the supramundane jhāna together with the mode of progress, the Buddha spoke the words beginning with 'painful progress with slow direct-knowledge' (dukkha-paṭipadā dandhābhiññā).

In that statement, for whoever from the very beginning, while suppressing the defilements, suppresses them with difficulty, with effort, and with exhaustion, for that person there is 'painful progress' (dukkha-paṭipadā). For whoever, having suppressed the defilements, reaches the manifestation of the Path only after a long time while dwelling in the vicinity of insight (vipassanā), for that person there is 'slow direct-knowledge' (dandhābhiññā). Thus, any such section is named 'painful progress with slow direct-knowledge.'

Which section do the teachers prefer? In whichever section the defilements, once suppressed, arise again; and being suppressed a second time, they arise once more; but when suppressed for the third time, they remain suppressed and are brought to absolute eradication by the Path—this is the section they prefer. This section is named 'painful progress with slow direct-knowledge.' However, the name is not yet clear by this much alone. Therefore, the explanation from the beginning should be understood here as follows:

Whoever, having grasped the four great elements, grasps derived matter (upādā-rūpa) and mentality (arūpa), and while grasping mentality and materiality (rūpārūpa), is able to grasp them only with difficulty, hardship, and exhaustion—for that person, it is called 'painful progress.' For that person who has grasped mentality and materiality, because the manifestation of the Path is slow while dwelling in the vicinity of insight, it is called 'slow direct-knowledge.'

Also, whoever, having grasped mentality and materiality, defines them as 'this group of five aggregates is merely mentality-materiality; there is no other being or such apart from mentality-materiality,' and defines them with difficulty, hardship, and exhaustion, and while dwelling in the vicinity of insight regarding the defined mentality-materiality, is able to produce the Path only after a long time—for that person also, it is called 'painful progress with slow direct-knowledge.'

Another person, having defined mentality-materiality, grasps the causes (paccaya) with difficulty, hardship, and exhaustion, and having grasped the causes, produces the Path only after a long time while dwelling in the vicinity of insight—in this way also, it is called 'painful progress with slow direct-knowledge.'
261:
Another person, having also grasped the causes, when striving to penetrate the characteristics (lakkhaṇa) such as impermanence, penetrates them with difficulty, hardship, and exhaustion. That person, having penetrated the characteristics, produces the Path only after a long time while dwelling in the vicinity of insight. This kind of practice is also called 'painful progress with slow direct-knowledge.'

Another person, having also penetrated the characteristics, while insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) is occurring sharply, courageously, and clearly, when exhausting the attachment to insight (vipassanā-nikanti) that has arisen, exhausts it with difficulty, hardship, and exhaustion. Having exhausted that attachment and dwelling in the vicinity of insight, he produces the Path only after a long time. This kind of practice is also called 'painful progress with slow direct-knowledge.' The teachers prefer this section. This name is given to this section. By this same method, the other three modes of progress should be understood.

In the passages beginning with 'contact occurs' (phasso hoti), these four terms are additional: the faculty 'I shall know the unknown' (anaññātaññassāmītindriya), Right Speech (sammā-vācā), Right Action (sammā-kammanta), and Right Livelihood (sammā-ājီva). Also in the section of definitions (niddesa-vāra), in the definitions of initial application (vitakka) and so on, terms such as 'factor of the path' (magganga) are additional. All the rest is just as stated below. However, by way of the difference in planes, the only distinction here is the supramundane nature.

Among those terms, the faculty 'I shall know the unknown' (anaññātaññassāmītindriya) is the faculty that arises through the prior reflection of one who practices with the thought: 'In the beginningless round of rebirth (saṃsāra-vaṭṭa), I shall know the Deathless state or the Four Noble Truths which have not been known before.' Its characteristics and so on should be understood in the same way as stated below under the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya).

Beautiful or praised speech is Right Speech (sammā-vācā). It is a designation for the abstinence from wrong speech which radically eradicates verbal misconduct. It has the characteristic of grasping (concomitant states), the function of abstaining, and is manifested as the abandoning of wrong speech. Beautiful or praised action is Right Action (sammā-kammanta). It is the name for the abstinence from killing and so on which radically cuts off wrong action. It has the characteristic of originating (good deeds), the function of abstaining, and is manifested as the abandoning of wrong action. Beautiful or praised livelihood is Right Livelihood (sammā-ājīva). It is a designation for the abstinence from wrong livelihood. It has the characteristic of purification, the function of proceeding with right livelihood, and is manifested as the abandoning of wrong livelihood.

Furthermore, the characteristics and so on here should be understood just as stated below under the three abstinences (virati). Thus, by way of these three states, the fivefold path (maggapañcaka) mentioned below should be understood as the eightfold path (maggaṭṭhaka) in this supramundane consciousness. And the absence of these states among the 'appertaining' (yevāpanaka) states should be understood. Likewise, Compassion (karuṇā) and Appreciative Joy (muditā) are also absent.
262:
These three factors, such as Right Speech (sammāvācā), are not included among the yevāpanaka (miscellaneous) states because they are explicitly mentioned in the Pāḷi text regarding this supramundane consciousness. Compassion (karuṇā) and appreciative joy (muditā), however, have sentient beings as their object, whereas these supramundane states have Nibbāna as their object. Therefore, compassion and appreciative joy are not included in this supramundane consciousness. This is the specific meaning in the Summary Section (uddesavāra).

In the Exposition Section (niddesavāra), regarding the phrase "a path factor, included in the path" (maggaṅgaṃ maggapariyāpannaṃ): first, it is called a path factor (maggaṅga) because it is a constituent part of the path; it means a portion of the path. Just as something belonging to a forest is called "included in the forest" (araññapariyāpanna), so too, because it is included in the path, it is called "included in the path" (maggapariyāpanna). It means a state dependent on the path.

In the phrase "the enlightenment factor of joy" (pītisambojjhaṅga), joy itself is the enlightenment factor, thus it is called the enlightenment factor of joy. In that term, it is called bojjhaṅga because it is a constituent part of the collection of states that lead to the knowledge of the Four Noble Truths. Alternatively, it is called bojjhaṅga because it is a cause for the Noble Disciple who knows the Four Noble Truths. The meaning is this: the Noble Disciple awakens by means of that collection of states—consisting of mindfulness (sati), investigation of states (dhammavicaya), energy (viriya), joy (pīti), tranquility (passaddhi), concentration (samādhi), and equanimity (upekkhā)—which arises at the moment of the supramundane path and which is the opposite of many afflictions such as sluggishness, restlessness, stagnation (patiṭṭhāna), toiling (āyūhana), devotion to sensual pleasures, devotion to self-mortification, the view of annihilation, and the view of eternalism. Therefore, that collection of states is called 'Awakening' (bodhi). "Awakens" (bujjhati) means waking up from the sleep of the continuum of defilements, or penetrating the Four Noble Truths, or realizing Nibbāna itself. Because it is a constituent part of that Awakening consisting of the collection of states, it is called an enlightenment factor (bojjhaṅga), like a factor of jhāna (jhānaṅga) or a factor of the path (maggaṅga). Furthermore, because the Noble Disciple awakens by means of this collection of states of the aforementioned kind, the Noble Disciple is called 'Awakening' (bodhi); because it is a constituent part (a cause) of that Awakening (the person), it is called bojjhaṅga, like a factor of an army (senaṅga) or a factor of a chariot (rathaṅga). Thus the teachers of the Commentaries said: "They are enlightenment factors (bojjhaṅga) because they are factors of the person who awakens."

Moreover, the meaning of bojjhaṅga should be understood by the method of the Paṭisambhidāmagga: "In what sense are they enlightenment factors? They are enlightenment factors because they lead to awakening, because they awaken, because they awaken subsequently, because they awaken towards, because they awaken fully." Sambojjhaṅga means a praised or excellent enlightenment factor. Thus, joy itself is the enlightenment factor, hence pītisambojjhaṅga. In the exposition of one-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā-niddesa) and so on, the meaning should be understood in this same way.

"Of those states" (tesaṃ dhammānaṃ) refers to the Four Noble Truths which are penetrated at that moment. "Of those not yet known" (anaññātānaṃ) means that although those states are known by the first path...
263:
...they are called 'known.' However, just as a person who has arrived at a monastery where they have never been before and stands in the middle of the monastery says, "I have come to a place where I have never been before," based on the fact that they had not previously been there; and just as one who wears a flower they have never worn before, puts on clothes they have never worn before, or eats food they have never eaten before, says, "I have eaten food I have never eaten before," based on the fact that they had not previously eaten it; so too in this supramundane path, because this person has not previously known these Four Noble Truths, they are called "of those not yet known" (anaññātānaṃ). The same method applies to "not seen" (adiṭṭha) and so on. In those terms, "of those not seen" (adiṭṭhānaṃ) refers to states not previously seen with the eye of wisdom before this first path. "Of those not reached" (appattānaṃ) refers to states not previously reached by way of attainment. "Of those not known" (aviditānaṃ) refers to states not previously made manifest by knowledge. "Of those not realized" (asacchikatānaṃ) refers to states not previously experienced personally. "For the sake of realization" (sacchikiriyāya) means for the purpose of personal experience. Just as it is connected with the term "not realized," it should also be connected with the remaining terms: "for the knowledge of states not yet known" (anaññātānaṃ ñāṇāya), "for the seeing of states not yet seen" (adiṭṭhānaṃ dassanāya), "for the reaching of states not yet reached" (appattānaṃ pattiyā), and "for the knowing of states not yet manifest" (aviditānaṃ vedāya).

In the phrases such as "from the four types of verbal misconduct" (catūhi vacīduccaritēhi), "verbal" (vacī) should be understood as verbal intimation (vacīviññatti). They are called "misconduct" (duccarita) because they are conducts corrupted by any one of the three faults: greed, hatred, and delusion. Misconducts arising from verbal intimation are "verbal misconducts" (vacīduccarita), or misconducts produced by verbal intimation are "verbal misconducts." Abstaining far from those verbal misconducts is called ārati. Refraining by being free from them is called virati. Refraining by turning back from each of those verbal misconducts and being free from them is called paṭivirati. Alternatively, the term is merely expanded by the power of prefixes. All these are synonyms for the state of abstaining (oramaṇa). It is called veramaṇī because it destroys the enmity (vera) of verbal misconduct. This term is also a synonym for abstaining (oramaṇa). The volition (cetanā) by which a person speaking falsehoods etc. is said to commit misconduct—this supramundane path-abstinence arises and prevents one from performing that act of falsehood etc. Because it cuts off the volition which is the cause for performing the act, it is called "non-action" (akiriya). Likewise, it prevents one from performing that act; because it cuts off the cause of doing, it is called "non-doing" (akaraṇaṃ). The volition by which one speaks the four types of verbal misconduct and thus transgresses—this abstinence arises and does not allow such transgression, therefore it is called "non-transgression" (anajjhāpatti).

In the phrase "non-transgression of the boundary" (velā-anatikkamo), in passages such as "at that time" (tāya velāya), velā is used to mean "time." In "He dwells at Uruvelā" (uruvelāyaṃ viharati), it is used to mean "a heap." In "The established law does not overstep the boundary" (velāṃ nātivattati), it is used to mean "boundary" (sīmā). Here also, velā means "boundary" (sīmā).
264:
Because they are not to be transgressed, the four types of good verbal conduct are meant by 'velā' (boundary/limit). In this way, a person who speaks the four types of verbal misconduct is said to transgress the velā. Since this (supramundane path abstinence) arises and prevents one from transgressing that velā, it is called 'velā-anatikkama' (non-transgression of the boundary). Alternatively, it is called 'velā' because it destroys; it means it shakes or destroys. What does it destroy? It destroys the four types of verbal misconduct. Because it destroys in this way, it is called 'velā'. Because it occurs without transgressing the welfare and happiness of beings, it is called 'anatikkama'. Thus, the meaning should be understood through these two words as well.

It is called 'setughāta' because it destroys the cause (bridge); it means the destruction or killing of the cause of the four types of verbal misconduct. Here, the cause (paccaya) is meant by 'setu'. The definition of that term is: lust and so forth, which are the causes of the four types of verbal misconduct, are called 'setu' because they bind the person within the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa). The destruction of that setu is called 'setughāta'. This is a designation for the abstinence (virati) that absolutely abandons the cause of verbal misconduct. This abstinence, known as Right Speech (Sammā-vācā), is obtained in various consciousnesses during the preliminary stage (pubbabhāga). The consciousness that abstains from false speech is of one kind, and the consciousness that abstains from slanderous speech and so forth is of another kind. However, at the moment of the supramundane path (lokuttara-magga), it is obtained in only a single consciousness. This is because a single abstinence arises, fulfilling the path factor while cutting off the cause of the four types of volitions for verbal misconduct.

'By bodily misconduct' (kāyaduccaritehi) refers to misconducts such as killing living beings that arise from the body or are performed by the body. The remaining meaning should be understood in the same way as the previous method. This abstinence, known as Right Action (Sammā-kammanta), is also obtained in various consciousnesses during the preliminary stage. The consciousness that abstains from killing living beings is of one kind, and the consciousness that abstains from taking what is not given and sexual misconduct is of another kind. However, at the moment of the supramundane path, it is obtained in only a single consciousness. This is because a single abstinence arises, fulfilling the path factor while cutting off the cause of the three types of volitions for bodily misconduct.

In the explanation of Right Livelihood (Sammā-ājīva-niddesa), regarding the terms such as 'non-action' (akiriyā), a person who makes a living through wrong livelihood by a certain volition is said to perform an action (of wrong livelihood). Since this (supramundane abstinence) arises and prevents one from performing that action, it is called 'akiriyā'. The application should be understood in this manner. Livelihood (ājīva) does not exist separately from speech and action; when Right Speech and Right Action are taken, it is already included because it belongs to their side. However, it is extracted and shown separately from those Right Speech and Right Action by way of constant practice (dhuva-paṭisevana). This being so, it is not that Right Livelihood has no separate function of its own...
265:
...it does; the eight path factors would not be complete. Therefore, Right Livelihood should be treated as having its own separate function, and the eight path factors must be fulfilled. In that (treating it as having a separate function), this is the method: Livelihood (ājīva), when it is broken, is broken only in the doors of body and speech. There is no such thing as the breaking of livelihood in the mind-door. Even when it is fulfilled, it is fulfilled only in those two doors. There is no such thing as the fulfillment of livelihood in the mind-door. In the body-door, however, there are transgressions caused by livelihood and also those not caused by livelihood. The same applies to the speech-door.

Among those (transgressions), when kings and royal ministers, being devoted to amusement and wishing to show their bravery, engage in hunting animals, or robbery on the road, or committing adultery, this is called unwholesome bodily action (akusala-kāyakamma). Abstinence from that (bodily action) is also called 'Sammā-kammanta'. When they speak the four types of verbal misconduct not for the sake of livelihood, this is called unwholesome verbal action (akusala-vacīkamma). Abstinence from that (verbal action) is also called 'Sammā-vācā'.

However, when hunters, fishermen, and so forth kill living beings, take what is not given, or engage in sexual misconduct for the sake of livelihood, this is called 'wrong livelihood' (micchā-ājīva). Abstinence from that is called 'Sammā-ājīva'. Also, when they speak falsely after taking bribes, or engage in slander, harsh speech, and frivolous chatter (for livelihood), this is also called 'micchā-ājīva'. Abstinence from that is called 'Sammā-ājīva'.

But Elder Mahā Siva said: 'Whether a transgression in the doors of body and speech is caused by livelihood or not, it is counted only as unwholesome bodily action or verbal action. Abstinence from that is also called only Sammā-kammanta or Sammā-vācā.' When asked, 'Then where is livelihood?', he said, 'It is the use of the four requisites after producing them by depending on the three grounds of scheming (kuhana).' This is wrong livelihood that has reached the climax. Abstinence from that is called Sammā-ājīva.

This Sammā-ājīva is also obtained in various consciousnesses during the preliminary stage (pubbabhāga), because one abstains from bodily transgression with one consciousness and from verbal transgression with another consciousness. However, at the moment of the supramundane path, it is obtained in only a single consciousness. The reason is that a single abstinence arises, fulfilling the path factor while cutting off the immoral volition known as wrong livelihood, which arises by way of the seven courses of action (kammapatha) in the doors of body and speech. This is the distinction in the section of the detailed exposition (niddesavāra).
266:
By virtue of the faculty 'I shall know the unknown' (anaññātaññassāmītindriya) developed among the faculties, and right speech (sammāvācā) etc. developed among the path factors, it is stated in the Saṅgahavāra (Summary Section) as "nine faculties and the eight-fold path." The Suññatavāra (Void Section), however, remains as usual. This is the distinction of the Suddhika-paṭipadā (Pure Practice).

Following this Suddhika, there is a classification of teachings such as Suddhika-suññata, Suññata-paṭipadā, Suddhika-appaṇihita, and Appaṇihita-paṭipadā. Among these, Suññata is a name for the Supramundane Path (lokuttara-magga). That path receives its name through three reasons: by way of its approach (āgamana), its own quality (saguṇa), and its object (ārammaṇa). How? In this Dispensation, a monk attends to [phenomena] as non-self (anatta) and sees conditioned things (saṅkhāra) as non-self. However, emergence of the path (vuṭṭhāna) cannot occur merely by seeing as non-self; it is also necessary to see them as impermanent (anicca) and as suffering (dukkha). Therefore, he practices by applying and investigating the three types of contemplation: "impermanence, suffering, and non-self." His insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā) sees the conditioned things of the three planes only as void (suññata). This insight is called Suññata. Standing in the position of the approach (āgamana), that insight gives the name "Suññata" to its subsequent path. Thus, the path receives the name Suññata by way of its approach (āgamana). Furthermore, because that path is void of lust and so on, it receives the name Suññata by way of its own quality (saguṇa). Nibbāna is also called Suññata because it is void of lust and so on. Because the path arises by taking that Nibbāna as its object, it receives the name Suññata by way of its object (ārammaṇa).

Among those ways of receiving the name, according to the Suttanta method (pariyāya), it receives the name by way of its own quality and its object. This is a figurative teaching (pariyāya-desanā). The Abhidhamma teaching, however, is a non-figurative teaching (nippariyāya-desanā). Therefore, in this Abhidhamma, it does not receive the name by way of its own quality or its object, but only by way of its approach (āgamana). The approach (āgamana) alone is the predominant factor (dhura). That approach is of two kinds: the approach of insight (vipassanāgamana) and the approach of the path (maggāgamana). Between these two, in the context of the path's arrival, the approach of insight is predominant; in the context of the fruit's arrival, the approach of the path is predominant. Here, because it concerns the arrival of the path, the approach of insight alone becomes the predominant factor.

In the word "Appaṇihita" (Desireless) as well, Appaṇihita is merely a name for the path. The path receives this name also through only three reasons. How? In this Dispensation, a monk first attends to [phenomena] as suffering (dukkha) and sees conditioned things only as suffering. However, emergence of the path cannot occur merely by seeing as suffering; it is also necessary to see them as impermanent and as non-self. Therefore, applying the three types of contemplation: "impermanence, suffering, and non-self"...
267:
...he practices by applying and investigating the three types of contemplation: impermanence, suffering, and non-self. Even while investigating thus, his insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā) dries up, exhausts, and relinquishes the longing of craving (taṇhā-paṇidhi) for conditioned things in the three planes. This insight is called Appaṇihita (Desireless). That Appaṇihita insight, standing in the position of the approach to the path, gives the name 'Appaṇihita' to the path that follows it. Thus, the path receives the name Appaṇihita by way of the preceding insight (āgamana). Because there are no longings (paṇidhi) such as lust, hatred, and delusion in that path, it also receives the name Appaṇihita by way of its own quality. Nibbāna is also called Appaṇihita because of the absence of those longings. Because the path arises by taking that Nibbāna as its object, it receives the name Appaṇihita by way of its object.

Among those reasons for receiving the name, according to the Suttanta method, it receives the name by way of its own quality and its object. This is a figurative teaching (pariyāya-desanā). The Abhidhamma teaching, however, is a non-figurative teaching (nippariyāya-desanā). Therefore, in this Abhidhamma, it does not receive the name by way of its own quality or its object, but only by way of the preceding insight (āgamana). The approach (āgamana) alone is the primary factor. That approach is of two kinds: the approach of insight (vipassanāgamana) and the approach of the path (maggāgamana). Of these two, when the path arises, the approach of insight is primary, and when the fruit arises, the approach of the path is primary. In this context, as it is a discussion about the path, the approach of insight alone becomes the primary factor.

Are there not three names for the path: Suññata, Animitta, and Appaṇihita? The Blessed One taught: "Monks, there are these three liberations (vimokkha): the void liberation (suññata-vimokkha), the signless liberation (animitta-vimokkha), and the desireless liberation (appaṇihita-vimokkha)." Among these three, why is only the two paths taken here and the signless path (animitta-magga) not taken? It is not taken because there is no approach (āgamana). This is because signless insight (animitta-vipassanā) is unable to stand in the position of the approach to the path and give its name to the subsequent path. Nevertheless, the Blessed One taught signless insight to his own son, the Elder Rāhula, saying: "Rāhula, develop the signless (animitta, i.e., contemplation of impermanence), and abandon the underlying tendency to conceit (mānānusaya); then, by the full understanding of conceit, you will live in peace."

Insight removes the sign of permanence (nicca-nimitta), the sign of stability (dhuva-nimitta), the sign of happiness (sukha-nimitta), and the sign of self (atta-nimitta). Therefore, it is called signless (animitta). Although that insight removes those signs, it itself still operates within conditioned phenomena which possess signs; thus, it is actually 'with signs' (sanimitta). For this reason, it is unable to stand in the position of the approach to the path and give its name to the subsequent path.
268:
Another way: Abhidhamma is the teaching of ultimate reality (paramattha-desanā). For the signless path (animitta-magga), there is simply a deficiency of the cause for receiving a name in the ultimate sense. How so? For the signless liberation (animitta-vimokkha) is taught by virtue of the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā). Along with that liberation, the faculty of faith (saddhindriya) is predominant. That faculty of faith is not even a single factor of the noble path (magganga); because it is not a path factor, it is unable to give a name to its own path in the ultimate sense. However, among the remaining two, the void liberation (suññata-vimokkha) is taught by virtue of the contemplation of non-self (anattānupassanā), and the undirected liberation (appaṇihita-vimokkha) is taught by virtue of the contemplation of suffering (dukkhānupassanā). Among those, the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya) is predominant through the void liberation, and the faculty of concentration (samādhindriya) through the undirected liberation. Since these (wisdom and concentration) are factors of the noble path, they are able to give a name to their own path in the ultimate sense. Even in the Triad of Path as Object (maggārammaṇattika), when analyzing the states having the path as predominant (maggādhipati), the state of being a path-predominant is not mentioned for desire (chanda) and consciousness (citta) when they are predominant, simply because they are not path factors. Thus, the completeness of this illustration should be understood. This is the decision of the opinion of a certain teacher, which is not directly included in the Commentary (Atthakathā).

Thus, in every way, because the signless contemplation (animitta-vipassanā), while standing in the position of being able to receive a name itself, is unable to give a name to its own path, the signless path (animitta-magga) is not taken. However, some teachers say, "Although the signless path does not receive a name by way of its occurrence (āgamana), it receives a name by way of its quality (saguṇa) and its object (ārammaṇa) according to the Suttanta method." They are refuted by saying this: if the signless path were to receive a name by its quality and object, then the void and undirected paths should also receive names here (in Abhidhamma) only by their quality and object. But they do not. Why? Because this path receives a name through two reasons: by way of its own nature (sarasa) and by way of opposition (paccanīka). Here, the void and undirected paths receive names both by nature and by opposition. For the void and undirected paths are "void" of lust, etc., and "undirected" from the desire for lust, etc.; thus they receive names by "nature". And "void" is the opposite of the adherence to self (attābhinivesa), and "undirected" is the opposite of desire (paṇidhi); thus they receive names by "opposition". But the signless path receives a name only by nature due to the absence of signs such as lust and signs such as permanence, but not by opposition. For it is not the opposite of the contemplation of impermanence which has the sign of formations as its object. Rather, the contemplation of impermanence stands in the state of being in conformity (anuloma) with that path. Therefore, in every way, there is no such thing as the signless path (animitta-magga) according to the Abhidhamma method.
269:
According to the Suttanta method, however, this signless path is shown by the commentators by bringing it in the following way: "The path of one who emerges through impermanence is called signless," and so on. When the emergence of the path (maggavuṭṭhāna) occurs, the three characteristics appear as if through a single adverting (āvajjana). However, there is no such thing as the three characteristics appearing together. This is said to show the clarity of the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). In the beginning, let there be reflection on any one of the characteristics such as impermanence; insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī vipassanā) emerges by contemplating whichever characteristic it may be, and standing in the position of arrival, it gives a name to its own path by virtue of that contemplated characteristic.

How does it give a name? Having first reflected on one of the characteristics such as impermanence, the remaining two characteristics are also certainly seen. This is because the emergence of the path cannot occur by merely seeing a single characteristic. Therefore, a monk who reflects by way of impermanence does not emerge through impermanence alone; he also emerges through suffering and non-self. The same method applies when reflecting on suffering and non-self. Thus, in the beginning, let there be reflection on any one characteristic; insight leading to emergence emerges by contemplating whichever characteristic it may be, and standing in the position of arrival, it gives a name to its own path by virtue of that contemplated characteristic. In that emergence, the path of one who emerges through impermanence is called signless (animitta); the path of one who emerges through suffering is called undirected (appaṇihita); and the path of one who emerges through non-self is called void (suññata). Thus, it is shown by bringing it in according to the Suttanta method.

What is the object of insight leading to emergence? It has the characteristics as its object (lakkhaṇārammaṇa). A characteristic is of the nature of a concept (paññatti) and is a type of state that cannot be described (as ultimate) such as limited (paritta) or exalted (mahaggata). For the monk who notes the three characteristics as impermanent, suffering, and non-self, the five aggregates appear like a rotting carcass tied around the neck. Only the knowledge that has formations as its object emerges from formations.

For example: a monk wishing to buy an alms-bowl sees a bowl brought by a bowl-merchant and, thinking with great joy that he will buy it, upon examining it, he sees three holes. Just as that monk becomes detached from the holes, he also becomes detached from the bowl. In the same way, by noting the three characteristics, one becomes detached from formations and emerges from formations through the very knowledge that has formations as its object. The same method applies to the cloth analogy.

Thus, the Blessed One, when classifying supramundane absorption (lokuttara-jhāna), brought in both the fourfold and fivefold methods in the Pure Progress (suddhika-paṭipadā). Likewise, He brought in the Void Progress (suññata-paṭipadā) in the Pure Void (suddhika-suññata), and the Undirected Progress (appaṇihita-paṭipadā) in the Pure Undirected (suddhika-appaṇihita). Why did He bring them in this way? He did so by virtue of the inclination of individuals (puggalajjhāsaya) and by virtue of the elegance of the teaching (desanā-vilāsa). Both of these should be understood according to the method mentioned above.
270:
It should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. In this context of 'developing supramundane jhāna,' there are two methods according to the pure path (suddhika-paṭipadā): the fourfold and the fivefold. Similarly, since there are two methods for each of the remaining categories (such as pure voidness, etc.), ten methods are analyzed across all five groups.

## Miscellaneous Discussion on Supramundane Wholesome States

The following is the miscellaneous discussion regarding the supramundane path:
Internal and external,
In form and the formless, in the five aggregates,
The transformation of the seven and eight factors,
Sign, path, and predominance (exist).

The supramundane path, having applied itself to the internal, emerges from the internal; having applied itself to the internal, it emerges from the external; having applied itself to the external, it emerges from the external; having applied itself to the external, it emerges from the internal. Having applied itself to form, it emerges from form; having applied itself to form, it emerges from the formless. Having applied itself to the formless, it emerges from the formless; having applied itself to the formless, it emerges from form. In a single moment, it emerges from all five aggregates.

‘Sattaṭṭhaṅga-pariṇāmaṃ’ means that the path may have eight factors or seven factors. The factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) may be seven or six. Jhāna may have five, four, three, or two factors. Thus, the transformation of factors such as seven, eight, and so on, should be understood.

In the phrase ‘nimittaṃ paṭipadāpati,’ ‘nimittaṃ’ refers to that from which emergence occurs. Regarding ‘paṭipadāpati,’ the movement and non-movement of the path and the predominance should be understood.

Among the terms ‘having applied itself to the internal, it emerges from the internal,’ etc., first the decision should be understood. In this Dispensation, a certain person initially enters by taking the five aggregates occurring within his own continuity (internal) as the object. Having applied himself, he sees those five aggregates as impermanent and so on. However, emergence into the path does not occur merely by seeing purely internal aggregates; the external must also be seen. Therefore, he sees the aggregates of others and also non-clung-to formations (anupādinnasaṅkhāra) as impermanent, suffering, and non-self. At times he contemplates the internal, and at times he contemplates the external. For him who contemplates thus, when he contemplates the internal, insight (vipassanā) connects with the path. In this way, it is said that ‘having applied himself to the internal, he emerges from the internal.’ If, however, when he contemplates the external, insight...
271:
...connects with the path, it is said that ‘having applied himself to the internal, he emerges from the external.’ This same method applies to emergence from the external and the internal after having applied himself to the external.

Another teacher [states that one] initially enters by taking form (rūpa) as the object. Having entered, he distinguishes between primary matter (bhūta-rūpa) and derived matter (upādā-rūpa) and sees them as impermanent and so on. However, since emergence into the path cannot occur merely by seeing form alone, mental states (arūpa) must also be seen with the eye of wisdom. Therefore, taking that form as the object, he distinguishes the arising feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as ‘this is the formless (mental states)’ and sees them as impermanent and so on. At times he contemplates form, and at times he contemplates the formless. For him who contemplates thus, when he contemplates form, insight connects with the path. When it connects thus, it is said that ‘having applied himself to form, he emerges from form.’ If, however, when he contemplates the formless, insight connects with the path, it is said that ‘having applied himself to form, he emerges from the formless.’ This same method applies to emergence from the formless and form after having applied himself to the formless.

When one emerges while applying the mind thus: ‘Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease,’ it is said that he emerges from the five aggregates in a single moment. This is the insight of a monk with sharp insight and great wisdom.

For example, suppose a lump of dung was placed in the middle of rice and a tray full of various delicious foods was brought to a hungry man. When that man pushes aside the curry with his hand and sees that lump of dung, he asks, ‘What is this?’ When told it is a lump of dung, he says, ‘How disgusting! Take it away!’ and becomes detached from both the rice and the tray. This example should be understood in the same way.

The time when the man was delighted upon seeing the food tray is like the time when this monk, as a foolish worldling, grasped the five aggregates as ‘I’ and ‘mine.’ The time when the lump of dung was seen is like the time when the three marks (tilakkhaṇa) are noted. The time of being detached from the rice and the tray should be understood as the time when the monk with sharp insight and great wisdom emerges simultaneously from the five aggregates, [realizing] ‘Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease.’

In the term ‘sattaṭṭhaṅga-pariṇāmaṃ,’ this transformation of factors with the stated distinctions should be understood as it occurs. For equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa) itself is the [precursor] of the Noble Path...
272:
(The knowledge of equanimity towards formations) determines the distinction of the factors of enlightenment, the path factors, and the jhana factors. Some elders, however, say: "The basic jhana determines the distinction of the factors of enlightenment, the path factors, and the jhana factors." Some say: "The aggregates which are the objects of insight determine [them]." Some say: "The individual's inclination determines [them]." Even in the views of those elders, it should be understood that only this emergence-leading insight, which occurs prior to the path and is called equanimity towards formations, determines [them].

In this regard, this is the sequential explanation: By the power of the determination of insight, the path that arises for a dry-insight practitioner, the path that arises for one who has attained meditative attainments without making a jhana the basis, and the path produced by making the first jhana the basis and contemplating various formations, all occur in association with the first jhana. In all these paths, there are 7 factors of enlightenment, 8 path factors, and 5 jhana factors. Whether the insight occurring prior to those paths is associated with joy or with equanimity, when it reaches the state of equanimity towards formations at the time of emergence, it is associated only with joy.

In the fivefold method, in the paths produced by making the second, third, and fourth jhanas the basis, the jhana has 4, 3, and 2 factors respectively. In all these paths, however, there are 7 path factors; in the fourth jhana, there are 6 factors of enlightenment. This distinction occurs due to the determination of the basic jhana as well as the determination of insight. The insight prior to those paths also occurs whether associated with joy or with equanimity. But emergence-leading insight is associated only with joy.

In the path produced by making the fifth jhana the basis, however, by the power of equanimity and one-pointedness of mind, there are only 2 jhana factors, 6 factors of enlightenment, and 7 path factors. This distinction also occurs by the power of both determinations. In this method, the prior insight occurs whether associated with joy or with equanimity, but emergence-leading insight is associated only with equanimity. This same method applies to the path produced by making the formless jhanas the basis. Thus, the attainment situated close to the path—which is produced by emerging from a basic jhana and contemplating certain formations—makes [the path] similar to itself, just as the color of the ground makes the color of a monitor lizard similar to itself.

In the view of the second elder, however, from whichever attainment one emerges and whichever attainment-factors one contemplates to bring about the path, that path becomes similar to that specific attainment; the meaning is that it is similar to the attainment being contemplated.
273:
If one contemplates sense-sphere states (kāmāvacaradhamma), the path is only of the first jhana level. In that case too, the determination of insight should be understood in the manner already stated.

In the doctrine of the third elder, according to one's own inclination (ajjhāsaya), such as "O, may I reach the seven-factored path, may I reach the eight-factored path," whichever jhana is made the basis or whichever jhana-states are contemplated to produce the path, that path is similar only to that particular jhana. However, without a basic jhana (pādakajjhāna) or a contemplated jhana (sammasitajjhāna), it cannot be achieved by mere inclination alone. This meaning should be clarified by the Nandakovāda Sutta.

For it is said: "Bhikkhus, just as on the fifteenth day of the Uposatha, the majority of people have no doubt or uncertainty as to whether the moon is waning or full, but rather it is simply the full moon; even so, bhikkhus, those bhikkhunīs were delighted with Nandaka's Dhamma teaching and had fulfilled their aspirations. Bhikkhus, among those five hundred bhikkhunīs, even the one who is the least is a stream-enterer (sotāpanna), no longer subject to downfall, assured, and bound for enlightenment." (Majjhima Nikāya 3.415).

Among those bhikkhunīs, she who had the supporting condition (upanissaya) for the fruit of stream-entry had her aspiration fulfilled by the fruit of stream-entry itself... she who had the supporting condition for arahantship, by arahantship itself. In this same way, according to one's own inclination, whichever jhana is made the basis or whichever jhana-states are contemplated to produce the path, that path is similar only to that particular jhana. However, without a basic jhana or a contemplated jhana, it cannot be achieved by mere inclination alone. In this case too, the determination of insight should be understood in the manner already stated.

Among those doctrines, the disciples of the Elder Tipitaka Cūḷanāga, who held the view that "Only the basic jhana determines it," asked: "Venerable sir, in a realm where there is a basic jhana, let it be determined by that; but in the formless realm (arūpabhava) where there is no basic jhana, what determines it?" "Friends, even there, only the basic jhana determines it. For a bhikkhu who has attained the eight attainments, having produced the path and fruit of stream-entry by making the first jhana the basis, dies without falling away from jhana and is reborn in the formless realm; emerging from the fruition attainment of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala-samāpatti) which is of the first jhana level, he begins insight..."
274:
