...produces the three higher paths and fruits. For that monk, those paths and fruits belong to the first jhāna only. The same method applies to the higher paths and fruits belonging to the second jhāna and so on. In the formless realm, the group of three jhānas or four jhānas arises. However, that jhāna is only supramundane (lokuttara), not mundane (lokiya). Thus, even in the formless realm, friends, only the basic jhāna (pādakajjhāna) determines [the path]. "Venerable sir, the question is well-explained," they replied.

"The aggregates (khandhas) which are the objects of insight (vipassanā) determine [the path]. Whichever of the five aggregates one contemplates and emerges from [insight], the path becomes similar to those aggregates," so said Elder Mahādatta residing at Moravāpi. His disciples said, "Venerable sir, a fault appears in your view. For a monk who emerges after contemplating matter (rūpa), the path should be indeterminate (avyākata) like matter. For one who emerges after grasping the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana) by method, the path should be similar to that, reaching the state of neither-perception-nor-non-perception." "Friends, it is not as you say. There is no supramundane path that has not reached absorption (appanā). Therefore, for one who emerges after contemplating matter, there is an eight-fold path accompanied by joy (somanassa). For one who emerges after contemplating the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the path is not similar to it in every aspect, but is a seven-fold path accompanied by equanimity (upekkhā)," the Elder said.

Bringing the view of Elder Cūḷābhaya, who held that "the person's inclination (ajjhāsaya) determines [the path]," they told it to Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga. That Elder said, "First, for a monk who has a basic jhāna (pādakajjhāna), let the person's inclination determine it. For one who does not have that basic jhāna, what kind of inclination will determine it? It would be like a time when a penniless person seeks interest [on wealth he doesn't have]."

Bringing that speech, they told it again to Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya. He said, "Friends, I said this regarding a monk who possesses a basic jhāna." Just as it is understood for one with a basic jhāna, so should it be understood for one with a jhāna used as an object of contemplation (sammasitajjhāna). Indeed, for a monk who emerges from the fifth jhāna and contemplates the first jhāna etc., the path that arises is a fifth-jhāna path according to the first Elder's view. According to the second view, it would be a first-jhāna path etc., thus the two views conflict. But in the third view, because it says "whichever jhāna he desires, the path belongs to that jhāna," those two views do not conflict, and the inclination becomes meaningful. Thus, these three Elders were wise, clever, and endowed with intellect. Therefore, their views were established as a tradition (tanti). However, in this [Atthasālinī], extracting only the meaning, it is shown that all three views are determined by insight (vipassanā) alone.
275:
Now, I shall state the decision regarding the phrase "nimittaṃ paṭipadāpati." When the path, which involves the transformation of factors (aṅgapariṇāma), arises, from where does the change-of-lineage (gotrabhu) emerge? From where does the path (magga) emerge? This is the question. Between the two, the change-of-lineage first emerges from the sign (nimitta, the object of insight), but it cannot cut the occurrence (pavatta, the continuity of aggregates); therefore, this change-of-lineage is called "emerging from one side" (ekatovutthāna). The path, however, emerges from the sign and also cuts the occurrence; therefore, this path is called "emerging from both sides" (ubhatovutthāna).

The sequence of their arising is as follows: In the occurrence of the emergence of the path, conformity (anuloma) does not occur only once, nor does it occur five times. This is because conformity occurring only once does not obtain the repetition condition (āsevana-paccaya). The fifth conformity would be unstable due to its proximity to the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). At that time, the impulsion (javana) is said to have "fallen" (patita). Therefore, conformity occurs neither once nor five times.

For a person of great wisdom (mahāpaññā), conformity occurs twice; at the third moment is change-of-lineage, at the fourth is the path-consciousness, then three moments of fruition (phala) occur, after which it descends into the life-continuum. For a person of medium wisdom (majjhimapaññā), conformity occurs thrice; at the fourth is change-of-lineage, at the fifth is the path-consciousness, then two moments of fruition occur, after which it descends into the life-continuum. For a person of dull wisdom (mandapaññā), conformity occurs four times; at the fifth is change-of-lineage, at the sixth is the path-consciousness, at the seventh is the fruition-consciousness, after which it descends into the life-continuum. Among these three, it should be explained by way of the person of medium wisdom, without speaking by way of the great or dull wisdom.

In the occurrence of the emergence of the path, the functional rootless mind-consciousness element (kiriya-ahetuka-manoviññāṇadhātu) accompanied by equanimity becomes the mind-door adverting (manodvārāvajjana), takes the aggregates which are the objects of insight as its object, and interrupts the life-continuum. Immediately after that adverting, taking the same aggregates grasped by that adverting, the first impulsion, the knowledge of conformity (anuloma-ñāṇa), arises. That knowledge, occurring as impermanent (anicca), suffering (dukkha), or non-self (anatta) regarding those aggregates, dispels the gross darkness that veils the truths (saccapaṭicchādakatama), makes the three characteristics more and more manifest, and ceases.

Thereafter, the second conformity arises. Among these conformities, the first one has not yet obtained the repetition condition. For the second conformity, the first conformity acts as the repetition condition. Because it has obtained the repetition condition, that second conformity becomes sharp, courageous, and clear; occurring in that same object in that same manner, it dispels the medium darkness that veils the truths, makes the three characteristics more and more manifest, and ceases. Thereafter, the third conformity arises. For that third conformity, the second conformity acts as the repetition condition. Because it has obtained the repetition condition, it becomes sharp, courageous, and clear; occurring in that same object in that same manner, it completely dispels the remaining subtle darkness that veils the truths, and makes the three characteristics more and more...
276:
## 
Having made the three characteristics manifest, it ceases. Thus, when the darkness that veils the Four Noble Truths has been dispelled by the three conformity knowledges (anuloma-ñāṇa), immediately following those conformity knowledges, the change-of-lineage knowledge (gotrabhū-ñāṇa) arises, taking Nibbāna as its object.

In this regard, there is this simile: A man with sight, wishing to know the conjunction of the moon with a constellation, went out at night and looked up at the sky to see the moon. Because it was covered by clouds, the moon was not visible to him. Then, a wind arose and blew away the thick clouds. Another wind blew away the medium clouds. Another wind blew away the subtle clouds. Only then did that man see the moon in the cloudless sky and thus know the conjunction of the moon with the constellation.

In this simile, the three types of clouds are like the darkness of defilements—thick, medium, and subtle—that veil the Four Noble Truths. The three winds are like the three conformity consciousnesses (anuloma-citta). The man with sight is like the change-of-lineage knowledge (gotrabhū-ñāṇa). The moon is like Nibbāna. Just as each wind successively destroys the three types of clouds, so each conformity consciousness dispels the darkness veiling the Truths. Just as that man sees the pure moon in the cloudless sky, when the darkness veiling the Truths is gone, the change-of-lineage knowledge arises, taking the extremely pure Nibbāna as its object.

Just as the three winds can only destroy the clouds covering the moon but cannot see the moon, so the conformity knowledges can only dispel the darkness veiling the Truths but cannot take Nibbāna as their object. Just as that man can only see the moon but cannot destroy the clouds, so the change-of-lineage knowledge can only take Nibbāna as its object but cannot dispel the darkness of defilements. Thus, conformity knowledge has formations (saṅkhāra) as its object, while change-of-lineage knowledge has Nibbāna as its object.

For if change-of-lineage knowledge were to take the same object as conformity knowledge, then conformity knowledge would follow it again, and there would be no emergence into the Path (magga-vuṭṭhāna). But the change-of-lineage knowledge, without taking the object of conformity knowledge, makes it so that there is no further occurrence [of that object], and though it is not itself an adverting (āvajjana), it stands in the place of adverting and ceases, as if giving a sign to the Path, saying, "Arise in this way." The Path, without letting go of the sign given by it, following that knowledge in an uninterrupted sequence, arises while piercing and breaking through the masses of greed, hatred, and delusion that have never been pierced or broken through before.
277:
## 
In this Path-process (magga-vīthi), there is this simile: An archer had a hundred planks placed at a distance of a hundred bow-lengths. He wrapped his face with a cloth, prepared his arrow, and stood on a wheeled vehicle. Another man turned the wheeled vehicle, and when the hundred planks were directly in front of the archer, he gave a sign by striking there with a stick. The archer, without letting go of the sign given by the strike of the stick, shot the arrow and pierced the hundred planks.

In this simile, the sign given by the strike of the stick should be understood as the change-of-lineage knowledge (gotrabhū-ñāṇa). The archer should be understood as the Path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa). Just as the archer pierces the hundred planks without letting go of the sign given by the strike of the stick, so the Path-knowledge, without letting go of the sign given by the change-of-lineage knowledge, takes Nibbāna as its object and pierces and breaks through the masses of greed and so on, which have never been pierced or broken through before. This breaking through of the masses of greed and so on is also described by the wise as the absolute uprooting of the defilements that bind one to the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa) found in the ground of the five aggregates of clinging.

Indeed, the Path has only one function: the abandoning of the underlying tendencies (anusaya). Thus, as that Path abandons the underlying tendencies, it is said to "emerge from the sign" (nimitta) and "cut the occurrence" (pavatta). "Sign" refers to the signs of materiality, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, which are the objects of insight. "Occurrence" refers to the continuous occurrence of materiality, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness in the round of rebirths. That occurrence is of two kinds: clung-to (upādinnaka) and not clung-to (anupādinnaka). Among these, it is said that the shadow of the Path's emergence from the "not clung-to" is evident, and thus teachers say it "emerges from the not clung-to."

Indeed, by the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga), five consciousnesses are abandoned: four associated with wrong view and one accompanied by doubt. These consciousnesses produce materiality. That materiality is called the "not clung-to" aggregate of materiality. Those consciousnesses are the aggregate of consciousness. The three mental aggregates—feeling, perception, and formations—associated with those five consciousnesses are called the immaterial aggregates (arūpa-kkhandha). Regarding the abandonment of those consciousnesses, if the Path of Stream-entry had not been developed by the Stream-enterer, those five consciousnesses would have reached the state of obsession (pariyuṭṭhāna) toward the six objects. However, the Path of Stream-entry, by preventing their arrival at obsession and by making them incapable of arising through the absolute uprooting of the defilements that break the round of rebirths, is said to "emerge from the occurrence" that is not clung-to.

By the Path of Once-returning (sakadāgāmi-magga), six consciousnesses—four dissociated from wrong view and two accompanied by aversion—are abandoned in terms of coarse sensual lust and ill will. By the Path of Non-returning (anāgāmi-magga), those same six consciousnesses are abandoned in terms of subtle sensual lust and ill will. By the Path of Arahantship (arahatta-magga), five unwholesome consciousnesses—four dissociated from wrong view and one accompanied by restlessness—are abandoned. Regarding the abandonment of those unwholesome consciousnesses, if those Paths had not been developed by those noble ones (ariya), those consciousnesses would have reached the state of obsession toward the six objects. However, those Paths, by preventing their arrival at obsession...
278:
Those Paths (the Path of Once-returning, the Path of Non-returning, and the Path of Arahantship) are said to emerge from unacquired phenomena (anupādinnaka) by completely eradicating the defilements that break the cycle of rebirth and by making it impossible for them to arise again. Teachers also say they 'emerge from acquired phenomena' (upādinnaka), stating that 'the shadow of emergence from the acquired cycle is evident.'

Indeed, if a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna) had not developed the Path of Stream-entry, the cycle of acquired aggregates—the round of suffering—would continue in the beginningless round of rebirths (saṃsāra), excluding seven lives. Why? Because the defilements that are the root causes for the occurrence of those acquired aggregates would still exist. However, as soon as the Path of Stream-entry arises, it completely eradicates these five defilements: the three fetters, the latent tendency to wrong view (diṭṭhānusaya), and the latent tendency to doubt (vicikicchānusaya). Now, for a Stream-enterer who has attained the Path, how could the cycle of acquired aggregates occur in the beginningless round of rebirths, excluding seven lives? Thus, the Path of Stream-entry is said to emerge from acquired phenomena by preventing the occurrence of the cycle of acquired aggregates.

If a Once-returner (Sakadāgāmi) had not developed the Path of Once-returning, the cycle of acquired aggregates would continue for five lives, excluding two lives. Why? Because the defilements that are the root causes for the occurrence of those acquired aggregates would still exist. However, as soon as that Path of Once-returning arises, it completely eradicates these four defilements: gross sensual lust (kāmarāga), gross ill-will (paṭigha), the gross latent tendency to sensual lust, and the gross latent tendency to ill-will. Now, for a Once-returner, how could the cycle of acquired aggregates occur in five lives, excluding two lives? Thus, the Path of Once-returning is said to emerge from acquired phenomena by preventing the occurrence of the cycle of acquired aggregates.

If a Non-returner (Anāgāmi) had not developed the Path of Non-returning, the cycle of acquired aggregates would continue in a second life, excluding one life. Why? Because the defilements that are the root causes for the occurrence of those acquired aggregates would still exist. (In this context, the commentators explain that 'one life' means the Non-returner does not return to the lower sense sphere.) However, as soon as that Path of Non-returning arises, it completely eradicates these four defilements: subtle sensual lust, subtle ill-will, the subtle latent tendency to sensual lust, and the subtle latent tendency to ill-will. Now, for a Non-returner, how could the cycle of acquired aggregates occur in a second life, excluding one life? Thus, the Path of Non-returning is said to emerge from acquired phenomena by preventing the occurrence of the cycle of acquired aggregates.

If an Arahant had not developed the Path of Arahantship, the cycle of acquired aggregates would continue in the fine-material and immaterial existences. Why? Because the defilements that are the root causes for the occurrence of those acquired aggregates...
279:
...because of the existence of (defilements), the Path of Arahantship, at the very moment of its arising, completely eradicates these eight defilements: lust for the fine-material realm (rūparāga), lust for the immaterial realm (arūparāga), conceit (māna), restlessness (uddhacca), ignorance (avijjā), the latent tendency to conceit (mānānusaya), the latent tendency to lust for existence (bhavarāgānusaya), and the latent tendency to ignorance (avijjānusaya). Now, for an Arahant, how could the cycle of acquired aggregates (the continuity of mind and matter) occur in a new existence? Thus, the Path of Arahantship is said to emerge from the acquired by preventing the occurrence of the cycle of acquired aggregates.

Among these four Paths, teachers say: the Path of Stream-entry emerges from the woeful existences; the Path of Once-returning emerges from a portion of the happy sense-sphere existences; the Path of Non-returning emerges from the sense-sphere existence; and the Path of Arahantship emerges from the fine-material and immaterial existences, and indeed from all existences.

To clarify this meaning, there is this canonical text: "With the cessation of kamma-formative consciousness (abhisaṅkhāravijñāṇa) through the knowledge of the Path of Stream-entry, the mind and matter that would have arisen in the beginningless round of rebirths, excluding seven lives, cease here, are stilled, disappear, and are further calmed."

"With the cessation of kamma-formative consciousness through the knowledge of the Path of Once-returning, the mind and matter that would have arisen in five lives, excluding two lives, cease here, are stilled, disappear, and are further calmed."

"With the cessation of kamma-formative consciousness through the knowledge of the Path of Non-returning, the mind and matter that would have arisen in two lives in the sense sphere, excluding one life, cease here, are stilled, disappear, and are further calmed."

"With the cessation of kamma-formative consciousness that would produce results in the fine-material or immaterial spheres through the knowledge of the Path of Arahantship, the mind and matter that would have arisen cease here, are stilled, disappear, and are further calmed. With the cessation of the final consciousness of an Arahant passing away into the Nibbāna element without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna), wisdom, mindfulness, mind, and matter cease here, are stilled, disappear, and are further calmed" (as stated in the Cūḷaniddesa). This is the decision regarding the sign (nimitta) first.

## In the phrase 'Paṭipadāpati'

In this context, does the practice (paṭipadā) fluctuate or not? It fluctuates. Indeed, for the Blessed One and the Elder Sāriputta, all four Paths were 'pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge' (sukha-paṭipadā khippābhiññā). For the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, the first Path was 'pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge,' but the three higher Paths were 'painful practice with quick direct knowledge' (dukkha-paṭipadā khippābhiññā). Why? Because he was oppressed by drowsiness.
280:
The Blessed One cared for the Elder Mahāmoggallāna for seven days as if he were a young prince. One day, the Elder sat nodding off. Then the Teacher said to him: "Moggallāna, are you nodding? Moggallāna, are you nodding?" (AN 7.61). If the practice (paṭipadā) of such a disciple who has attained great supernormal powers (mahābhiññā) still fluctuates, how could the practice of others not fluctuate? It will certainly fluctuate. For some monks, all four paths are of painful practice and slow intuition (dukkha-paṭipadā dandhābhiññā). For some, painful practice and quick intuition (dukkha-paṭipadā khippābhiññā). For some, pleasant practice and slow intuition (sukha-paṭipadā dandhābhiññā). For some, pleasant practice and quick intuition (sukha-paṭipadā khippābhiññā). For some, the first path is painful practice and slow intuition, the second path is painful practice and quick intuition, the third path is pleasant practice and slow intuition, and the fourth path is pleasant practice and quick intuition.

Just as the practice fluctuates, so does the predominance (adhipati). For some monks, all four paths are governed by desire (chanda). For some, by energy (viriya). For some, by consciousness (citta). For some, by investigation (vīmaṃsā). For some, the first path is governed by desire, the second by energy, the third by consciousness, and the fourth by investigation.

## Conclusion of the Miscellaneous Discussion.

## The Twenty Great Methods of the First Path

Now, one who develops supramundane wholesome states (lokuttara-kusala) does not develop only jhāna in the sense of closely contemplating; he also develops the path (magga) in the sense of leading out [from saṃsāra]; the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) in the sense of establishing [mindfulness]; the right efforts (sammappadhāna) in the sense of striving; the bases of power (iddhipāda) in the sense of succeeding; the faculties (indriya) in the sense of predominance; the powers (bala) in the sense of being unshakable; the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) in the sense of awakening; the truths (sacca) in the sense of being real; tranquility (samatha) in the sense of non-distraction; phenomena (dhamma) in the sense of being void; the aggregates (khandha) in the sense of a heap; the sense bases (āyatana) in the sense of exerting; the elements (dhātu) in the sense of being void of self and non-living; nutriment (āhāra) in the sense of supporting; contact (phassa) in the sense of touching; feeling (vedanā) in the sense of experiencing; perception (saññā) in the sense of perceiving; volition (cetanā) in the sense of willing; and consciousness (citta) in the sense of cognizing. Therefore, to show these nineteen terms, the text says again, "Which states are wholesome?" and so on. Thus, these twenty methods are taught according to the dispositions of individuals (puggalajjhāsaya) and the beauty of the teaching (desanāvilāsa), saying "he develops this, and he develops that."
281:
Among the assembly of devas sitting to hear the Dhamma, to those who understand the supramundane when it is called 'jhāna' in the sense of closely contemplating, it is taught as 'jhāna' according to their suitability. ... To those who understand it when it is called 'consciousness' (citta) in the sense of cognizing, it is taught as 'consciousness' according to their suitability. This is called 'the disposition of the person' (puggalajjhāsaya) in this context.

The Fully Enlightened One, however, because of his own perfect enlightenment, being endowed with the ten powers (dasabala), the fourfold fearlessness (vesārajja), the fourfold analytical knowledge (paṭisambhidā), and the six uncommon knowledges (asādhāraṇañāṇa), shows the teaching by determining it as he wishes. If he wishes, he shows the supramundane as 'jhāna' in the sense of closely contemplating; if he wishes, in the sense of leading out... in the sense of cognizing, he shows the supramundane as 'consciousness'. This is called 'the beauty of the teaching' (desanāvilāsa). Just as the ten methods are analyzed in the section called supramundane jhāna, so should they be understood in the sections on the path and so on. Thus, by making ten methods for each of the twenty categories, two hundred methods are analyzed.

Now, to show the different types of predominance (adhipati), the text begins again with "Which states are wholesome?" and so on. Therein, the supramundane jhāna that arises by making desire (chanda) the chief, the head, and the precursor is called 'predominance of desire' (chandādhipateyya). The same method applies to the remaining ones like predominance of energy, etc. Thus, with the two hundred methods in the previous pure (suddhika) section and two hundred for each of the four predominances like desire, etc., the King of Dhamma showed the first path by dividing it into one thousand methods.

## The First Path is Finished.

## The Second Path

Now, to show the second path and so on, the text begins again with "Which states are wholesome?" and so on. Therein, "for the attenuation of sensual lust and ill-will" means for the purpose of making those defilements thin. In that context, attenuation should be understood through two reasons: occasional occurrence (adhiccuppatti) and the weakness of obsession (pariyuṭṭhānamandatā). Indeed, for a Sakadāgāmī (Once-returner), defilements do not arise frequently as they do for the multitude of people following the round of rebirths; they arise only occasionally. Even when they arise, they do so in a sparse manner, like sprouts in a sparsely sown field. Furthermore, they do not arise by trampling, pervading, covering, and creating darkness as they do for the multitude of people following the round of rebirths. Being abandoned by the two paths, they are weak...
282:
(The defilements) arise weakly. They arise in a thin manner, like a layer of clouds or like a fly's wing.

In this matter (of the thinning of sensual lust and ill-will), some elders say: "Even if the defilements of a Sakadāgāmin arise after a long time, they arise thickly; for this reason, his sons and daughters are seen." This statement is not a standard (to be taken as authoritative). For sons and daughters can be born even by the mere touching of major and minor limbs. Since they have been abandoned by the two paths, there is no thickness or strength of defilements. The thinning of defilements for that Sakadāgāmin should be understood by two reasons: by accidental occurrence (adhiccuppatti) and by the weakness of obsession (pariyuṭṭhānamandatā).

"Dutiyāya" means second by way of counting and by way of the second occurrence. "Bhūmiyā pattiyā" means for the sake of attaining the fruit of recluseship (sāmaññaphala). In the third and fourth paths, the method is the same. However, I shall speak only of the distinction.

"Aññindriya" is the faculty of knowing. It means the faculty of knowing those very four noble truths known by the first path, without overstepping the limit known by that path. In the Niddesavāra (Section of Exposition), the meaning of this term should be understood in this way. In the Koṭṭhāsavāra (Section of Classification), there are nine faculties together with this (aññindriya). The rest should be understood according to the previous method.

## The Second Path is finished.

## The Third and Fourth Paths

In the third path, "anavasesappahānāya" means for the sake of abandoning without remainder those very fetters that were thinned by the path of the Sakadāgāmin.

In the fourth path, "for the sake of abandoning without remainder rūparāga, arūparāga, māna, uddhacca, and avijjā" means for the sake of abandoning these five higher fetters (uddhambhāgiya saṃyojana) without remainder. Among them, rūparāga is the desire and lust for the fine-material existence. Arūparāga is the desire and lust for the immaterial existence. Māna is only the conceit that is to be killed by the path of Arahantship. Likewise, uddhacca and avijjā. In these two paths also, the ninth faculty is only aññindriya.
283:
## A Thousand Methods of the Four Paths

In all paths, there are 60 terms identical in the sequence of words; together with the four unwavering factors (apaṇṇakaṅga), they are 64. In an unmixed way, however, there are 33. The Koṭṭhāsavāra and Suññatavāra are just as usual. Just as there are a thousand methods in the first path, so also in the second path and so on, there are only a thousand methods each; thus the King of Dhamma, the Buddha, showed the four paths by dividing them into four thousand methods.

In the Saccavibhaṅga, however, sixty thousand supramundane methods are laid down by the power of these very thousand methods. In the Satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅga, twenty thousand supramundane methods; in the Sammappadhānavibhaṅga, twenty thousand; in the Iddhipādavibhaṅga, thirty-two thousand; in the Bojjhaṅgavibhaṅga, thirty-two thousand; in the Maggaṅgavibhaṅga, twenty-eight thousand supramundane methods are laid down by the power of these very methods.

In this (Dhammasaṅgaṇī), however, there are only four thousand methods in the four paths. Among those paths, in the first path which has the first jhāna, eight factors are analyzed; so also in the second path and so on. Therein, in the first path, Right View is called "Right View" because it abandons wrong view. Right Intention and so on should also be understood by the nature of abandoning wrong intention and so on. This being so, (a question may be raised): "Since the sixty-two types of wrong views have been abandoned by the first path alone, there is no such thing as a view to be abandoned by the three higher paths; if so, how does the name 'Right View' occur in the higher paths?" (The answer is): "Just as an antidote is called 'antidote' whether poison exists or not, so this Dhamma is called 'Right View' whether wrong view exists or not."

"If it is so, this would be a mere name; in the three higher paths, it would result in Right View having no function, and the path factors would not be fulfilled; therefore, Right View should be made to have its own function, and the path factors should be fulfilled." In these three higher paths, Right View should be shown as having its own function according to the rule of whatever is obtainable. For there is one conceit (māna) to be killed by the three higher paths, and that conceit stands in the place of view. That Right View is called "Right View" because it abandons that conceit. In the path of Stream-entry, Right View abandons wrong view. For a Stream-enterer, there is conceit to be killed by the path of Once-returning, and that conceit stands in the place of view; that Right View is called "Right View" because it abandons that conceit. For that very person, there is thought (sankappa/vitakka) associated with seven unwholesome consciousnesses. By those very consciousnesses, there is the movement of the vocal organs, the movement of the bodily organs, and the use of requisites,
284:
There is effort conjoined with unwholesome consciousness (sahajāta-vāyāma); there is the state of lack of mindfulness (asatibhāva), which is the opposite of mindfulness; there is one-pointedness of mind conjoined with unwholesome consciousness (sahajāta-cittekaggatā). These states, such as thought (vitakka) and so forth, are called wrong intention (micchā-saṅkappa) and so forth. It should be understood that in the Path of Once-Returning (sakadāgāmi-magga), by abandoning those wrong intentions and so forth, right intention (sammā-saṅkappa) and so forth arise. Thus, in the Path of Once-Returning, the eight path factors come performing their respective functions. For the Once-Returner, there is conceit (māna) to be eradicated by the Path of Non-Returning (anāgāmi-magga). That conceit stands in the place of wrong view (diṭṭhi). For that person, the thoughts and so forth conjoined with the seven unwholesome consciousnesses are called wrong intention and so forth. By abandoning those wrong intentions and so forth, the fact that the eight path factors in the Path of Non-Returning have their respective functions should be understood. For the Non-Returner, there is conceit to be eradicated by the Path of Arahantship (arahatta-magga). That conceit stands in the place of wrong view. For that Non-Returner, the thoughts and so forth conjoined with the five unwholesome consciousnesses that arise are called wrong intention and so forth. By abandoning those wrong intentions and so forth, the fact that the eight path factors in the Path of Arahantship have their respective functions should be understood.

Among these four paths, the Four Noble Truths are seen by the first path (the Path of Stream-Entry). Regarding the question, "Do the three higher paths see only the truths already seen, or do they see truths not yet seen?" the statement "They see only the truths already seen" is the unanimous explanation of the teachers. However, the sophist (vitanḍavādī) says, "They see new truths not yet seen." That sophist should be asked, "Which faculty (indriya) do you assign to the first path?" If he is knowledgeable, he will say, "I assign the faculty 'I shall know the unknown' (anaññātaññassāmītindriya)." When asked, "Which faculty do you assign to the three higher paths?" he will say, "I assign the faculty of final knowledge (aññindriya)." That sophist should be told: "If there is the seeing of truths not yet seen, then assign only the faculty 'I shall know the unknown' to the three higher paths as well; in this way, your problem will be consistent." When asked, "Does one path abandon different defilements, or does it abandon only those defilements already abandoned?" he answers, "One path abandons different defilements." To a person with such a view who says, "If one path abandons different defilements not yet abandoned, then it sees only truths not yet seen," it should be asked: "How many truths are there?" A knowledgeable person will say, "There are four truths." He should be told: "In your view, there would be sixteen truths. You see what even the Buddhas have not seen. You are indeed one who knows many truths (bahusaccaka). Do not hold such a view. There is no seeing of new truths; however, it abandons defilements not yet abandoned."

In this context of the path, regarding the fact that seeing the truths is not new, the simile of the boxes (peḷopama) is taken. It is said that a certain man had four boxes containing treasures placed in a noble inner chamber. That man, having business with the boxes at night, opened the door and lit a lamp. When the darkness was dispelled by the lamp, the boxes became manifest. Having performed his business with those boxes, he closed the door and left. Once again, darkness overwhelmed the place. He did the same for the second and third times. On the fourth time, when the door was opened, the boxes were not visible within the darkness...
285:
While he was investigating, the sun arose. When the darkness disappeared due to the sunlight, he performed his business with the boxes (baskets) and left.

In that simile, the four boxes are like the Four Noble Truths. When business arises regarding those boxes, the time of opening the door is like the time of directing insight (vipassanā) towards the Path of Stream-Entry (sotāpatti-magga). The darkness is like the delusion (moha) that covers the Four Noble Truths. The light of the lamp is like the radiance of the Path of Stream-Entry. When the darkness disappears, the manifestation of the boxes to that man is like the manifestation of the Four Noble Truths to the knowledge of the path (magga-ñāṇa). The truths manifest to the knowledge of the path are also manifest to the person possessed of the path. The time of performing business with the boxes and leaving is like the time when the Path of Stream-Entry, having abandoned the defilements to be abandoned by it, ceases. The darkness overwhelming again is like the delusion covering the truths that is to be abandoned by the three higher paths.

The time of opening the door for the second time is like the time of directing insight towards the Path of Once-Returning (sakadāgāmi-magga). The light of the lamp is like the radiance of the Path of Once-Returning. The time of performing business with the boxes and leaving is like the time when the Path of Once-Returning, having abandoned the defilements to be abandoned by it, ceases. The darkness overwhelming again is like the delusion covering the truths that is to be abandoned by the two higher paths.

The time of opening the door for the third time is like the time of directing insight towards the Path of Non-Returning (anāgāmi-magga). The light of the lamp is like the radiance of the Path of Non-Returning. The time of performing business with the boxes and leaving is like the time when the Path of Non-Returning, having abandoned the defilements to be abandoned by it, ceases. The darkness overwhelming again is like the delusion covering the truths that is to be abandoned by the higher Path of Arahantship.

The time of opening the door for the fourth time is like the time of directing insight towards the Path of Arahantship (arahatta-magga). The rising of the sun is like the arising of the Path of Arahantship. The dispelling of darkness is like the Path of Arahantship dispelling the delusion that covers the truths. When the darkness disappears, the manifestation of the boxes to that man is like the manifestation of the Four Noble Truths to the knowledge of the Path of Arahantship. The truths manifest to the knowledge are also manifest to the person. The time of performing business with the boxes and leaving is like the Path of Arahantship exhausting all defilements. The time from the rising of the sun when the light arises and persists is like the time from the arising of the Path of Arahantship when once again...
286:
It is the absence of delusion (moha) that covers the Four Noble Truths. This is the simile for the fact that the vision of the Truths is not [entirely] new [for the higher paths].

In truth, the three higher paths see only the same Truths that have already been seen by the Path of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-magga). In this context, where it is said, "Another path abandons other defilements," the simile of the soap (alkali) should be taken. A man gives a soiled cloth to a washerman. The washerman applies three types of soap—salt-earth alkali, ash alkali, and cow-dung alkali—and knowing that the dirt has been acted upon by the soaps, he rinses it in water and removes the coarse impurities. Then, thinking, "It is not yet pure," he applies the soaps a second time in the same way, rinses it in water, and removes the impurities that are not very subtle, which lie beneath the coarse ones. Then, thinking, "It is not yet pure," he applies those soaps a third time, rinses it in water, and removes the more subtle impurities. Then, thinking, "It is not yet pure," he applies those soaps a fourth time, rinses it in water, and completely removes even the impurities residing within the fibers, then gives it to the owner. The owner places it in a perfume casket and wears it whenever he desires.

In this simile, the mind obsessed by defilements (kilesa) should be understood as the soiled cloth. The period of practicing the three contemplations (anupassanā) should be understood as the time of applying the three types of soap. The exhausting of the five defilements by the Path of Stream-entry should be understood as rinsing in water and removing the coarse impurities. The practice of those same three contemplations while thinking, "This mind is not yet pure," should be understood as applying those soaps a second time. The exhausting of the two coarse fetters (saṃyojana) by the Path of Once-returning (Sakadāgāmi-magga) should be understood as removing the impurities that are not very subtle. The practice of those same three contemplations while thinking, "This mind is not yet pure," should be understood as applying the three types of soap again, like thinking, "The cloth is not yet pure." The exhausting of the two subtle fetters by the Path of Non-returning (Anāgāmi-magga) should be understood as removing the subtle impurities. The practice of those same three contemplations while thinking, "This mind is not yet pure," should be understood as applying the three types of soap again, like thinking, "The cloth is not yet pure." Then, just as the pure cloth, which is like a silver plate, is placed in a perfume casket and worn whenever desired after the impurities within the fibers have been removed by washing, so too should one understand the spending of time in the bliss of the Attainment of Fruition (phalasamāpatti) at any desired moment by the mind of an Arahant, which is pure because the eight defilements have been exhausted by the Path of Arahantship (Arahatta-magga).

This is the simile for the statement, "Another path abandons other defilements." This has also been stated [by the Blessed One]:

"Friends, suppose there were a cloth, soiled and stained, and its owners gave it to a washerman. The washerman [would scrub it] with salt-earth alkali..."
287:
"...or with ash alkali, or with cow-dung, and rinse it in clear water. Even though that cloth becomes pure and clean, there still remains in it a residual smell of salt-earth alkali, ash alkali, or cow-dung that has not been removed. The washerman gives it back to the owners. The owners place it in a casket scented with perfume. Then, whatever residual smell of salt-earth alkali, ash alkali, or cow-dung remained in it, that too is completely eliminated.

In the same way, friends, even though an ultimate disciple (ariya-sāvaka) has abandoned the five lower fetters (pañcorambhāgiya saṃyojana), there still remains in him a residual conceit 'I am' (asmīti māna), a desire 'I am' (asmīti chanda), and an underlying tendency 'I am' (asmīti anusaya) regarding the five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandha) that have not been removed. At a later time, he dwells contemplating the rise and fall (udayabbayānupassī) of the five aggregates of clinging: 'Such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the passing away of form. Such is feeling, such is perception, such are mental formations, such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the passing away of consciousness.' As he dwells contemplating the rise and fall of these five aggregates of clinging, the residual conceit 'I am', the desire 'I am', and the underlying tendency 'I am' regarding the five aggregates of clinging are completely eliminated." (Saṃ. Ni. 3.89)

Among those [four paths], by the Path of Stream-entry, five unwholesome consciousnesses (akusala citta) are abandoned along with the evil states that arise by way of mental components (cittaṅgavaőena). By the Path of Once-returning, the two consciousnesses accompanied by displeasure (domanassa) are weakened along with the evil states that arise by way of mental components. By the Path of Non-returning, those same [displeasurable] consciousnesses are completely abandoned along with their associated states. By the Path of Arahantship, the [remaining] five unwholesome consciousnesses are abandoned along with the evil states that arise by way of mental components. From the time these twelve unwholesome consciousnesses are abandoned, there is no such thing as a defilement that arises again later by way of mental components for the Arahant.

In this regard [the abandoning of the 12 unwholesome states by the four paths], there is this simile: A noble king lives enjoying sovereignty in a great city, having established guards at the border. Then his border region becomes turbulent. At that time, twelve bandit leaders, together with many thousands of men..."
288:
The twelve great thieves, together with a large number of men, plundered and destroyed the kingdom. The great ministers living at the border sent word to the king, saying, "The border region is in turmoil." The king sent back a message, saying, "Capture them freely; I will do what needs to be done for you." With the very first clash, those ministers killed five great thieves along with many thousands of men. The remaining seven men took their respective followers and fled into the mountains. The ministers sent news of this to the king. The king sent rewards, saying, "I know the reward that should be given to you; capture those others as well." In the second clash, those ministers struck down two great thieves and weakened their followers. All those thieves fled and entered the mountains. The ministers sent news of this to the king as well. Again, the king sent rewards, saying, "Let them capture them freely." In the third clash, they killed two great thieves along with their companions and sent news of this to the king. Again, the king sent rewards, saying, "Let them capture the remaining ones freely." In the fourth clash, they killed five great thieves along with their followers. From the time the twelve great thieves were killed, there were no more thieves. The people of the countryside lived in peace, as if dancing with their children on their chests. The king, surrounded by victorious warriors, enjoyed great prosperity in his noble palace.

In this simile, the one like the great king is the Buddha, the King of Dhamma. Those like the ministers living at the border are the noble sons who are practitioners (yogāvacara). The states like the twelve great thieves are the twelve unwholesome consciousnesses (akusala citta). The states like their thousands of companions are the evil states that arise by way of mental factors. The time of reporting to the king that "the border is in turmoil" is like the time of reporting to the Teacher, the Buddha, when defilements arise regarding an object, saying, "Venerable Sir, defilements have arisen in me." The giving of rewards, saying "Capture them freely," is like the King of Dhamma teaching the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), saying, "Monk, suppress the defilements." The time of killing the five great thieves along with their followers is like the abandoning of the five unwholesome consciousnesses associated with the Path of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-magga).
289:
Again, the sending of news to the king is like reporting the attained qualities to the Fully Enlightened Buddha. The giving of rewards again, saying "Capture the remaining thieves as well," is like the Blessed One teaching insight (vipassanā) for the Path of Once-returning (Sakadāgāmi-magga). The weakening of the two great thieves along with their followers in the second clash is like the thinning out of the two consciousnesses accompanied by displeasure (domanassa) along with their associates by the Path of Once-returning.

Again, the sending of news to the king is like reporting the attained qualities to the Teacher. The giving of rewards again, saying "Capture them boldly," is like the Blessed One teaching insight for the Path of Non-returning (Anāgāmi-magga). The killing of the two great thieves along with their followers in the third clash is like the total abandonment of the two consciousnesses accompanied by displeasure along with their associates by the Path of Non-returning.

Again, the sending of news to the king is like reporting the attained qualities to the Tathāgata. The giving of rewards again, saying "Capture them boldly," is like the Blessed One teaching insight for the Path of Arahantship (Arahatta-magga). From the time the five great thieves along with their followers were killed in the fourth clash, it is like the period of safety for the country; when the five unwholesome consciousnesses associated with the Path of Arahantship are abandoned, from the time all twelve unwholesome consciousnesses are abandoned, it should be understood as the absence of unwholesome states that arise by way of mental factors. Just as the king, having won the battle and surrounded by his ministers, enjoys great prosperity in his noble palace, so too the King of Dhamma, surrounded by the assembly of Arahants, enjoys the bliss of Fruition Attainment (phala-samāpatti) as desired among the types of attainments such as the void (suññata), the signless (animitta), and the undirected (appaṇihita).

## The explanation of the term 'Kusalā Dhammā' is finished.

## Unwholesome Terms (Akusala-pada)

## Discussion on the Section of the Summary of States (Dhammuddasavāra)

## The First Consciousness

Now, in order to analyze and show the section on unwholesome states, the passage beginning with "Which states are unwholesome?" (katame dhammā akusalā) is commenced. Therein, the classification of the sections such as the "Section on the Determination of States" (dhamma-vavatthāna-vāra) and the decision on the meaning of the terms appearing below should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. However, I will explain only the specific differences in various places. First, in the "Section on the Determination of the Occasion" (samaya-vavatthāna-vāra), because there is no division of planes (bhūmi) in the unwholesome as there is in the wholesome, even though this is strictly of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), it is not called "sense-sphere". In the term "associated with wrong view" (diṭṭhigata-sampayuttaṃ)...
290:
Only view itself is called 'gone to view' (*diṭṭhigata*). It is like the terms 'gone to excrement' (*gūthagata*) or 'gone to urine' (*muttagata*). Alternatively, because there is no essence to be known, it is called *diṭṭhigata* as it is merely the occurrence of view. That which is associated with that view is called 'associated with wrong view' (*diṭṭhigata-sampayutta*).

In that state associated with wrong view, the arising of this wrong seeing (*micchā-dassana*) known as *diṭṭhigata* should be understood as occurring through causes such as unwise attention (*ayoniso manasikāra*), which includes listening to false Dhamma (*asaddhamma-savana*), having bad friends (*akalyāṇamittatā*), and the lack of desire to see the Noble Ones (*ariyānaṃ adassanakāmatā*). It should be understood that this view arises through: listening to false doctrines related to wrong views, preceded by great esteem and exceeding indifference, without investigation; through bad friendship (*akalyāṇamittatā*) characterized by leaning towards bad friends who have fallen into wrong views; through the lack of desire to see the Noble Ones and virtuous persons such as the Buddha; through lack of proficiency in the Noble Dhamma such as the four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*); through lack of discipline (*avinaya*) characterized by the failure of restraint (*saṃvara*) in the Noble Dhamma and the Dhamma of virtuous persons, specifically the failure of restraint in the Pātimokkha (*pātimokkha-saṃvara*), restraint of the senses (*indriya-saṃvara*), restraint of mindfulness (*sati-saṃvara*) (here meaning restraint of patience, *khanti-saṃvara*), restraint of knowledge (*ñāṇa-saṃvara*), and restraint of abandonment (*pahāna-saṃvara*) (restraint of energy, *vīriya-saṃvara*); through unwise attention nurtured by those causes; and through devotion to omens of things seen and heard (*diṭṭha-maṅgala*, *suta-maṅgala*), etc. The unprompted (*asaṅkhārika*) nature of that consciousness should be understood in the same way as mentioned below.

In the section on the summary of phenomena (*dhammuddesa-vāra*), 'contact' (*phassa*) refers to the contact that arises together with unwholesome consciousness. The same method applies to feeling (*vedanā*) and so on. Thus, the only difference from the previously mentioned wholesome contact and feeling is that these are merely unwholesome. 'One-pointedness of mind (*cittassa ekaggatā*) occurs' means that even in acts such as killing (*pāṇātipāta*), there is one-pointedness of mind in the sense of non-distraction. This is because people, having concentrated their minds and becoming undistracted, strike the bodies of beings with weapons that do not miss. Those with well-concentrated minds steal the property of others. With a mind of single-minded purpose, they commit sexual misconduct (*micchācāra*). Thus, even in the occurrence of the unwholesome, there is one-pointedness of mind.

Wrong view (*micchā-diṭṭhi*) means improper view, or a distorted view because it is held wrongly. It is also called *micchā-diṭṭhi* because it is a view loathed by the wise as it brings about harm. The same method applies to wrong intention (*micchā-saṅkappa*) and so on. Furthermore, it is called *micchā-diṭṭhi* because one sees wrongly by it, or it sees wrongly itself, or it is merely a wrong seeing. It has the characteristic of unwise conviction (*ayoniso abhinivesa*), the function of misinterpretation (*parāmāsa*), the manifestation of wrong conviction (*micchā-abhinivesa*), and the proximate cause of not desiring to see the Noble Ones. It should be regarded as a supreme fault.
291:
In wrong intention (*micchā-saṅkappa*) and so on, the only difference is the word 'wrong' (*micchā*). The remaining meaning should be understood in the same way as stated in the section on the wholesome.

In the terms 'power of shamelessness' (*ahirika-bala*) and 'power of fearlessness' (*anottappa-bala*), the meaning of 'power' (*bala*) will become clear in the section of definitions (*niddesa-vāra*). As for the other terms: one is 'shameless' (*ahirika*) because one is not ashamed. The state of being shameless is 'shamelessness' (*ahirikaṃ*). That which is not dread (*ottappa*) is 'fearlessness' (*anottappa*). Between these two, shamelessness has the characteristic of not loathing bodily misconduct and so on, or the characteristic of lack of shame (*alajja*). Fearlessness has the characteristic of lack of dread regarding those same bodily misconducts, or the characteristic of lack of fear. Shamelessness itself being a power is the 'power of shamelessness'. Fearlessness itself being a power is the 'power of fearlessness'. This is the summary of the meaning here. The detailed explanation should be understood by way of the opposites of shame (*hiri*) and dread (*ottappa*) mentioned below.

One lusts by it, or it lusts itself, or it is merely lusting; therefore, it is 'greed' (*lobha*). One is deluded by it, or it is deluded itself, or it is merely deluding; therefore, it is 'delusion' (*moha*). Between these two, greed has the characteristic of grasping an object like monkey-glue. It has the function of sticking to an object like a piece of meat thrown onto a hot pan. It manifests in knowledge as being unable to let go, like an oil stain. It has the proximate cause of seeing enjoyment in things that are fetters (*saṃyojaniya-dhamma*). It should be understood that as it grows into the river of craving (*taṇhā-nadī*), it carries beings away to the states of loss (*apāya*), just as a river with a swift current flows into the great ocean.

Delusion has the characteristic of blindness of mind or the characteristic of ignorance. It has the function of non-penetration or the function of covering the true nature of the object. It manifests in knowledge as wrong practice or manifests as darkness. It has unwise attention as its proximate cause. It should be regarded as the root of all unwholesome states.

One covets the wealth of others by it, or it covets itself, or it is merely coveting; therefore, it is 'covetousness' (*abhijjhā*). That covetousness has the characteristic of desiring to make others' wealth one's own. It has the function of seeking in that manner. It manifests in knowledge as being directed towards others' wealth. It has great delight in others' wealth as its proximate cause. Indeed, that covetousness manifests only as being directed towards others' wealth. Moreover, it arises when there is delight in that wealth. It should be regarded as the stretching out of the mind's hand towards others' wealth.

In 'tranquility occurs' (*samatho hoti*) and so on, it is 'tranquility' (*samatha*) because it calms distraction from other tasks. It is 'exertion' (*paggāha*) because it upholds the mind in the occurrence of the unwholesome. It is 'non-distraction' (*avikkhepa*) because it does not allow distraction.
292:
In this (first unwholesome) consciousness, these factors—faith, mindfulness, wisdom, and the six pairs—are not included. Why? Because in a mind devoid of faith, there is no such thing as devotion (pasāda). Therefore, faith is not included first. If it is asked, 'Do those with wrong views not believe in their own teachers?'—they do believe. However, that is not what is called faith; it is merely the acceptance of words. In essence, it is either delusion (moha) lacking investigation or it is wrong view (diṭṭhi). Since there is no mindfulness in a mind devoid of mindfulness, it is not included. If it is asked, 'Can those with wrong views not remember what they have done?'—they can remember. However, that is not what is called mindfulness. It is merely the occurrence of unwholesome consciousness in that mode. Therefore, mindfulness is not included. Then why is it called 'wrong mindfulness' (micchā-sati) in the Suttas? Because unwholesome aggregates are devoid of mindfulness and are the opposite of mindfulness, it is taught there figuratively (pariyāya) for the purpose of completing the factors of the wrong path and wrongness (micchatta). In the literal sense (nippariyāya), however, it does not exist. Therefore, it is not included. Since there is no wisdom in a blindly foolish mind, it is not included. If it is asked, 'Do those with wrong views not have deceptive wisdom?'—they do. However, that is not wisdom; it is called illusion (māyā). In essence, that illusion is just craving (taṇhā). This consciousness is accompanied by distress, and is heavy, burdensome, coarse, rigid, unwieldy, ailing, crooked, and devious. Therefore, the six pairs beginning with tranquility (passaddhi) are not included.

Having shown the thirty-two terms presented in the Pāḷi text by way of the constituents of consciousness through this sequence of words, the text now says 'or whatever other' (ye vā pana) etc., to show the 'or-whatever-other' factors (yevāpanaka). Among them, in all unwholesome consciousnesses, only these ten factors—intention (chanda), decision (adhimokkha), attention (manasikāra), conceit (māna), envy (issā), avarice (macchariya), sloth (thina), torpor (middha), restlessness (uddhacca), and remorse (kukkucca)—are said to be the 'or-whatever-other' factors that appear in the Sutta passages. However, in this specific consciousness, only four factors known as the invariable factors (apaṇṇakanga)—intention, decision, attention, and restlessness—are the 'or-whatever-other' factors.

Among those four, the three beginning with intention should be understood according to the method mentioned below. The only difference is that those mentioned below are wholesome, while these are unwholesome. As for the remaining factor, restlessness (uddhacca), it is the state of being distracted. It has the characteristic of unpeacefulness of mind, like water stirred by the impact of the wind; the function of instability, like a banner or flag fluttering in the wind; the manifestation of turmoil, like ashes flying up when struck by a stone; and it has inappropriate attention (ayoniso manasikāra) to the unpeacefulness of mind as its proximate cause. It should be regarded as the distraction of the mind.

Thus, there are thirty-two factors beginning with contact, and four mentioned by way of the 'or-whatever-other' factors; therefore, in this summary of phenomena (dhammuddesa-vāra), there are thirty-six factors in total. These are the four invariable factors.
293:
Excluding the four invariable factors, there are only thirty-two factors directly appearing in the Pāḷi text. However, by taking the factors not yet included in this summary of phenomena, there are sixteen factors: the group of five starting with contact (phassa-pañcaka), initial application (vitakka), sustained application (vicāra), zest (pīti), one-pointedness of mind (ekaggatā), the faculty of energy (vīriyindriya), the life-faculty (jīvitindriya), wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi), lack of shame (ahirika), lack of dread (anottappa), greed (lobha), and delusion (moha). Among these sixteen factors, seven are undivided (avibhattika) and nine are divided (savibhattika). Which are the seven? Contact, perception, volition, sustained application, zest, the life-faculty, and delusion—these seven are undivided. Feeling, consciousness, initial application, one-pointedness of mind, the faculty of energy, wrong view, lack of shame, lack of dread, and greed—these nine are divided.

Among them, six factors are divided into two places, one factor into three places, one factor into four places, and one factor into six places. How? Consciousness, initial application, wrong view, lack of shame, lack of dread, and greed—these six are divided into two places. Among them, consciousness is first called 'consciousness' (citta) when it reaches the group of five starting with contact, and it is called the 'mind-faculty' (manindriya) when it reaches the faculties. Initial application is called 'initial application' (vitakka) when it reaches the jhana factors, and it is called 'wrong intention' (micchā-saṅkappa) when it reaches the path factors. Wrong view is called 'wrong view' (micchā-diṭṭhi) both in the path factors and in the courses of action (kammapatha). Lack of shame is called the 'power of shamelessness' (ahirika-bala) when it reaches the powers, and it is called 'shamelessness' (ahirika) when it reaches the dyad of world-destroyers. The same method applies to the lack of dread (anottappa). Greed is called 'greed' (lobha) when it reaches the roots (mūla), and it is called 'covetousness' (abhijjhā) when it reaches the courses of action. These six factors are divided into two places.

As for feeling (vedanā), it is called 'feeling' when it reaches the group of five starting with contact, 'happiness' (sukha) when it reaches the jhana factors, and the 'faculty of joy' (somanassindriya) when it reaches the faculties. Thus, this single factor is divided into three places.

As for energy (vīriya), it is called the 'faculty of energy' (vīriyindriya) when it reaches the faculties, 'wrong effort' (micchā-vāyāma) when it reaches the path factors, the 'power of energy' (vīriya-bala) when it reaches the powers, and 'exertion' (paggāha) when it reaches the End Dyads (piṭṭhiduka). Thus, this single factor is divided into four places.

As for concentration (samādhi or ekaggatā), it is called 'one-pointedness of mind' (ekaggatā) when it reaches the jhana factors, the 'faculty of concentration' (samādhindriya) when it reaches the faculties, 'wrong concentration' (micchā-samādhi) when it reaches the path factors, the 'power of concentration' (samādhi-bala) when it reaches the powers, and when it reaches the End Dyads, in the second dyad, by way of a single...
294:
... It is called 'calm' (samatha), and in the third dyad, it is called 'non-distraction' (avikkhepa). Thus, this single dhamma is analyzed in six places.

All these dhammas form nine groups by way of the fivefold contact (phassa-pañcaka), the factors of absorption (jhāna-aṅga), the faculties (indriya), the path factors (maggaṅga), the powers (bala), the roots (mūla), the courses of action (kammapatha), the world-destroyers (lokanāsaka), and the concluding dyads (piṭṭhiduka). What should be said in this Summary of Dhammas (Dhammuddessavāra) has already been stated in the exposition of the first wholesome consciousness (pathama-kusala-citta-niddesa).

## The Commentary on the Summary of Dhammas (Dhammuddessavāra-kathā) is finished.

## The Commentary on the Exposition (Niddesavāra-kathā)

In the Exposition (Niddesavāra), within the exposition of one-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā-niddesa), first, the two terms 'steadfastness' (saṇṭhiti) and 'fixity' (avaṭṭhiti) are merely synonyms for 'stability' (ṭhiti). However, the statement made in the wholesome exposition (kusala-niddesa) that "it is called fixity (avaṭṭhiti) because it stands having entered and penetrated the object" is not applicable here in this unwholesome exposition (akusala-niddesa). It has already been shown below that one-pointedness of mind is weak in unwholesome consciousness.

The meaning of 'non-shifting' (avisāhāra) as being the opposite of 'shifting' (visāhāra) to various objects occurring by way of restlessness (uddhacca) and doubt (vicikicchā) is also not applicable here. However, it is called 'non-shifting' (avisāhāra) because it does not cause the co-nascent dhammas to shift. It is called 'non-distraction' (avikkhepa) because it does not scatter. The state of a mind that is not shifted by the power of unwholesome one-pointedness of mind is called 'the state of a non-shifted mind' (avisāhaṭamānasatā). It is called 'the power of concentration' (samādhibala) because it does not waver regarding co-nascent dhammas. It should be understood in this unwholesome exposition that it is called 'wrong concentration' (micchāsamādhi) because it is a wrong way of focusing on an object.

In the exposition of the faculty of energy (viriyindriya-niddesa), the method stated below starting with "this energy is an exit for the removal of sense desires" is not applicable here. It should be known as 'the power of energy' (viriyabala) only in the sense of not wavering regarding co-nascent dhammas.

In the exposition of wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi-niddesa), it is called 'wrong view' (micchādiṭṭhi) in the sense of seeing incorrectly. This seeing has gone into views; it is called 'resorting to views' (diṭṭhigata) because it is included within the sixty-two views. The meaning of this has also been stated below. Just like a thicket of grass, a thicket of forest, or a thicket of mountains, view itself is called 'the jungle of views' (diṭṭhigahana) in the sense of being difficult to cross. View itself, in the sense of being accompanied by danger and suspicion...
295:
Wrong view is called 'the wilderness of views' (diṭṭhikantāra) because it is full of danger, like a wilderness frequented by robbers, a wilderness of wild beasts, a sandy wilderness, a waterless wilderness, or a famine-stricken wilderness. It is called 'the thorn of views' (diṭṭhivisūkāyika) in the sense of piercing right view and in the sense of being contrary to it. Indeed, when wrong view arises, it both pierces and opposes right vision (sammā-dassana). It is called 'the agitation of views' (diṭṭhivipphandita) because it is a distorted trembling of view due to sometimes holding the eternalist view (sassata) and sometimes the annihilationist view (uccheda). A person with wrong views cannot stand in a single view but follows sometimes the eternalist view and sometimes the annihilationist view. View itself is called 'the fetter of views' (diṭṭhisaṃyojana) in the sense of binding.

It is called 'a grip' (gāha) because it firmly grasps the object, just as creatures like crocodiles seize a man. It is called 'a standing place' (patiṭṭhāha) because it stands firmly having arisen with great force. Indeed, this dhamma of view grasps by standing firmly due to its powerful occurrence. It is called 'adherence' (abhinivesa) because it strongly attends to things as permanent, etc. It is called 'misapprehension' (parāmāsa) because it touches upon things as permanent, etc., by transcending the true nature of dhammas. It is called 'the wrong path' (kummagga) because it leads to harm and because it is the path to the loathsome woeful states. It is called 'the false path' (micchāpatha) because it is an incorrect road. Just as a person confused about the directions, though taking a road thinking 'this is the road to such-and-such a village,' cannot reach that village, so too a person with wrong views, though taking a view thinking 'this is the path to a happy destination,' cannot reach a happy destination; thus it is 'the false path' (micchāpatha) because it is an incorrect road. It is called 'wrongness' (micchatta) because it is of a false nature. It is called 'a landing-place' (tittha) like a ferry-port because fools wander back and forth within that view. It is called 'the resort of the landing-place' (titthāyatana) because that view is the basis for harm. Or, it is called 'titthāyatana' in the sense of being the place of origin and the dwelling place of sectarians (titthiya). It is called 'the grip of perversion' (vipariyesaggāha) because it grasps in a perverted way. The term 'vipalatthagāha' has the same meaning.

387-388. In the expositions of shamelessness (ahirika) and fearlessness of wrongdoing (anottappa), the meaning should be understood as the opposite of the method stated in the expositions of shame (hiri) and fear of wrongdoing (ottappa). They should be known as 'the power of shamelessness' (ahirika-bala) and 'the power of fearlessness' (anottappa-bala) only in the sense of not wavering regarding co-nascent dhammas.

In the expositions of greed (lobha) and delusion (moha), it is called 'greed' (lobha) because it covets. 'Lubbhana' is the manner of coveting. A mind associated with greed, or a person, is called 'covetous' (lubbhita), and the state of such a person is 'covetousness' (lubbhitatta). It is called 'intense passion' (sārāga) because it is intensely lustful. 'Sārajjanā' is the manner of being intensely lustful. The state of an intensely lustful mind or person is called 'the state of being intensely lustful' (sārajjitatta). In the sense of 'scheming' (abhijjhāyana)...
296:
Abhijjhā (Covetousness). Again, the reason for the word 'greed' (lobha) has already been stated. It is called an unwholesome root (akusalamūla) because it is both unwholesome and a root, or because it is the root of unwholesome states.

It is called non-knowledge (aññāṇa) and non-seeing (adassana) because it is the opposite of knowledge and vision (ñāṇadassana). It is called non-realization (anabhisamaya) because it occurs in the presence of phenomena but does not rightly understand or meet them. Understanding phenomena in accordance [with truth] is called anubodha; because it is the opposite of that, it is called non-understanding (ananubodha). It is called non-enlightenment (asambodha) because it does not understand in conjunction with [the characteristics of] impermanence and so on. It is also called non-enlightenment because it understands what is non-existent and improper. It is called non-penetration (appaṭivedha) because it does not penetrate the Four Noble Truths. It is called non-comprehension (asaṅgāhanā) because it does not grasp even a single phenomenon among form and so on by way of the common characteristics such as impermanence. It is called non-plunging (apariyogāhanā) because it does not plunge into that very phenomenon. It is called improper looking (asamapekkhaṇā) because it does not look [at things] evenly. It is called non-reflection (apaccavekkhaṇā) because it does not reflect based on the nature of phenomena.

Because of perverse activity regarding wholesome and unwholesome actions, or because of the absence of grasping the nature [of things], not even a single action is direct to this [delusion]; or because it does not itself make any action direct, it is called non-direct action (appaccakkhakamma). When this delusion does not arise, the mental continuum would be pure and bright; because this delusion corrupts that pure mental continuum, it is called bad wisdom (dummejjha). It is called folly (bālya) because it is the state of fools. It is called delusion (moha) because it deludes. Intense delusion is pamoha. It is called complete delusion (sammoha) because it deludes all around. It is called ignorance (avijjā) because it is not knowledge, being the opposite of knowledge (vijjā). The meanings of flood (ogha) and yoke (yoga) have already been stated. It is called a latent tendency (anusaya) because it lies dormant in the sense of being firmly established. It is called obsession (pariyuṭṭhāna) because it overwhelms or pervades the mind. Because it does not grasp what is beneficial, it cannot go towards what is beneficial, but rather slips away; thus it is called laṅgī, meaning it slips. Or it is called laṅgī in the sense of being difficult to open. Indeed, just as a door-bolt called a mahāpaligha is difficult to open, so too this delusion is like a door-bolt; thus it is called laṅgī. The remaining words have clear meanings. The Summary Section (Saṅgahavāra) and the Voidness Section (Suññatavāra) should also be understood by way of meaning according to the method already stated below.

## Second Consciousness

In the second consciousness, the word 'with prompting' (sasaṅkhārena) is the distinction. The meaning of that word has also been stated below. Although this consciousness arises for one who, being joyful regarding the six objects, produces greed and misapprehends them by way of 'a being, a being,' and so on, yet because it is prompted (sasaṅkhārika), it arises with effort and with means...
297:
When a young man of good family desires a maiden from a family of wrong view, and they do not give the maiden, saying, 'You are of a different view,' then other relatives say, 'He will do whatever you do,' and cause them to give her. That man approaches the sectarians along with them. At first, he is full of doubt. As time goes by, he thinks, 'The behavior of these people is pleasing,' and he comes to like their doctrine and adopts the wrong view. It should be understood that this [second] consciousness arises at such a time.

Among the remaining (yevāpanaka) states, sloth (thina) and torpor (middha) are predominant here. Therein, the state of being slothful is 'sloth' (thina). The state of being torpid is 'torpor' (middha). It means lack of enthusiasm, shrinking, lack of capability, and exhaustion. Sloth and torpor combined are called 'sloth and torpor' (thina-middha). Therein, sloth has the characteristic of lack of enthusiasm, the function of dispelling energy, and is manifested as sinking. Torpor has the characteristic of unwieldiness (incapability), the function of enveloping [the doors of perception], and is manifested as dejection or as nodding and sleepiness. Both have unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra)—arising from dissatisfaction, laziness, stretching the body, and so on—as their proximate cause.

## Third Consciousness

The third consciousness arises for one who, being joyful regarding the six objects, produces greed but does not misapprehend them (wrongly) by way of 'a being, a being,' and so on, such as for one watching the Nārāyaṇa festival, wrestling matches, boxing matches, dramatic performances, and so on, or for one devoted to listening to pleasing sounds and so on. In this consciousness, there are five invariable factors along with conceit (māna). Therein, it is called 'conceit' (māna) because it is proud. That conceit has the characteristic of loftiness, the function of self-exaltation, is manifested as the desire to fly a banner, has greed disconnected from wrong view as its proximate cause, and should be regarded as being like madness.

## Fourth Consciousness

The fourth consciousness arises in the aforementioned situations, such as when one is spat upon on the head or has dust thrown on one's feet, and one looks around from time to time with effort to avoid that danger; or when royal plays are being performed and the crowd is being cleared, for those who are peeking through various gaps; it arises in such situations.
298:
In this fourth consciousness, however, there are seven *yevāpanaka* states together with sloth and torpor (*thina-middha*). In both (the third and fourth), wrong view (*micchā-diṭṭhi*) is excluded. Setting aside that wrong view, the enumeration of states should be understood by way of the remaining states.

## The Fifth Consciousness

The fifth consciousness arises in a person who, being indifferent towards the six objects by way of feeling, arouses greed and misapprehends them in such ways as "a being, a being," etc. In this fifth consciousness, equanimity (*upekkhā-vedanā*) occurs in the place of joy (*somanassa*), and the term zest (*pīti*) is excluded. All the rest is exactly the same as the first consciousness.

## The Sixth Consciousness and Others

409-412. The sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses should also be understood in the same manner as described for the second, third, and fourth consciousnesses, by changing the feeling and excluding the term zest (*pīti*). In these eight consciousnesses rooted in greed, both types of predominance—predominance of co-nascence (*sahajātādhipati*) and predominance of object (*ārammaṇādhipati*)—are obtained.

## The Ninth Consciousness

The ninth consciousness arises in one who is displeased with the six objects and arouses aversion (*paṭigha*). In the section on the delimitation of the occasion (*samayavavatthānavāra*) for that ninth consciousness, first (the analysis should be understood): a mind that is bad (because it is destroyed by anger), or a mind that is contemptible because of the inferior nature of its feeling, is called *dummana* (bad-minded). The state of being *dummana* is *domanassa* (displeasure). Because it arises together with that displeasure, it is called "accompanied by displeasure" (*domanassasahagata*). Because it strikes against the object with a nature of non-endearedness, it is called *paṭigha* (aversion). Because it is associated with that aversion, it is called "associated with aversion" (*paṭighasampayutta*).

In the enumeration of states (*dhammuddesa*), only the feeling of displeasure (*domanassavedanā*) appears in all three places. There, the term for feeling (*vedanā*) has the meaning already stated. Likewise, the terms pain (*dukkha*) and displeasure (*domanassa*) also have the meanings already stated. By way of characteristics, etc., displeasure (*domanassa*) has the characteristic of experiencing an undesirable object; its function is the enjoyment of the undesirable aspect in its true nature, or in any way; its manifestation is the affliction of the mind; and its proximate cause is invariably the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*).

Just as in the root courses of action (*mūlakammapatha*) for the previous consciousnesses it was stated that "greed occurs" and "covetousness occurs," so here it is stated that "hatred occurs" and "ill-will occurs." There, one offends by means of it, or it offends by itself, or it is merely the act of offending...
299:
Hatred (*dosa*) has the characteristic of fierce anger, like a cobra struck by a stick. Its function is to spread like poison, or its function is to consume its own support like a forest fire consuming its own base (the heart-base or the whole body). It is manifested as a state that destroys oneself and others, like an enemy who has found an opportunity. It should be understood as having the grounds of resentment (*āghātavatthu*), such as doing harm, as its proximate cause, like putrid urine mixed with poison.

By that hatred, the mind is corrupted and reaches a state of putrefaction; or, because it destroys the practice of discipline, the perfection of appearance, and welfare and happiness, etc., it is called ill-will (*byāpāda*). In essence, this ill-will is just hatred. In this ninth unwholesome consciousness, there are 29 terms in the sequence of words. By taking only those not yet taken, there are 14. By way of those 14, the distinction between the group with inflections and the group without inflections should be understood.

Among the *yevāpanaka* states, intention (*chanda*), decision (*adhimokkha*), attention (*manasikāra*), and restlessness (*uddhacca*) are fixed. Among envy (*issā*), avarice (*macchariya*), and remorse (*kukkucca*), they arise in groups of five along with any one of them. Thus, these three states are called unfixed *yevāpanaka* states. Among those three, envy (*issā*) is so called because it envies; it has the characteristic of being jealous of the prosperity of others, its function is dissatisfaction with that very prosperity, its manifestation is turning one's face away from it, and its proximate cause is the prosperity of others.
